text:
This is the second story of a two-part series. Read part one here.

NEW CARLISLE — On the frigid morning of Jan. 27, the Department of Energy ordered Amazon’s massive data center in northern Indiana to cut off 50 megawatts of electricity, about the amount needed to power 40,000 homes for one hour.

Backup diesel generators fired up, but the outside air was so cold that air lines froze in five of them. Cold lines disrupted the generators’ pollution control equipment, causing three pollutants that contribute to smog, acid rain and respiratory irritation to waft into the wind for five hours.

Bob Humbarger, who lives just east of the data center, said he was never notified of the leak that morning. But he knows the winds blow east toward the house where he’s lived for more than 50 years. Now, he’s worried about the lack of protections guarding him and his neighbors from big tech and county government interests.

Humbarger, 85, said his monthly electric rates have increased 9% from February 2023 to February this year. Meanwhile, he has watched from his front window as Amazon Web Services’ (AWS) $26 billion hyperscale data center expands just south of State Route 2, near his 20 acres of farmland. He spent dozens of hours at zoning meetings over the last year, voicing concerns that he and other members of his community feel aren’t being adequately addressed.

“I wasted a lot of my time going to public hearings,” he said. “The people who live below State Route 2 are sacrificial lambs.”

Once the other 14 of the project’s 32 buildings are built on its 1,200-acre New Carlisle campus, the development can consume up to 2.25 gigawatts, enough to power more than 1.4 million homes, or around half of the state of Indiana’s residential households. At $11 billion, the AWS data center announced in 2024 that it was the largest private investment in state history, and then the plan grew by another $15 billion the next year.

Local residents are concerned that its colossal energy needs will increase their utility rates and spike demand for dirtier forms of energy. They don’t feel they have any control over how their hometown is changing.

In many ways, the experience of New Carlisle residents is a sign of things to come for Hoosiers across the state, including in the Indianapolis area. Residents successfully pushed back against a proposed Google data center in Franklin Township, but plans for other data centers in Martindale-Brightwood, Decatur Township and near Irvington are still on track. And Meta is planning a $10 billion hyperscale development in Lebanon.

Ben Inskeep, program director of the advocacy group Citizens Action Coalition (CAC), said the public wasn’t informed about the January grid emergency at the Amazon facility, and he only found out because the state requires a pollution emissions report.

“To my knowledge, this is the first specific instance of a data center in America being ordered to temporarily reduce their power consumption from the grid by utilizing their onsite emergency backup generators to help maintain grid reliability during an extreme weather event,” Inskeep said.

In an email response, AWS spokesperson Adrienne Talbot said Amazon serves millions of customers and must maintain service to continue life-saving care, emergency communications and vital infrastructure. “Total emissions remained below 1 percent of our annual permitted levels,” she wrote.

Last December, a petition to rezone more New Carlisle farmland — making way for an unidentified company’s proposed data center near Amazon’s — failed. Since then, locals have continued to oppose big tech’s momentum. Microsoft is poised to develop another data center in Granger and forego potential tax incentives or abatements.

As tech firms eye Indiana for its economic incentives and natural resources, Indiana Michigan Power (I&M) is poised to triple its electricity sales to nearly 35 terawatt-hours — more than demand of Ireland in 2024 — within the next four years.

As many as 120 built or proposed data center buildings across Indiana will cause state power use to nearly double within 10 years, according to a report by Purdue University that sourced data from the utility companies.

“What we’re seeing in the state is unprecedented load growth,” said Timothy Phillips, lead analyst for the State Utility Forecasting Group that conducted the report. “We have a situation where Indiana Michigan Power’s electricity demand is going to double or more in the next five years.”

Other Midwest states are coordinating response efforts to circumvent troubles in meeting this surge. In central Ohio, a new hub for big tech, electricity bills have spiked 10% year-over-year, but billions of private dollars are funding upgrades to the electric grid to prevent blackouts.

In Wisconsin, a community passed a measure requiring voter approval for developments valued above $10 million to receive tax incentives, after a hyperscale data center moved into town. In Illinois, Champaign County banned data center infrastructure for 12 months.

But in Indiana, the state Senate rejected a bill that would have required centers to disclose how much power and water they are using.

Across the country, wholesale electric prices, which are eventually passed on to customers, have risen by as much as 267% over the last five years in areas around data centers that consume a substantial amount of resources, according to a Bloomberg report.

“Grid experts are very worried about these data centers,” Inskeep said, “because they’re unprecedented stressors on the grid.”

In an email, Amazon wrote that its data center would receive power from I&M’s regional grid. That grid relies on a mix of power sources, including renewable energy, but the Cook Nuclear Plant in Michigan represents “a significant part of I&M’s generation portfolio.”

Many living or working in New Carlisle and South Bend say they want safeguards for their electricity bills, environmental regulations, higher power rates for AI industries, and legislation enacting higher hurdles for AI firms to develop.

Some protections currently exist to prevent disruptions on locals. A tariff structure imposed by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) imposes a minimum monthly payment of 80% of expected grid demand from hyperscalers, a 12-year minimum contract term, and a large exit fee costing up to five years of electricity demand.

American Electric Power, the parent company of I&M, says they’re looking to cut rates for all customers across their network in an IURC filing that will be heard this summer, said Bill Schalliol, St. Joseph County’s executive director of economic development.

Reduced rates are possible because large load users like Amazon have paid millions to upgrade the regional grid, Schalliol and Amazon said.

But a promise to reduce rates isn’t enough to calm residents.

Fulfilling promises

St. Joseph County has granted property tax abatements totaling over $9 billion over 35 years for AWS’s data center. An additional 85% sales tax break exists on technological hardware, including specific computer hardware and powerful cables to support Amazon’s many processing chips.

“I don’t think we have a comprehensive tally of just how much we’re subsidizing this,” Inskeep said. “These subsidies are going to one of the wealthiest corporations in human history while a lot of Hoosiers are struggling to put food on the table.”

Previously, AWS agreed to help pay for improvements on certain public works, including water treatment plants and grid infrastructure upgrades. Amazon also said they would fund $7 million for road improvements, according to local reports.

“All of those costs are required by the state to be paid by AWS,” Schalliol said.

Schalliol said that AWS is bringing substantial benefits to the county tax base at a time when it is facing a projected shortfall due to changes in state property tax collection. Even with the tax breaks, each data shell is projected to bring the county more than $1 million in taxes. Then there are payroll taxes from about 4,000 construction jobs, hotel taxes from non-local technicians, and all the support services that benefit from a huge investment.

It’s unclear how future utility rates will change for New Carlisle users. Utilities themselves cannot raise rates; they must seek approval from the IURC, which holds hearings and approves measures.

For the last year, rates have increased among all five of Indiana’s major utility providers. I&M residential bills increased 4% year-over-year starting July 1, 2024, according to a survey. This summer’s rate case is the newest battleground for data center opponents to clash with pro-development local officials.

“That’s really where rubber is going to be hitting the road,” said Inskeep, whose nonprofit group opposes rapid expansion. “I&M is going to have to put forth a lot of evidence, open their books, provide a cost of service study where you can really trace the math, to make sure the data centers are paying their fair share.”

Talbot, the AWS spokesperson, said the company’s investments and guaranteed payments are driving the potential rate reduction.

“Amazon’s energy agreements are structured to benefit the communities where we operate, and we are committed to ensuring our presence delivers tangible benefits to local ratepayers,” Talbot wrote in an email.

To meet larger demand, I&M is looking to buy existing gas plants and keep aging coal plants online, Inskeep said. It’s unknown when new energy sources will be built. Nuclear power may help charge the electric grid and support tech firms, but it also creates inefficient water use and redirects power from existing customers.

“These data centers are going to use enormous amounts of energy and the significant portion of that is going to be coming from fossil fuels,” Inskeep said. “So we have a really big concern about how data centers are taking us backwards away from sustainability.”

Power dynamics

All of these changes, planned or enacted, have happened because of strained dynamics among environmental advocates, residents and local officials. Residents have faced conflicting statements on the topic of power: officials promise rate reductions and enormous economic benefits, while critics warn of double-dipping water use and higher utility bills.

“It’s driving prices higher across the market at the same time it’s increasing pollution,” said Inskeep. “And that’s because all of these data centers are taking a lot of power plants off the market for citizens.”

County leaders have long boasted about the surplus of jobs created from Amazon’s construction, but it’s unclear how long those jobs will last.

“The project itself was required — per the development agreement — to provide 1,000 jobs for the project,” said Schalliol. Of those new jobs, about 80% are Hoosiers. Around 60 workers are expected to be employed per building constructed, he said. Every direct job usually supports an equal number of indirect jobs.

“We believe that number will exponentially grow,” Schalliol said.

Inskeep said there may be a large boom in short-term jobs, but AI is designed to eliminate the number of long-term jobs across the country, especially as the technology yields stronger capabilities. He also said similar industrial projects, such as the nearby electric battery plant, bring in far more jobs with far less power usage. CAC estimates that data centers create a quarter of a job per megawatt of energy used, compared to an average of 41 jobs per megawatt in other industries.

Another gray area is how sustainable the project’s power is.

“This is the biggest energy-using facility I had ever heard about in my entire career,” Inskeep said. Despite this new demand — roughly 18% of the state’s daily consumption — no clean energy requirements were written into Amazon’s tax abatement plan.

Brian Will, co-leader of the South Bend chapter of Citizens Climate Lobby, said the gas power plants to expand the regional grid emit methane, which contributes to climate change. The challenge is exacerbated because state and federal laws were changed this year to make enforcing many pollution standards voluntary rather than mandatory.

“Data centers aren’t necessarily bad, but what we are realizing as a society is that they have a huge environmental footprint that we can no longer tolerate,” Will said.

Amazon previously said that the grid will expand capacity by 3 gigawatts to exceed its added demand. The company also said their commitment to the area “includes enabling four solar farms and a wind farm” that would serve less than 30% of its added demand.

AWS isn’t the only tech company building data centers. The expected energy demand of nine new hyperscale projects, including New Carlisle, is projected to consume half of Indiana’s total electric output, according to 2023 data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

This has kept locals worried about their future and vocal during zoning hearings, where they have the most leverage.

Public pushback

The tension between residents and powerful economic development interests was palpable at a hearing in December for another hyperscale data center in New Carlisle with an unidentified owner. Dozens of residents raised their concerns about big tech taking swaths of farmland and stressing their utilities and aquifers. The meeting lasted until 4 a.m.

“I would rather pay the property tax than to have you guys destroy beautiful property out here,” said Sandra Ralph, a New Carlisle resident. “We don’t need another data center to poison our land.”

A week prior to the meeting, South Bend Mayor James Mueller, Mishawaka Mayor Dave Wood and three county commissioners signed a letter supporting the proposed data center that would provide millions of dollars in taxes and infrastructure funds. Two are Democrats and three are Republicans.

Later, it was revealed that Larry Garatoni, an influential businessman and charter school operator, hired a right-wing public relations firm to write the letter.

"The money is going to win out," said Steve Sass, a New Carlisle resident, at the meeting. "These people have all been bought off. It’s all a predetermined deal. And you know that’s heartbreaking to our democratic process."

Brandon Dickinson, an attorney based in Indianapolis who represents the development, said that a swarm of misinformation about the project’s footprint has poisoned social media. He also said recent surges in electricity rates were from EPA compliance rates and decommissioning coal plants, not from AWS.

But faced with public opposition, the St. Joseph County Council struck down the rezoning plan in a 7-2 vote.

Marcy Kauffman, New Carlisle’s council president, said the town deserved time to “absorb the impacts” of Amazon and other existing projects “without having to accommodate an unplanned, inappropriately placed second data center.”

Despite public outcry dragging into the morning, Bill Shalliol believes the proposed nearby project will return for a second try.

“We think there’s an opportunity again based on the utility infrastructure that’s been built,” Schalliol said. “I’m an economic development guy; we always want more.”

Future infrastructure

New Carlisle hasn’t felt the full effect of AWS’s data center. With the project being about half completed as of May, residents say disruptions to their daily life outweigh any monetary benefits for the county. Roads are blocked. Traffic congests an otherwise rural town. Bob Humbarger pointed to tire tracks plowing right through his roadside garden.

Other aging infrastructure projects — once promising to be an economic boon for the region — now lay abandoned. The College Football Hall of Fame convinced city and state officials to provide generous tax incentives, then moved to Atlanta and left an empty building downtown.

While artificial intelligence is driving much of the investment in Indiana and across the nation, residents and consumer advocates worry that rapid shifts in the nascent industry could leave them saddled with the costs of expensive energy upgrades.

“One of our big concerns is the uncertainty of the industry,” Inskeep said. “We’re going to need 2,250 megawatts, but what happens if they end up needing half that?”

Over Bob Humbarger’s farmland, industrial light leaks into the night sky. Chris Humbarger, his son, lives nearby and said he used to be able to see the Milky Way but now can’t see any stars. He worries about the environmental impacts the nearby developments could deliver.

He and his father have voiced their concerns, but they feel like it’s a losing game. “We don’t have any political clout,” Bob Humbarger said.

text:
Senator Alan Armstrong (R-OK) is growing momentum behind comprehensive permitting reform, announcing 13 additional Senate cosponsors for S. 4944, the American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure (AEMI) Act: Senators Tom Cotton (R-AR), Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), David McCormick (R-PA), Bernie Moreno (R-OH), John Cornyn (R-TX), Tim Sheehy (R-MT), Marsha Blackburn (R-TN), Steve Daines (R-MT), Roger Marshall (R-KS), John Kennedy (R-LA), Ted Budd (R-NC), Roger Wicker (R-MS), and Jon Husted (R-OH).

The newly-added cosponsors join original sponsors Senators Cynthia Lummis (R-WY), Rick Scott (R-FL), Katie Britt (R-AL), and James Lankford (R-OK) for a total of 17 cosponsors, expanding a base of Senate support that reaches into Republican leadership and both committees with jurisdiction over permitting reform.

The growing support comes as the Senate left Washington for the August recess without producing a bipartisan permitting reform package. Negotiators say they are making progress and hope to unveil an agreement in September, but significant issues remain unresolved — including Clean Water Act and National Historic Preservation Act reviews — and the shrinking legislative calendar leaves little time to turn a deal into law. Against that backdrop, Armstrong is working to reinvigorate conversations on permitting reform in the Senate by advancing concrete provisions that find bicameral and bipartisan support.

As power demands skyrocket across the nation — driven by rapid advancements in artificial intelligence, domestic high-tech manufacturing, and industrial expansion — America’s outdated and duplicative permitting framework continues to stall critical projects. The AEMI Act cuts through bureaucratic red tape, provides long-overdue certainty for builders, and prevents project delays that threaten economic growth and national security.

Senator Alan Armstrong (R-OK) said, “Our national energy infrastructure is like a bridge: nobody really cares about it until it falls down, and the cracks are starting to show right now. We have a narrow window to act, and we cannot afford to let this opportunity pass us by. I am grateful to my 17 Senate colleagues who are co-sponsoring the AEMI Act. Together, we recognize that America cannot afford another year of delay.”

Senator Cynthia Lummis (R-WY) said, “Wyoming’s energy industry and infrastructure future depends on our ability to build. For far too long, environmental extremists have weaponized permitting processes to kill critical projects before they ever break ground. I am proud to partner with Senator Armstrong to streamline reviews and ensure Wyoming’s minerals and energy can reach the market.”

Senator Rick Scott (R-FL) said, “Previous generations of Americans built the greatest economic powerhouse the world has ever seen. Nowadays, however, government seems to be doing everything it can to kill the American spirit with needless bureaucracy. While Communist China cuts corners to get ahead, a mountain of red tape has America fighting the energy war with one hand tied behind our backs. This bill slashes red tape and meets 21st century demands to help President Trump restore American energy dominance.”

Senator Katie Britt (R-AL) said, “As America continues to lead in industries that require a higher energy demand, like artificial intelligence and manufacturing, it’s critical that we are modernizing our infrastructure to keep up with that demand. This bill creates regulatory certainty for energy and critical mineral projects alike, and it continues to execute on President Trump’s promise to unleash American energy dominance and compete with the People’s Republic of China by slashing burdensome red tape, ensuring environmental decision-making is based on sound science, and preventing partisan politics from inhibiting this necessary growth.”

Senator James Lankford (R-OK) said, “Oklahomans know how to build, produce, and deliver. The problem is not our workers or our resources. The problem is a federal permitting system that stands in the way of the people doing the work. I am proud to join Senator Armstrong to advance ideas to cut the red tape and let Oklahoma do what Oklahoma does best.”

Senator Tom Cotton (R-AR) said, “Bureaucratic red tape and radical environmentalists’ delay vital energy projects needed to advance American manufacturing. Our bill would streamline the federal permitting process to ensure we can accelerate critical energy infrastructure projects.”

Senator Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) said, “For Alaska, few issues are more important than federal permitting reform. We have just about every resource our nation needs in great abundance, but almost every project is challenged, costing us investment, jobs, and security. We can’t even build simple roads without facing lawsuits these days. That’s why I have cosponsored Senator Armstrong’s American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act, which includes a number of good ideas to make lasting improvements to what is currently a failing system.”

Senator Dave McCormick (R-PA) said, “Pennsylvania has the workers, resources, and infrastructure to power America for decades, but Washington’s broken permitting system is standing in the way. I’m proud to support this bill to bring clear rules and predictable timelines, get America building again, and help the United States achieve energy dominance and outcompete Communist China.”

Senator Bernie Moreno (R-OH) said, “Ohio is leading energy production in the United States, and we refuse to let Washington’s bureaucratic red tape get in the way. It is time to slash burdensome regulations to give our companies the tools and freedom they need to out-compete any country in the world.”

Senator John Cornyn (R-TX) said, “As energy use rises, we must remove unnecessary barriers holding us back from building reliable infrastructure that can keep up with demand. I am proud to join Senator Armstrong as a cosponsor of the American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act, which would help streamline the process for federal permitting and construction and allow Texas to continue fueling the nation.”

Senator Tim Sheehy (R-MT) said, “America cannot achieve energy dominance if critical projects are tied up in years of unnecessary permitting delays and litigation. We need a permitting process that is efficient, predictable, and grounded in common sense to develop Montana’s abundant critical mineral resources and unleash American energy. The American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act gets rid of burdensome red tape, provides certainty for job creators, and ensures radical politics doesn’t stand in the way of projects that strengthen our economy and national security.”

Senator Marsha Blackburn (R-TN) said, “America’s energy demand is surging due to advanced technology and manufacturing, but our outdated federal permitting process remains a massive barrier to building the infrastructure we need to stay competitive. The American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act would cut red tape and accelerate construction of the critical energy and mineral projects essential to our nation’s future.”

Senator Steve Daines (R-MT) said, “Montana is rich in natural resources, from wind and hydro to coal and natural gas. It’s critical that we optimize the ability to build and provide consistent and reliable Made-In-America energy infrastructure. I’m thrilled to work with Senator Armstrong to streamline reviews and ensure Montana’s energy can reach the market.”

Senator Roger Marshall (R-KS) said, “Every unnecessary regulation and every year a project sits tied up in red tape comes with a price tag, and eventually that bill gets passed on to American families. We have the energy and resources right here at home to power our country and lower costs. This legislation cuts through the regulatory maze, gets projects moving again, and lets American producers do what they do best.”

Senator Ted Budd (R-NC) said, “America cannot achieve true energy dominance with red tape standing in the way. By cutting the burdensome bureaucratic barriers that hold back American energy, undermine our national security, and stifle economic growth, we can ensure access to the reliable infrastructure needed to power the future. North Carolina is proud to lead the nation in high-tech manufacturing, and by making reliable power more accessible, we can lower energy bills and reshore key industries that create good-paying jobs.”

Senator Roger Wicker (R-MS) said, “If we hope to secure America’s energy future, the government must get out of the way. This legislation would reduce unnecessary permitting rules, providing greater certainty for those investing in American energy.”

Senator Jon Husted (R-OH) said, “Permitting reform is affordability. Cutting unnecessary red tape lowers costs, strengthens American competitiveness and helps make life more affordable for working families. America has the energy resources and innovation needed to lead the world, and we need to make sure we can build the infrastructure needed to meet growing demand.”

S. 4944: THE AMERICAN ENERGY AND MINERAL INFRASTRUCTURE ACT OF 2026

· Strengthens the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (FERCs) role as the lead agency for interstate natural gas pipelines and LNG facilities, ensuring that no single state can unilaterally block federally authorized projects and reducing delays caused by duplicative or overlapping reviews.

· Ensures consistent evidence-based environmental decision-making and includes targeted reforms to the Clean Water Act 401 review process for all types of infrastructure.

· Provides certainty with the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) general permits and nationwide permits by eliminating duplicative review, extending permit terms, and incorporating meaningful judicial reforms to avoid baseless lawsuits.

· Provides statutory clarification necessary to re-enable essential mining activities on federal lands.

· Clarifies the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) by codifying a targeted scope of review, preventing overly expansive environmental analyses, reaffirming the statute’s procedural nature, and establishing meaningful judicial review standards to ensure NEPA cannot be misused to stall critical infrastructure projects.

The section by section can be found here.

Read about the American Energy and Mineral Infrastructure Act in Fox News here.

BROAD COALITION OF SUPPORT

The addition of new Senate cosponsors follows a surge of endorsements from outside stakeholders across the country. Scores of energy producers, mining enterprises, labor unions, manufacturing associations, and policy groups have united behind the AEMI Act, recognizing it as an essential step toward restoring American infrastructure leadership and lower energy costs for families and businesses.

Companies and organizations supporting Senator Armstrong’s permitting agenda include: ONE Gas, Inc., TC Energy, Williams, EQT, Woodside Energy USA, NextEra Energy, Expand Energy, Labor organizations, United Association of Union Plumbers and Pipefitters (UA), South Central Pennsylvania Building Trades, Brotherhood of Boilermakers Local 154, Pipe Line Contractors Association (PLCA), American Public Power Association, National Rural Electric Cooperative Association (NRECA), Interstate Natural Gas Association of America (INGAA), American Gas Association (AGA), American Petroleum Institute (API), American Exploration & Production Council (AXPC), Natural Gas Supply Association (NGSA), Center for LNG (CLNG), GPA Midstream, GPSA, Liquid Energy Pipeline Association (LEPA), The Petroleum Alliance of Oklahoma, Virginia Oil & Gas Association, National Mining Association (NMA), National Hydropower Association (NHA), Energy Infrastructure Council (EIC), Essential Minerals Association, Colorado Oil and Gas Association, Petroleum Association of Wyoming (PAW), Texas Pipeline Association, Electric Power Supply Association (EPSA), Partnership to Address Global Emissions (PAGE), American Council for Capital Formation (ACCF), Americans for Prosperity (AFP), ClearPath Action, ACC Action, America First Policy Institute, Cato Institute, and the Pacific Legal Foundation.

text:
The U.S. Grains & BioProducts Council recently hosted a high-level delegation from Guatemala for a trade and learning mission to Washington, D.C. and Indiana to strengthen bilateral cooperation and support the country’s national E10 ethanol blending program. Guatemala is preparing to become the first Central American country to implement an E10 gasoline blending program in more than 40 years, creating new long-term opportunities for U.S. ethanol exports.

“Guatemala is writing a new chapter for transportation fuels in Central America,” said Federico Salcedo, USGBC Latin America ethanol strategy lead.

“This mission allowed policymakers to experience how ethanol supports energy security, cleaner transportation, rural prosperity and economic growth. As Guatemala advances its E10 program, these exchanges and partnerships will strengthen confidence in the market while creating new opportunities for long-term trade between Guatemala and U.S. agricultural producers.”

The delegation included leaders from Guatemala’s Congress, officials from the Ministry of Energy and Mines and ethanol industry representatives.

Salcedo and USGBC Ethanol Consultant Lady Gómez accompanied the mission, facilitating exchanges with U.S. government agencies, industry associations and private-sector leaders to strengthen technical knowledge, institutional relationships and understanding of the U.S. ethanol industry.

In Washington, D.C., the delegation met with stakeholders and policymakers including the Council, the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA), the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the Renewable Fuels Association (RFA) and Growth Energy. Discussions focused on ethanol policy, fuel quality standards, market oversight, consumer education and ethanol’s role in strengthening energy security, reducing emissions and supporting rural economic development.

In Indiana, the Indiana Corn Marketing Council coordinated visits across the ethanol value chain. Delegates toured POET’s Alexandria ethanol plant, observed storage and blending operations at a U.S. Energy terminal , met with Family Express to discuss retail fuel marketing and consumer outreach and visited Chris Eck’s family farm in Boggstown. The visits demonstrated how ethanol production supports farming communities, delivers economic and environmental benefits and succeeds through collaboration between the agricultural and energy sectors.

title: Clean Air Act: Dismantling One of the Country's Bedrock Environmental Laws
description:
Amid the deregulatory flurry, the administration set up an inbox within the EPA where executives who run chemical plants, coal power stations, copper smelters and other factories could email to request a temporary exemption to Clean Air Act rules.
As of mid-July, the administration had granted Clean Air Act exemptions to about 200 polluting facilities across 39 states and Puerto Rico, issuing its decisions in presidential proclamations full of typos and errors.
The factories and plants that were given a temporary pass on Clean Air Act rules, while scattered across the country, fall disproportionately in majority nonwhite neighborhoods, according to EPA and U.S. Census Bureau data collected by the Environmental Defense Fund.
Congress and executive agencies are currently working to undo several dozen other rules and regulations meant to safeguard air quality.
In this session, ProPublica reporter Mark Olalde joins fellow environment journalists from across the country to discuss the unprecedented rollback of the Clean Air Act and what it means for public health in urban and rural communities, in red and blue states.
text:
In partnership with the Chicago Tribune and Deep South Today.

Shortly after President Donald Trump returned to the White House, political appointees at the Environmental Protection Agency announced the “biggest deregulatory action in U.S. history.” Foundational environmental laws, rules and regulations that for decades had been used to clean up the nation’s air and waterways, protect its plants and animals, and reduce its greenhouse gas emissions were suddenly on the chopping block.

Amid the deregulatory flurry, the administration set up an inbox within the EPA where executives who run chemical plants, coal power stations, copper smelters and other factories could email to request a temporary exemption to Clean Air Act rules. The president said it was a matter of national security because disruptions to the affected industries could interrupt supply chains. EPA staff and others disagreed. No rigorous application was necessary, no public comment, no EPA oversight — all it took was an email sent to that EPA inbox stating your case, which was passed to the White House for approval.

ProPublica obtained thousands of pages of EPA communications that told the inside story of how quickly and sloppily the Trump administration received, processed and accepted these requests. As of mid-July, the administration had granted Clean Air Act exemptions to about 200 polluting facilities across 39 states and Puerto Rico, issuing its decisions in presidential proclamations full of typos and errors. In one case, a factory that doesn’t appear to exist received an exemption. The factories and plants that were given a temporary pass on Clean Air Act rules, while scattered across the country, fall disproportionately in majority nonwhite neighborhoods, according to EPA and U.S. Census Bureau data collected by the Environmental Defense Fund. Roughly 250,000 people live within a mile of at least one of the exempted facilities.

An EPA spokesperson told ProPublica that the agency “played no role” in the decisions and “any requests sent to the EPA’s electronic mailbox were forwarded to the White House.” A spokesperson for the White House said that the “exemptions were issued due to crushing Biden-era regulations that required large swaths of our industrial base to adopt technologies that don’t exist outside the imagination of Biden’s EPA bureaucrats.”

But the exemptions, which granted a two-year reprieve from complying with specific Clean Air Act rules, are just the tip of the spear. Congress and executive agencies are currently working to undo several dozen other rules and regulations meant to safeguard air quality.

In this session, ProPublica reporter Mark Olalde joins fellow environment journalists from across the country to discuss the unprecedented rollback of the Clean Air Act and what it means for public health in urban and rural communities, in red and blue states.

text:
Rhode Islanders are facing higher-than-usual energy bills and a significant increase in utility shutoffs.

State officials are providing temporary bill credits, but there is no consensus on a long-term solution to the energy crisis.

Proposed long-term fixes range from expanding natural gas pipelines to increasing investment in renewable energy sources like offshore wind.

Rhode Island Energy is requesting further rate increases, citing inflation and market forces beyond its control.

The phones keep ringing at the George Wiley Center. They're people looking for help with their energy bills from the Pawtucket nonprofit that advocates for the poor.

Camilo Viveiros, executive director at the center for the last decade, is used to getting more calls from people in need around this time of year after the annual winter moratorium on utility shutoffs ends each spring. But the call volume is even higher this year.

"It may be double what we usually get," Viveiros said.

Rhode Island and the other New England states consistently rank among the highest in the nation for energy prices, driven by constraints on the region's natural gas pipelines and what many experts say is an overdependence on the fossil fuel for heating and electric generation.

But while electric supply rates, in particular, usually subside in the summer months as heating use goes down and wholesale gas prices follow, they've remained higher than usual this summer. For comparison, the summer rate this year is steeper than the winter rate of 2021-22.

Combine the inflated rate with periods of extreme heat that are pushing up the use of air conditioning and it means that many electric customers are getting hit with more burdensome bills.

And now, after COVID-era rules that allowed customers to make smaller payments on their debts to Rhode Island Energy finally expired at the beginning of the year, shutoffs are climbing. There were 5,668 on the electric side alone in May and June, nearly twice as many as in the same period last year.

More increases in electric rates on the horizon

There's no letup in sight. Rhode Island Energy is requesting another increase in supply rates for the coming winter, and it has a proposal to raise delivery charges pending with state regulators that could take effect as soon as September.

"Rhode Islanders are at a breaking point," Gov. Dan McKee said on July 23 in announcing the use of $28 million in state money to help offset ratepayer bills in the winter.

The executive order, which would work out to a combined $61 credit for each Rhode Island Energy customer between January and March, isn't the first time the McKee administration has stepped in to defray electric costs.

The state Public Utilities Commission tapped into funds set aside for energy efficiency and storm repairs to credit customers for the same months last winter. And in previous years, the administration has adopted temporary measures to reduce bills for low-income customers.

But finding long-term solutions to the state's energy affordability crisis has been much more difficult.

No consensus on long-term fixes

Some groups argue that New England must expand its pipeline capacity to meet the needs of a region that got 55% of its electric generation from natural gas in 2025.

A just-released analysis from Daymark Energy Advisors found that the Constitution Pipeline that would deliver more shale gas from Pennsylvania could reduce wholesale electric prices in New England by $2.8 billion over 20 years.

Others argue that the region needs more renewable energy supplies to reduce its dependence on gas. Daymark has also estimated more than half a billion dollars in winter bill savings with the development of more offshore wind.

But while McKee has backed Revolution Wind, an offshore wind farm that would supply power to Rhode Island for less than current retail rates, he hasn't been as supportive of clean energy as a whole.

His most recent budget proposal would have capped spending on energy efficiency and pulled back on commitments to ramp up renewable energy offsets. His administration said the changes would save Rhode Islanders $1 billion over five years.

Others vying for the governorship have put forward their own plans.

Helena Foulkes, McKee's rival for the Democratic nomination, has said she would ramp up investments in renewables, aiming to reduce consumer costs by diversifying energy sources.

Ken Block, an independent running for governor, proposes reassessing all fees and surcharges on electric bills with a goal of cutting bills by 25%.

Republican candidate Aaron Guckian has called for forming a commission to look at solar and wind, but also small nuclear reactors in a bid to expand energy sources for the state.

What is making electricity in Rhode Island less affordable?

Rhode Island Energy blames the high electric rates on a combination of factors outside of its control – the war in the Middle East, state renewable energy mandates and regional grid costs. (On the last one, the operator of the New England grid disputes Rhode Island Energy's numbers.)

Greg Cornett, president of Rhode Island Energy, said he understands the burden on ratepayers, but he also said that costs are going up because of inflation and larger forces on energy markets.

"It's not a matter of folks just trying to grab more money," he said. "It's the fact that it's more expensive to do business today."

He believes that small changes, such as allowing nuclear power to qualify as a clean energy source under state law, could help control costs. In the longer term, he argues that amending state law to allow his company to develop its own generating sources would help.

He also said the company is doing more to help customers now. As part of its request with the Public Utilities Commission to increase delivery fees, Rhode Island Energy has also proposed a revamped low-income program with more discounted rates that aims to help a greater number of people.

But while Viveiros says the Wiley Center is supportive of the new program, he correctly points out that Rhode Island Energy is also seeking a higher cap on its profits. (Cornett said the request is in line with what other states allow their utilities.)

The Wiley Center has fought unsuccessfully to strengthen state rules that suspend utility shutoffs during heat waves and others that protect people who are seriously ill. But Viveiros believes that those proposed changes are Band-Aids on a larger problem that can only be solved by reworking the state's energy system.

"Without rate restructuring, you can pour all the money you want in the pot, but every rate increase puts another hole into it," he said.

text:
The Trump administration has quietly let lapse a program for young leaders at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, The Times has learned. In its place, California will launch its own council for young people looking to get involved with environmental issues at the state level.

The California EPA’s Environmental Youth Advisory Council is doing a callout for people ages 14 to 20 years old who want to build leadership skills, learn from environmental decision-makers and make recommendations on state environmental policy, officials said.

The move comes after a similar group within the federal EPA, the Biden-era National Environmental Youth Advisory Council, appears to have expired under the Trump administration.

Launched in 2023, the federal program hosted 16 members ages 16 to 29, appointed to two-year terms. While the Trump administration has not officially announced the program’s termination, no new cohort was appointed at the end of the term last year, and its website has been taken down.

When asked whether the program has been terminated, EPA officials said simply that the committee’s charter expired on June 5, 2025. Under the Federal Advisory Committee Act, such groups automatically end after two years unless explicitly renewed.

California’s program hopes to fill the gap by “giving young people a seat at the table,” Gov. Gavin Newsom said in a statement.

“By establishing the CalEPA Youth Council, we are ensuring that young people can engage directly in climate action, serve California’s communities, and have a say in the future of our environment,” Newsom said.

The program comes as young people in the state face worsening hazards fueled by climate change including extreme heat, wildfires and dangerous air pollution. People under the age of 20 make up about a quarter of the state’s population, or about 9.75 million residents, according to demographic data from the California Department of Finance.

Not only will young people experience more climate extremes and damage, but children are also disproportionately affected as “developing bodies make it harder for them to cope with the physical and psychological stresses,” according to UNICEF’s 2026 Children’s Climate Risk report.

At the same time, Trump’s EPA has moved to roll back bedrock environmental protections in the state and across the U.S., including California’s clean car standards and the federal government’s longstanding scientific conclusion that planet-heating pollution seriously threatens Americans, known as the endangerment finding. The administration has said the rollbacks will reduce regulatory costs and lower prices for taxpayers.

“Young people everywhere will inherit the environmental legacy we build today,” said Yana Garcia, California secretary for environmental protection. “That’s why, at CalEPA, we believe young people should get a say in the decisions we make, and that their diverse perspectives should be heard and honored.”

In April, Sen. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) and Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) introduced legislation that would cement the status of youth groups within the EPA as well as the U.S. departments of the Interior, Energy, Agriculture and Commerce — with Markey noting at the time that “young people have the most to lose from climate change.”

However, neither bill has advanced beyond committee referral, meaning they are unlikely to pass under the current Congress.

CalEPA officials did not provide a precise dollar amount for the new program but said it will make use of existing funds for travel and in-person training, and that the inaugural class will help the agency determine future budget needs. There is no cost to applicants.

The program is open to applicants from small towns and cities, tribal communities and underrepresented groups. No previous advocacy or leadership experience is required.

The inaugural cohort will include 10 appointees and run for a one-year pilot term before expanding to 20 appointees and a full two-year term, according to CalEPA. The application period runs through Sept. 21.

title: California lost the EV mandate. Why is the fight just getting started? - CBT News
authors: Lauren Fix, CBT News Editorial Team
description:
I can’t tell you how many times I’ve heard people say, “Didn’t California already lose?” The answer is NO.
The latest Congressional Review Act resolutions introduced in the Senate don’t target the 2035 EV mandate itself.
American families should not face higher costs or fewer choices because of policies imposed by a single state.” California’s response speaks for itself.
Rather than backing away after Congress overturned the EV mandate, California introduced the My First EV program.
Or should the courts decide where state authority ends and federal authority begins?
text:
If you’ve been reading my columns over the past year, you may have noticed that I keep returning to California. One week it’s the EV mandate. Another week it’s replacement tire regulations. Then it’s emissions waivers, Section 177, Right to Repair, insurance companies collecting driving data, or new incentives designed to push consumers toward electric vehicles. On the surface, these stories don’t appear to have much in common.

They do.

Each one is another piece of a much larger puzzle. Individually, they’re easy to dismiss as another regulatory fight that only affects California. Together, they reveal a coordinated effort that has been reshaping the American automotive market for years, often without consumers realizing it.

That’s why the latest action in Washington deserves far more attention than it’s getting.

Last year, Congress voted to overturn California’s Advanced Clean Cars II waiver, the rule that would have effectively banned the sale of new gasoline-powered passenger vehicles in California by 2035. President Trump signed the Congressional Review Act resolutions, and many people assumed the fight was over. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve heard people say, “Didn’t California already lose?”

The answer is NO.

California lost one battle, not the war. If anything, what’s happening now shows just how determined the state is to preserve the influence it has built over decades. The latest Congressional Review Act resolutions introduced in the Senate don’t target the 2035 EV mandate itself. They go after something much bigger: the legal foundation California has relied on for years to build much of its vehicle emissions program.

Sign up for CBT News’ daily newsletter and get the latest industry stories delivered straight to your inbox.

That may sound like inside-the-Beltway legal jargon, but it has real-world consequences for every driver. California’s Clean Air Act waivers allow the state to adopt emissions standards that are stricter than federal requirements. Under Section 177 of the Clean Air Act, other states can choose to adopt California’s standards instead of the federal government’s. Today, California and the states following many of its rules represent a substantial portion of the U.S. auto market.

Automakers don’t like building one version of a vehicle for California and another for everyone else. It’s expensive, inefficient, and complicates manufacturing. More often than not, they build vehicles that satisfy the toughest standards across the markets they serve. That’s how policies written in Sacramento can influence what’s available in showrooms from New York to Texas.

Once you understand that, a lot of my previous reporting starts fitting together. When I wrote about California’s attempt to regulate replacement tires, it wasn’t just about tires. It was about California setting standards that could ripple into other states. When I covered Right to Repair, the debate wasn’t only about fixing your own vehicle. It was about who controls access to the technology built into modern cars. When we discussed insurance companies collecting driving data or automakers expanding connected vehicle systems, the bigger issue wasn’t convenience. It was who controls the information generated by your vehicle and how that information could eventually influence insurance rates, repairs, ownership, and consumer choice.

Now we’re watching the same pattern unfold again. Congress is trying to roll back decades of California regulatory authority through new Congressional Review Act resolutions targeting four additional EPA waiver decisions. Supporters say the effort is necessary to prevent one state from effectively dictating national vehicle policy. Opponents argue California has long held special authority under the Clean Air Act because of its unique air quality challenges and should continue leading on emissions policy.

The American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers applauded the resolutions. AFPM President and CEO Chet Thompson said, “Congress already rejected California’s effort to force its vehicle policies on the rest of the country. Yet California continues looking for new ways to advance the same agenda. American families should not face higher costs or fewer choices because of policies imposed by a single state.”

California’s response speaks for itself. Rather than backing away after Congress overturned the EV mandate, California introduced the My First EV program. The initiative offers rebates for qualifying new and used electric vehicles to first-time buyers in an effort to keep EV adoption moving after federal incentives were reduced. The program also relies on participation from automakers, placing manufacturers in the middle of California’s continuing push toward electrification.

At the same time, California Attorney General Rob Bonta has made it clear the state intends to fight the Congressional Review Act actions in court. His position is that Congress improperly used the CRA to overturn EPA waiver decisions and that California’s authority under the Clean Air Act remains intact.

That’s why I don’t view these as separate stories anymore. Congress is trying to limit California’s regulatory authority. California is using incentive programs to keep its electrification goals moving forward. The courts are being asked to decide whether Congress even has the authority to revoke these waivers. Meanwhile, automakers are left trying to navigate conflicting political and regulatory demands while designing vehicles years before they ever reach a dealership.

If you only look at one headline, you miss what’s really happening. But when you step back and connect the dots, a different picture emerges. This is no longer just a debate over electric vehicles. It’s a debate over who gets to shape the future of transportation in America.

That’s the question consumers should be asking. Should one state have the ability to influence what vehicles are sold across much of the country? Should Congress establish one national standard? Or should the courts decide where state authority ends and federal authority begins? This is why Congress is pushing the Congressional Review Act resolutions.

However this ends, one thing is becoming increasingly clear. The biggest battle over your next vehicle isn’t happening inside the engineering departments at Ford, General Motors, Toyota, or Tesla. It’s unfolding in Congress, state capitols, federal agencies, and courtrooms. By the time the average consumer notices the outcome, many of those decisions may already have shaped the vehicles sitting on dealership lots.

That’s why these stories matter. They’re not isolated headlines. They’re chapters in a much bigger story that’s still being written. Your freedoms to choose what to drive should be yours not some unelected bureaucrat.

title: GM-LG Energy Solution Ohio Battery Plant Restarts After Seven-Month Halt - BigGo Finance
description:
Ultium Cells, the joint venture between General Motors (GM) and LG Energy Solution, will restart its battery cell plant in Warren, northeastern Ohio, next week.
The Ohio plant, which began mass production in August 2022, was the first joint battery production facility for GM and LG Energy Solution.
Battery Production Strategy The Ohio plant restart is part of a broader trend in which GM's U.S. battery production strategy is becoming differentiated by facility.
Another joint venture plant operated by GM and LG Energy Solution in Spring Hill, Tennessee, has been converted to produce batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) instead of EV batteries.
It would be premature to conclude that the Ohio plant restart signals a broad-based demand recovery in the North American EV market.
text:
Ultium Cells, the joint venture between General Motors (GM) and LG Energy Solution, will restart its battery cell plant in Warren, northeastern Ohio, next week. The restart comes approximately seven months after production was halted in January amid slowing electric vehicle demand.

According to Reuters on the 12th (local time), Tom Gallagher, Ultium Cells' vice president of operations, said in an interview that most furloughed workers will return on the 17th to resume battery production. The plant is expected to employ approximately 1,400 people once operations restart.

The Ohio plant, which began mass production in August 2022, was the first joint battery production facility for GM and LG Energy Solution. It has an annual production capacity exceeding 35 GWh and announced in December 2024 that it had produced its 100 millionth EV battery cell.

However, as consumer demand for EVs proved weaker than expected, battery cell production was halted in January. According to Reuters reporting from May, the Ohio plant employed approximately 1,330 workers as of October last year, with roughly 480 laid off indefinitely and about 850 placed on temporary furlough during the shutdown.

Major Overhaul of U.S. Battery Production Strategy

The Ohio plant restart is part of a broader trend in which GM's U.S. battery production strategy is becoming differentiated by facility. Another joint venture plant operated by GM and LG Energy Solution in Spring Hill, Tennessee, has been converted to produce batteries for energy storage systems (ESS) instead of EV batteries. GM had previously announced plans in July 2025 to add lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery production equipment at the plant to expand production of lower-cost EV batteries.

GM has also exited its joint venture with Samsung SDI. Samsung SDI (006400.KS) officially announced this week that it has acquired GM's 49.99% stake in Synergy Cells, the joint venture established for a battery plant under construction in New Carlisle, Indiana. As a result, Synergy Cells becomes a wholly owned subsidiary of Samsung SDI, giving the company its first standalone battery plant in North America.

Synergy Cells was established in 2024 with a total investment of $3.5 billion (approximately 5 trillion won) from Samsung SDI and GM, with an annual production capacity of 27 GWh. Mass production was originally targeted for 2026, but the start date was pushed back to 2027 as EV market conditions weakened. Samsung SDI plans to operate the plant as a facility producing both EV batteries and ESS batteries, with a particular focus on aggressively targeting the rapidly growing North American ESS market.

While the joint venture structure with GM is ending, the two companies will continue their partnership. They signed a joint development agreement (JDA) for a next-generation prismatic battery co-development project for EVs. A JDA is a more concrete arrangement than a memorandum of understanding (MOU) and carries legal binding force as a formal contract. Under the agreement, the two companies will jointly conduct R&D on prismatic batteries incorporating Samsung SDI's high-energy-density and fast-charging technologies, with the resulting products slated for installation in GM's next-generation EV models.

GM's Broader EV Investment Pullback

GM's exit from the Indiana joint venture extends a multi-year trend of scaling back EV manufacturing investments. GM previously transferred its stake in the Lansing, Michigan battery plant to LG Energy Solution and has delayed production plans and adjusted capacity across multiple EV operations.

As GM has reassessed its EV investment and production outlook, it has recorded substantial impairment charges. In October 2025, the company announced a $1.6 billion (approximately 2.3 trillion won) asset write-down related to its EV business, followed by an additional $6 billion (approximately 8.5 trillion won) write-down in January 2026 as management further revised investment plans.

The U.S. EV market environment has also deteriorated. The federal EV purchase tax credit of $7,500 expired in September 2025, intensifying pressure on automakers already facing slowing growth and affordability challenges. GM shares closed down 2.89% at $86.77 on the day Samsung SDI's acquisition of the Synergy Cells stake was reported.

It would be premature to conclude that the Ohio plant restart signals a broad-based demand recovery in the North American EV market. Rather, it is more appropriately interpreted as GM adjusting production volumes and battery applications on a plant-by-plant basis in response to market conditions. The company is resuming EV cell production in Ohio, producing ESS batteries in Tennessee, and unwinding its joint venture structure in Indiana—demonstrating a differentiated battery investment strategy across its U.S. footprint.

For LG Energy Solution, the restart of a major North American production hub that had been idle for seven months is notable. However, the restart announcement did not include details on future utilization rates, production volumes, or additional capacity expansion timelines for the Ohio plant. Whether this production resumption translates into a meaningful rebound in North American EV battery demand will require further monitoring of GM's EV sales performance and plant utilization rates going forward.

text:
As global biomass markets continue to shift, attention is increasingly turning to opportunities closer to home. Pellet Mill Magazine spoke with industry leaders about the prospects for developing domestic markets for industrial wood pellets, biocarbon and black pellets, where, despite the volumes being produced, demand remains modest compared with well-established export markets. In 2025, U.S. producers manufactured approximately 9.5 million tons of utility wood pellets; 9.4 million tons were exported, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Darrell Smith, president of the Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, explains that the forest industry in the southern U.S. needs a market for their trees in order to maintain the region’s forested acreage. Approximately 85% to 86% of agricultural land is privately held. Without healthy forest products markets, landowners may be forced to find a different use for their land, which could include selling it for commercial property development. And, wildfire risks could increase if low-grade material is not removed. “As demand for low-grade material declines and it winds up laying on the forest floor—or if forests aren’t thinned out or utilized as quickly as they used to be—there can be a lot of extra fuel for forest fires,” Smith says.

Finding additional markets is critical, agrees Thomas Reilley, chair of AWBA and chairman at Highland Pellets. “Markets will solve the long-term decline of our working forests, our rural communities—a way of life—and will help preserve them from what will otherwise be inevitable land use change, and the loss of both billions of tons of carbon and tremendous economic value,” he adds.

Economic Drivers and

Decarbonization

Subsidies have driven wood pellet use internationally, explains Smith. Though the U.S.’ well-established biomass supply chain has historically served international markets, aiding decarbonization efforts around the world, Smith says the industry’s next chapter will leverage the same infrastructure to help American industries decarbonize. “We’re international companies and we’ll go where the market demands, whether that’s new domestic plays or international markets that have shaped our industry and been buoyed by subsidies for years,” Smith says. “I think the common theme is that these markets value biomass not simply as a fuel anymore, but as a solution to decarbonization. And that’s the direction we’re moving in.”

He views the pursuit of domestic outlets as finding additional markets, rather than replacing exports. The three major domestic opportunities for the pellet industry include direct use, feedstock application and carbon capture, he says. The white pellet markets in Europe and Asia remain valuable to the industry and it does not plan to pivot away from exports, but conversations are being had about opportunities closer to home, according to Smith.

Direct use applications include many of the same uses that U.S. pellets find abroad, such as energy generation or industrial power production. Data centers may be a big contender for the next large-scale pellet consumer. At these power-hungry facilities, energy use is projected to jump from 4.1% of the U.S. peak summer power demand in 2025 to 8.5% in 2027, according to Goldman Sachs. Increased energy demand constitutes a great opportunity for every player in the energy world, explains Smith. Due to the optics, data center hyper-scalers are “very interested” in finding renewable energy sources.

“We’re going to need everybody to play a role in what’s coming with our energy needs,” Smith says. “And I think for woody biomass, not only can we play a role in supplying power, but we can supply power in a renewable, sustainable way that helps with decarbonization efforts.”

Harold Arnold, president of pellet producer Fram Renewable Fuels and AWBA board member, explains that the economics for converting coal-powered energy facilities to biomass don’t work without some type of subsidy because biomass is not cost-competitive with coal. “Policies that require biomass to be used as a fuel or coal replacement are needed to give the market the push it needs,” he says. “The infrastructure is in place, at least for the start, as some white pellet plants could be converted while greenfield sites are being built.”

Woody biomass could also serve as a feedstock for renewable fuels like sustainable aviation fuel, methanol and marine fuel, and play a critical role in steel production. Public policy, logistics and economics must work in concert for these projects to reach fruition, Smith adds.

Arnold believes the market for biocarbon in the U.S. will develop, though he estimates it will be five years before a meaningful market for it will come to fruition. He highlights Aymium’s biocarbon joint venture with Steel Dynamics and notes that some parties may be observing the project, waiting to see if it succeeds. The joint venture, SDI Biocarbon Solutions, located in Columbus, Mississippi, is built to produce 228,000 metric tons of biocarbon to supply Steel Dynamics’ nearby steel mill.

The third opportunity, carbon capture’s integration with bioenergy—also known as bioenergy with carbon capture and storage (BECCS)—has attracted interest from some companies. “We need other [domestic] industries to understand the value that we have and how that we can help them in their decarbonization efforts,” Smith says. “And we look forward to having that conversation with as many people as possible.”

Scaling Strategy

In Canada, production capacity is well above 4 million metric tons per year, with actual production hovering around 3.5 million metric tons per year, most of which is exported. Therefore, industrial pellet use remains low. Although some projects are underway and interest in using both black and white pellets is present, market demand and development remains slow. Part of the reason for low industrial-scale utilization is the country’s use of hydroelectric power as its main energy source. Gordon Murray, executive director of the Wood Pellet Association of Canada, explains that industrial demand often is driven by countries searching for a more sustainable option for their power grid, and swapping to wood pellets from coal makes sense. However, Canada’s abundance of cheap, sustainable power eliminates this demand driver.

Murray notes that the Atikoken Generating Station, located in northwestern Ontario, uses between 90,000 and 100,000 metric tons of wood pellets each year, but it runs as a peaking facility—operating only when the grid’s energy demand increases—so the pellet consumption is inconsistent.

An opportunity on the horizon is the Belledune project in the province of New Brunswick, which would see three to four white pellet producers change their process to black pellets, supplying a converted coal power station with fuel. The scale of the project—300,000 to 500,000 metric tons of pellets each year—comes with risk and financing has been difficult for producers to find, explains Murray.

“All the potential suppliers that would be converting their plants right now are still in the throes of trying to secure capital,” he says. “The financial markets are still a little bit nervous about it.”

Government support could help bring the project to completion, but support at the provincial level has been lacking. Murray hopes the government’s mandate to end coal-fired power production by 2030 will spur further interest.

Competing with cheap natural gas is a challenge for pellet-fired power production across much of North America, he explains. However, Canada’s eastern provinces, which rely on heating oil to meet their needs, may become much more interested in wood pellets if the Belledune project succeeds.

Export market demand has remained steady in recent years, but the changes made to the United Kingdom’s Contracts for Difference program will shrink that market for pellet producers in eastern Canada. However, Murray believes the Belledune project—when completed—would utilize the volume producers currently sell to the U.K. and Europe.

Mid-scale pellet use, such as burning pellets in boilers for heating in hospitals, schools and residential buildings, is WPAC’s current focus, he explains. Pellet use is gaining traction in northern provinces, such as the Northwest Territories, where wood pellets have reached 35% market penetration in commercial and institutional heating, according to Murray.

Industrial Interest

In April this year, Norwegian metallurgical company Elkem sold its biochar-related assets in Saguenay, Quebec, to CHAR Technologies Ltd. and agreed to purchase 62,500 metric tons of biocarbon pellets from the company over five years when production begins. Inge Grubben-Strømnes, senior vice president for foundry alloys at Elkem, outlines how biocarbon fits into Elkem’s sustainability goals. Elkem’s Saguenay, Quebec, facility, Elkem Silicon Products Chicoutimi, makes ferrosilicon and ferrosilicon-based alloys. Grubben-Strømnes explains that the process reduces quartz to disconnect the oxygen atoms from the silicon atoms using carbon. The carbon source can be fossil-based, such as coke or coal, or renewable, like wood chips, charcoal or other forms of biocarbon. The smelter operates at more than 2,000 degrees Celsius, which requires a significant amount of electricity.

Elkem aims to meet sustainability goals by only using renewable energy and implementing biocarbon in the smelting process whenever possible. Other strategies such as carbon capture and storage and the “revolutionary production processes of carbon looping” could also play a role in the future, according to Grubben-Strømnes. Elkem’s use of hydropower enables the company to emit two-thirds less carbon than the global average. Ultimately, the company plans to increase biocarbon utilization and further reduce its carbon footprint, targeting 50% biocarbon use in its facilities by 2030.

Although wood chips and charcoal have been utilized at Elkem’s facilities in Norway and Paraguay, biocarbon has higher density than wood chips or charcoal, which makes it a better replacement for coal and lowers the logistical costs for handling.

Grubben-Strømnes explains Elkem decided to sell its pilot facility and equipment therein, including a pyrolysis kiln, binder technology and other assets needed for pilot-scale production. The company selected CHAR Tech because the acquisition price and terms of the supply contract were acceptable, he says. Also, Elkem perceived CHAR Tech as a company with a good likelihood of industrialization success. “We want to sell to someone we think is capable of industrializing this technology, and then at the end of the day, supply us biocarbon,” he says.

Progress toward a domestic U.S. industrial pellet market is evident in growing interest among industrial companies in converting from coal to biomass, explains Reilley. “There is a growing understanding of the application domestically in the U.S. given the constraints of the grid, the rise of AI and the need for baseload power,” he says.

In the past, carbon capture technology needed to advance further in order to increase large-scale demand domestically, which is no longer the case.

Communicating Value

Smith explains that industries across the U.S. need to hear and understand the opportunity that biomass offers and become educated on its story. Mitigating the initial reactions people might have to the concept of turning wood into energy requires explanation, education and time. “When I'm talking about other businesses, they don’t really know we are an option,” he says.

Biomass has been overlooked in several public policy documents, and AWBA is pursuing the inclusion of woody biomass in policy definitions. A clearer recognition of forest residues, thinnings, low-value material and mill residuals as eligible feedstocks under the Renewable Fuels Standard is one example.

Reilley and Smith identify several key changes that would support market growth in the U.S. Getting woody biomass included in the emissions rate tables and models for tax credit access would keep each facility from being treated as a new project, Smith explains. Under 45Y, 48E and 45V, a provisional emissions rate (PER) is needed for each project, since biomass is not modeled or included in the table. The 45Z emissions-rate table does not include most woody biomass-to-fuel pathways and, when the PER process is finalized, ABWA is advocating to favor pathway-level inclusion of woody biomass, rather than individual project review. Alignment between U.S. EPA, the Department of Energy and the U.S. Department of Agriculture to create standards would help solve this problem, according to Reilley. Extending tax credit programs such as 45V and 45Z would also help the industry grow.

Domestic industries need to understand the value and impact that woody biomass could bring to a variety of industries. “We are a reliable feedstock,” Smith says. “We obtain these materials in a sustainable way that has been certified and audited for years and years. We can sign multiyear contracts. We’re dependable. We can help you with your decarbonization efforts.”

text:
Samsung SDI has acquired GM’s 49.99% stake in their $3.5 billion Indiana battery venture, giving the Korean battery maker full ownership of the facility.

The plant will shift part of its focus toward stationary energy storage systems as U.S. demand rises, while retaining capacity for advanced battery applications.

The deal follows similar EV battery venture restructurings by Ford, Stellantis and LG Energy Solution as automakers adjust to slower EV growth.

Samsung SDI is taking full control of a $3.5 billion battery plant originally planned with General Motors, as slower electric vehicle demand reshapes North America’s battery manufacturing sector.

The South Korean battery maker acquired GM’s entire 49.99% stake in the SynergyCells joint venture in New Carlisle, Indiana. Samsung SDI announced the transaction on August 11.

The acquisition will make the facility Samsung SDI’s first wholly owned battery factory in North America. The plant remains under construction.

Rather than relying solely on EV demand, Samsung SDI plans to use the facility for stationary energy storage system batteries. It will also manufacture high-tech batteries for other applications.

The strategy gives Samsung SDI greater exposure to the fast-growing U.S. energy storage market. Demand is being supported by renewable energy deployment, grid investment and electricity-intensive data centers.

$3.5 billion EV project adapts to weaker demand

Samsung SDI and GM announced the joint venture in 2023. The companies planned to invest about $3.5 billion and support approximately 1,600 jobs.

Production of high-performance, nickel-rich prismatic batteries was expected to begin in 2027.

Since then, weaker-than-anticipated EV demand has forced GM to revise its electrification strategy. Other major U.S. and international automakers have made similar adjustments.

GM’s withdrawal does not end its relationship with Samsung SDI. The companies have signed a separate agreement covering future battery development.

They will work on high-energy-density and fast-charging prismatic cells for potential EV applications.

“While reflecting recent market changes, this acquisition decision is to continue the strategic partnership with GM,” said a Samsung SDI official in a statement. “We will continue our commitment to an electrified future with the partner, while utilizing the plant to proactively respond to the fast-growing ESS market in the U.S.”

The arrangement allows GM to reduce its capital exposure while retaining access to battery technology development.

RELATED ARTICLE: Stellantis, Samsung SDI Invest over $3.2 billon in New Battery Plant Gigafactory

Battery makers pivot toward energy storage

The Indiana transaction is part of a wider restructuring across North America’s battery sector.

Ford and SK On agreed last December to dissolve their BlueOval SK joint venture. The partnership was established in 2021 as part of a planned $11.4 billion investment in three U.S. battery plants.

Ford is now repurposing its Kentucky facility to manufacture 5-megawatt-hour energy storage batteries through its Ford Energy subsidiary. Large-scale batteries are seeing stronger demand as AI data centers increase electricity requirements.

Stellantis has also retreated from a battery partnership. In February, it agreed to sell its 49% stake in Canada’s NextStar Energy venture to LG Energy Solution for $100 million.

The transaction formed part of Stellantis’ broader $26 billion EV write-down and strategic reset.

LG Energy Solution plans to use the Windsor, Ontario facility for lithium iron phosphate energy storage batteries. The company is targeting more than 60 GWh of global ESS capacity in 2026. More than 50 GWh is expected to be located in North America.

LG Energy Solution has separately agreed to sell its stake in an Ohio battery plant to Honda Development and Manufacturing of America for $2.85 billion.

Energy storage offers a second market for battery capital

For executives and investors, these restructurings show how battery manufacturing strategies are adapting to changing demand rather than simply retreating from electrification.

Automakers are reducing exposure to expensive manufacturing ventures as EV adoption develops more slowly than earlier forecasts. Battery producers, meanwhile, are seeking alternative markets for factories and supply chains already under development.

Energy storage provides one of the clearest opportunities.

That shift could help preserve manufacturing capacity while supporting grid resilience, renewable integration and growing power demand from data centers.

Samsung SDI’s Indiana acquisition places that strategy inside a facility initially designed around the EV expansion. Its next phase reflects a broader change across North America: battery investment is increasingly serving both transportation and the power system.
