title: So Much Solar: Digging Into the List of Every US Power Plant That Went Online This Year
authors: Derek Harrison, Dan Gearino, Avril Silva
description:
Next is Trumbull Energy Center in Ohio, a 900-megawatt combined-cycle natural gas plant that is part of an expansion of natural gas power in the PJM Interconnection grid region, which covers parts of the Mid-Atlantic, Midwest and South.
Indeed, the story of power plant completions in the first half of 2026 was mainly about utility-scale solar and batteries.
Next were natural gas combustion turbines, with 22, and natural gas internal combustion engines, with 21.
A perpetual caveat: Power plant technologies have important differences to keep in mind when comparing generating capacity.
A 2.8-megawatt biomass power plant went online just a few miles from my house in Ohio, operated by the Columbus city government.
text:
It’s been a wild first half of the year in the U.S. power sector, with announcements of gigantic natural gas power plants and some long-awaited renewable energy projects coming online.

At times of rapid change, forecasting is difficult. So I feel a measure of comfort focusing on something concrete like the list of 368 utility-scale plants that began operation from January to June, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The group is dominated by utility-scale solar.

This is a top-heavy list, led by SunZia Wind South and SunZia Wind North in New Mexico, which went online this spring and are the largest wind farms in the country, with a combined generating capacity of 3,650 megawatts. SunZia has been in the works for about a decade and arrives at a time when U.S. onshore wind power development has dwindled for a host of reasons related to regulations and public opinion.

In other words, the SunZia is not indicative of an onshore wind-energy boom. It is more like an echo from a past boom.

Next is Trumbull Energy Center in Ohio, a 900-megawatt combined-cycle natural gas plant that is part of an expansion of natural gas power in the PJM Interconnection grid region, which covers parts of the Mid-Atlantic, Midwest and South.

The fourth-largest new power plant—if we’re counting SunZia as two—is Vineyard Wind, the offshore wind project near Massachusetts, which, much like SunZia, has been in development for a long time and whose completion doesn’t reveal much about future trends.

It isn’t until the fifth-largest new plant that we see one that is connected to the broader trend in the data: Green River Energy Center in Utah, with 800 megawatts that includes 400 megawatts of solar and 400 megawatts of batteries.

Indeed, the story of power plant completions in the first half of 2026 was mainly about utility-scale solar and batteries.

Utility-scale solar led in the number of projects coming online, with 207, followed by batteries, with 95.

Next were natural gas combustion turbines, with 22, and natural gas internal combustion engines, with 21.

Onshore wind had 9 projects.

Combined-cycle natural gas, despite having massive amounts of announced capacity in development, had just 3 projects that went online. The high tide of new gas plants won’t arrive for another few years.

If we look at projects in terms of generating capacity, utility-scale solar led with 11,458 megawatts, followed by batteries, 8,207 megawatts, and then onshore wind, mostly because of the SunZia projects, with 5,473 megawatts.

The three largest types of natural gas plants added a total of 2,707 megawatts of new capacity.

Small-scale solar, including rooftop solar, is not part of this database.

A perpetual caveat: Power plant technologies have important differences to keep in mind when comparing generating capacity. The most obvious one is that solar doesn’t produce power at night. Another is that many gas plants only run a few days or weeks per year, when they’re needed to handle peak demand.

What do these numbers tell us? I asked Eric Gimon, a senior fellow at Energy Innovation, a San Francisco-based think tank.

Gimon explained that the bulk of new projects are small and mid-size utility-scale solar. They are not attention-grabbing. But they’re almost everywhere. Many of the solar projects are paired with batteries.

“These kinds of smaller-size projects are just easier to build, and the site possibilities are much more diverse and easy to find,” he said.

Now, let’s look at the new power plants in terms of where they were built. Three states account for about half of the country’s new generating capacity: Texas, New Mexico and Arizona.

Texas was the leader, with a power mix that leaned more heavily on batteries and gas than other states. The leading category in Texas was batteries, with 3,067 megawatts, followed by utility-scale solar, with 2,311 megawatts, and then natural gas combustion turbines or natural gas internal combustion engines, with 1,154 megawatts.

Texas’ policies have prioritized gas and battery plant construction to help bolster the power grid’s reliability at times of high demand.

Also, Texas illustrates how challenging the market is for new onshore wind. The state is the national leader in onshore wind, but brought no new projects online in the first half of the year.

One of Gimon’s takeaways is that the first half of 2026 is that we’re firmly in the era of utility-scale solar, with batteries playing a supporting role.

“The real underlying workhorse is solar plus battery,” he said.

Some other observations from this data:

Illinois ranked first in the number of new utility-scale solar projects, with 36, ahead of California, with 22, and Texas, with 16. Illinois’ projects tended to be on the small side, which is why it could lead in the number of projects but barely cracked the top 10 in overall generating capacity coming online. This is policy-driven and shows that state laws encouraging small and medium-size solar are leading to completed projects.

The “other” category of power technologies almost always has something interesting, with some tiny plant that isn’t indicative of anything, but is probably a good story. One that caught my eye is the 4 megawatts of hydropower that went online in Dakota County, Minnesota, which is in the Minneapolis-St. Paul metro area. The project at the Byllesby Dam is a replacement of hydropower turbines that have operated on the Cannon River since 1910, and got local media coverage when the county government announced the project a few years ago.

A 2.8-megawatt biomass power plant went online just a few miles from my house in Ohio, operated by the Columbus city government. It’s fueled by methane captured from waste at a sewage-treatment plant. I was unaware of this project and now want to take a closer look.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

Looking ahead, the Energy Information Administration’s list of planned power plants shows that the utility-scale solar boom is likely to continue, and the final years of this decade are shaping up to bring a boom in natural gas power plants.

But it’s tough to pin down the size of the solar and gas booms because of uncertainty about many factors, including how much electricity demand will grow and what share of the growth will be driven by AI data centers.

So take some comfort in what we know for sure, which is the stuff that’s actually built, and realize that just about everything else comes with a question mark.

Other stories about the energy transition to take note of this week:

Here’s What the New Solar Tariffs Do, and What They Mean: The Trump administration last week announced new tariffs on imported polysilicon and related products used in solar panels, part of an attempt to impose a price floor to respond to what the administration has said is unfair competition. Julian Spector of Canary Media explains the new tariffs and how they fit into the history of the push and pull between reliance on inexpensive imports and policymakers’ efforts to help U.S.-based solar manufacturers compete.

Sunrun Focuses on Direct Sales Amid Larger Market Challenges: Sunrun, the country’s largest rooftop solar provider, reported disappointing second-quarter financial results as the company deals with a slowdown in rooftop solar and is trying to shift its business to focus less on sales through affiliates, as Brian Martucci reports for Utility Dive. Sunrun’s sales were affected by the bankruptcy of Freedom Forever, a partner company that does installations.

Amazon’s Plans to Use Texas Gas Plant at Odds With Climate Commitments: Amazon has confirmed that it plans to be the primary user of a proposed 7.6-gigawatt natural gas power plant in Texas, which would be one of the largest of its type in the world, as Hiroku Tabuchi reports for The New York Times. The company, which plans to use the plant to power a data center, has said this major expansion into gas power does not affect the company’s commitment to reach net-zero emissions by 2040, but it’s not clear how this is possible. We wouldn’t know of Amazon’s involvement in the gas plant if not for reporting from Michael Thomas of the market intelligence firm Cleanview, who has used satellite images, government filings and general sleuthing to track the growth of data centers and their power plants.

The Offshore Wind Bust Is Leaving Workers Behind: Building trades spent years preparing to spend at least a generation building offshore wind farms but have now been abandoned by U.S. policies hostile to development, as my colleague Ajani Stella reports. The scale of the reversal is shocking, with billions of dollars in investment and thousands of jobs vanishing in the face of obstruction from the Trump administration.

title: A call for power: energy poverty vs data centres | SEI - Stockholm Environment Institute
description:
Regardless of the technical solutions put in place, Sweden is continually expected to see higher and more volatile electricity prices.
This has to do with increasing energy use in northern Sweden, driven in part by data centres, and with electricity generation across northern Europe becoming more weather-dependent.
The establishment of new data centres has expanded over the past years as cold climate, access to land and renewable electricity are drawing these massive infrastructures to Sweden.
Electricity prices also remain relatively low on average, but with sharp regional and seasonal peaks, often coinciding with when households’ energy demand for heating is the highest.
Fears of continuing price increases surge alongside debates on the governmental subsidies to data centres, enacted through electricity tax reliefs of around 97% .
text:
As an energy poverty researcher, I usually try to schedule interviews during winter, assuming people are more willing to talk when cold homes and high bills are top of mind. But it is the end of June when we talk on the phone. He has not forgotten the electricity bills that exceeded his pension in February. And there is an election coming up.

Households across the country are increasingly discontented as the Swedish electricity system struggles with capacity shortages, regional imbalances, and tangible price peaks. Regardless of the technical solutions put in place, Sweden is continually expected to see higher and more volatile electricity prices. This has to do with increasing energy use in northern Sweden, driven in part by data centres, and with electricity generation across northern Europe becoming more weather-dependent. Both put higher demand on user flexibility to maintain balance on increasingly strained grids during both short-term and long-term moments of scarcity .

Swedish households are adapting: between 2015–2024, Swedish households had the 3rd highest reductions in energy use among EU member states (-7%). But despite this, and despite still having relatively low electricity prices, energy poverty increased more rapidly in Sweden than in any other EU member state between 2021–2025, with a more than 300% increase in number of households unable to keep their homes adequately warm (from around 3% to 10% of households).

Nontheless, Sweden is still, from the outside, seen as a haven for electricity access. The establishment of new data centres has expanded over the past years as cold climate, access to land and renewable electricity are drawing these massive infrastructures to Sweden. Electricity prices also remain relatively low on average, but with sharp regional and seasonal peaks, often coinciding with when households’ energy demand for heating is the highest. Some researchers are calling this rapid expansion of digital infrastructure “digital colonialism ”, referring to the way important assets, such as land and electricity, are being distributed without due democratic processes and with limited local benefits.

The cell reception is quite poor on his end, and at times we have a hard time hearing each other. But the man on the phone’s words echo many of the same fears and frustrations that I have seen online. In different forums, people are raging about the establishment of these energy-intensive facilities that are adding further unbalanced power struggles to an already volatile grid. Fears of continuing price increases surge alongside debates on the governmental subsidies to data centres, enacted through electricity tax reliefs of around 97% . Tech giants are thus granted both political and material advantages in accessing electricity, while households are left to manage the price volatility of an increasingly strained grid. Local businesses that are not granted the same subsidies as the international data centres might also struggle to make ends meet, potentially leading to what some researchers call “energy gentrification ” where unfair struggles for electricity on a strained grid push away smaller and local businesses.

After telling me about how the energy efficiency investments he has made have not been enough to reduce his stress around electricity costs, the man on the phone mentions the promise of 30 000 jobs as Facebook (now Meta) set up in Luleå, and the outcome of merely 56 employees . He says that we are all being fooled. While scholars argue that we could create more jobs with less energy use in a care economy – one where the energy and CO2 intensity of paid labour is reduced by employing a larger share of the population in healthcare, care, education, and social services – data centres are rushing in the opposite direction: maximizing energy use, minimizing jobs (at facilities and beyond through the AI boom they enable). For anyone interested in a transformative sustainable transition – one that fundamentally redirects the values of our economies – this development is not only concerning, but detrimental.

We know that underconsumption and overconsumption of energy are connected, literally linked through cords in the ground and in the sky, yet we rarely consider how they could be mutually addressed. The reason for this is, of course, that it remains unpopular to talk about the reality of energy demand, let alone the potential limits of demand. We avoid the daunting question: “what is energy for ?” As the number of energy-poor households is rapidly increasing in Sweden, I see through my research not only how political distrust is growing, but how distrust in the energy system’s ability to provide for them is growing as well. To the question “what is energy for?”, they are receiving a clear message: not for them.

People are gearing up with back-up generators, preparing to move into trailers, and keeping energy inefficient holes in the floor to store food. The ability to go off-grid is not only useful in case of power cuts, but also when prices are high. It is both protection and a privilege, and one that is far from available for everyone.

As we are about to hang up, the man on the phone emphasizes that he has done everything in his power to keep his energy costs down, but it has not been enough. I contemplate how to respond, but before I get the chance to say anything, the line breaks up. Can you hear me? he asks.

Can you hear me?

text:
Battery manufacturer Samsung SDI announced that it has agreed to acquire General Motors’ entire 49.99% stake in their SynergyCells electric vehicle (EV) battery joint venture project, with plans to shift the plant from an EV battery focus to address growing demand for broader energy storage systems.

The companies initially signed an agreement in August 2024 to establish the $3.5 billion battery manufacturing joint venture, establishing a plant in New Carlisle, Indiana, expected to have an initial production capacity of 27GWh up to 36GWh, and a production target of 2027. The facility was expected to produce NCA-based high-performance nickel-rich prismatic batteries for use in GM electric vehicles.

The companies said that the ownership change was made in consideration of market changes since the joint venture was announced, including the slower-than-expected growth of electric vehicle demand.

The acquisition will make the New Carlisle facility Samsung’s first wholly owned battery manufacturing plant in North America. Samsung said that it plans to utilize the plant for producing high-tech batteries for use in various applications, with an initial focus on producing batteries for energy storage systems (ESS), responding to rapidly growing demand in the U.S. ESS market. The plant could also potentially produce prismatic battery cells jointly developed with GM in the future, the companies added.

As part of the transaction, Samsung SDI and GM also signed a new agreement to jointly develop next-generation prismatic battery cells for potential future EV applications. The new batteries will be designed to provide high energy density and fast-charging capabilities.

Samsung said:

“While reflecting recent market changes, this acquisition decision is to continue the strategic partnership with GM. We will continue our commitment to an electrified future with the partner, while utilizing the plant to proactively respond to the fast-growing ESS market in the U.S.”

title: MIT Just Gutted The Most Popular Argument Against EVs - Carscoops
description:
A new study out of MIT appears to completely crush the claim that EVs simply move pollution from the tailpipe to a smokestack.
It’s that battery-electric vehicles beat comparable gas cars on lifecycle emissions across the U.S., including where electricity still comes heavily from fossil fuels.
Published in Environmental Research Letters, the MIT-led research first reported by InsideEVs found that EVs cut emissions by 40 to 60 percent in most locations.
What The Study Doesn’t Claim Before the angry comments come in, though, it’s worth being clear about what this study does and doesn’t say.
Even with the country’s most carbon-intensive electricity mix, the researchers found battery EVs do not increase lifecycle emissions compared to combustion vehicles.
text:
Well, there’s no way that this information will be controversial at all. A new study out of MIT appears to completely crush the claim that EVs simply move pollution from the tailpipe to a smokestack. The analysis tackled the variables usually missing from that argument, like where drivers live, what powers their grid, what they drive, how far they travel, and even the weather.

Its conclusion isn’t that EVs are perfect. It’s that battery-electric vehicles beat comparable gas cars on lifecycle emissions across the U.S., including where electricity still comes heavily from fossil fuels.

Published in Environmental Research Letters, the MIT-led research first reported by InsideEVs found that EVs cut emissions by 40 to 60 percent in most locations. That’s not cherry-picking statistics either. The researchers considered vehicle and battery manufacturing, fuel and electricity production, regional grids, local temperatures, vehicle types, and how people actually drive. Re-read that maybe, because that’s a dearth of variables and considerations.

Read: Should Fossil Fuel Ads Be Banned Like Tobacco

The reason is pretty simple. Internal-combustion engines waste an enormous amount of the fuel they burn as heat. EVs lose energy too, including at the power plant and during transmission, but electric motors are so much more efficient that they retain a massive advantage even after those losses are counted. A dirty grid narrows the gap. It doesn’t magically erase it.

What The Study Doesn’t Claim

Before the angry comments come in, though, it’s worth being clear about what this study does and doesn’t say. It is a lifecycle greenhouse-gas analysis, so battery production is already in the equation. But it doesn’t claim EVs have no environmental cost, nor does it settle every issue people may cram under the word “green.”

Mining, water use, local air pollution, labor practices, battery recycling, and grid reliability all deserve their own scrutiny. Like every model, its results also depend on assumptions about battery life, manufacturing, charging behavior, and future electricity mixes. Those details can affect the size of an EV’s advantage from place to place.

Still, the core finding holds. Even with the country’s most carbon-intensive electricity mix, the researchers found battery EVs do not increase lifecycle emissions compared to combustion vehicles. That’s a remarkably direct answer to the smokestack argument.

The Grid Only Gets Cleaner

title: Achieving Environmentally Friendly “Green” Dialysis Takes a Village
description:
In the past 4 years, there has been growing adoption of green dialysis initiatives in the United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, and many other countries, according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) controversies conference report on Green dialysis: environmentally sustainable care, growth, and innovation.
The Role of the Medical Community Green dialysis isn’t a single fix.
Nephrologists should also push procurement decisions, both their own and their institution’s, toward equipment and products that use less water, energy, and packaging.

The aim is to reduce waste and unnecessary resource use without compromising safe and effective dialysis,” Dr Stuard said.
text:
In the past 4 years, there has been growing adoption of green dialysis initiatives in the United Kingdom, European Union, Australia, and many other countries, according to the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) controversies conference report on Green dialysis: environmentally sustainable care, growth, and innovation. However, significant barriers still exist. The report cites an urgent need for new technologies and changes in models of care.

Participants included physicians, nurses, patients, and engineers who examined how existing hemodialysis (in-center and at home) and peritoneal dialysis practices might be optimized to promote environmental sustainability.

The report states that key areas for innovation include the development of more efficient water purification systems and energy-saving equipment in hemodialysis (HD). Point-of-care dialysate generation for peritoneal dialysis (PD) could significantly reduce carbon emissions associated with transport. Across both modalities, the introduction of novel bioplastics or other strategies to reduce harmful disposable materials could greatly mitigate the environmental impact.

The Role of the Medical Community

Green dialysis isn’t a single fix. It’s a shift in mindset, applied across many small and large decisions. “It requires staff education, standardized monitoring, and transparent reporting. Broader integration of sustainability into routine dialysis care represents a critical opportunity to reduce the environmental footprint of kidney replacement therapy without compromising patient safety or treatment efficacy,” said Jennifer Flythe, MD, professor of medicine and chief of the University of North Carolina (UNC) division of nephrology and hypertension, Chapel Hill, North Carolina. “For nephrologists, that starts with recognizing environmental sustainability as a genuine domain of care quality, on par with safety and effectiveness, not a side project.”

In clinical practice, this involves personalizing dialysis initiation and considering incremental dialysis where clinically appropriate. Dr Flythe said clinicians should question routine high dialysate flow rates (Qd) that offer little clinical benefit. Nephrologists should also push procurement decisions, both their own and their institution’s, toward equipment and products that use less water, energy, and packaging. “It also means becoming comfortable citing the evidence. Many green changes, like lowering Qd to 500-600 mL/min or adopting incremental PD, are backed by outcome data showing no compromise in care, which should reassure clinicians who worry sustainability efforts might mean cutting corners,” Dr Flythe said.

Rupesh Raina, MD, who is the co-chair of the International Pediatric Nephrology Association (IPNA) green dialysis working group and a member of the International Society of Nephrology (ISN) dialysis working group, noted that dialysis is one of the most resource-intensive therapies in medicine. From water and energy use to plastics and transportation resources, millions of patients on dialysis will utilize enormous amounts of resources over their lifetimes.

He said dialysis organizations can quantify and publicly report metrics on their environmental impact as they do with infections and clinical outcomes. “Green dialysis starts with awareness. Clinicians can begin by tracking and assessing opportunities to decrease waste, conserve water and energy, minimize unnecessary laboratory tests and supplies, and encourage evidence-based medicine that limits over-utilization of healthcare resources without negatively affecting outcomes,” said Dr Raina, an adult and pediatric nephrologist at Akron Children’s Hospital and Cleveland Clinic Akron General Medical Center, Akron Ohio. “Over time, green dialysis should be ingrained into daily clinical decision-making just like we consider cost, access, quality, and other patient-centered measures when striving to provide the best care possible.”

He said clinicians can practice evidence-based medicine, minimize waste, support home dialysis and telehealth options when feasible, and promote early initiation of chronic kidney disease management and transplantation. “Educating patients about medication adherence, vascular access preservation, home dialysis when applicable, and sustainability efforts within their dialysis organization are also crucial. Industry partners can aid in this effort by developing recyclable materials, biodegradable components, more efficient dialysis machines, and greener manufacturing processes,” Dr Raina said.

Dialysis patients, providers, and industry leaders are not the only ones who can drive environmental sustainability in kidney care. “Researchers, professional societies, and lawmakers play a critical role as well. By working together to advance green dialysis innovation without compromising patient safety and clinical outcomes, we can make sustainability an inherent part of providing exceptional care to our patients rather than treating it as an inconvenient afterthought,” said Dr Raina.

Mihran Naljayan, MD, who is chief medical officer of clinical transformation, home modalities and pediatrics at DaVita, said it is important to call attention to this issue for a host of reasons. “As nephrologists, we can work together to adopt and encourage intentional behaviors like prioritizing water and energy efficiency in daily operations and ongoing education on initiatives like facility recycling programs for non-medical waste, reducing general water and energy use, and other sustainable practices to support patients with their care,” said Dr Naljayan.

At DaVita, they have started a new focus with 3 main initiatives to help offset the environmental impact of delivering life-sustaining care. One is water conservation: DaVita saved hundreds of millions of gallons of water over the past 5 years through initiatives to reduce water consumption. “Another is energy efficiency, including updates like LED lighting, modernized water heaters, and advanced HVAC heat pump technology to optimize energy use while keeping patients comfortable. We also have a focus on renewable energy, which led to the launch of our first ever net-zero dialysis center in Georgia.” Dr Naljayan said.

Geovana Basso, MD, who is head of medical affairs at Vantive, a vital organ therapy company with a 70-year legacy of kidney care innovation in Deerfield, Illinois, said it is also necessary to view green dialysis through the lens of health care sustainability, which is the capacity of a health system to deliver care over time. “This requires measuring health outcomes relative to social, financial, and environmental costs,” Dr Basso said. “Because sustainable kidney care requires progress across clinical practice, technology, infrastructure, policy, and patient engagement, continued collaboration among clinicians, academic societies, providers, manufacturers, patients, researchers, and policymakers will be important.”

Patients’ Role

For patients, engagement looks different but is just as important. Dr Flythe said patients are the ones who live daily with the volume of supplies and waste that dialysis generates, and the report specifically highlights how patient perspectives shaped the conference’s conclusions. “Patients being treated with home therapies can participate in recycling programs where available, such as peritoneal dialysis bag recycling schemes now operating in several countries, ask their care teams about incremental or personalized prescriptions, and importantly have a voice in shared decision-making about modality and treatment frequency, where environmental impact is now recognized as a legitimate factor alongside clinical suitability and personal preference,” Dr Flythe said.

Patient Safety Remains a Top Priority

Both clinicians and their patients need to understand that the green changes are meant to be additive to care, not subtractive. The report repeatedly frames sustainability as something to pursue without compromising, and ideally while improving, patient outcomes. Stefano Stuard, MD, PhD, senior vice president and global clinical officer for hemodiafiltration (HDF) at Fresenius Medical Care, said before adopting new green products it is important to look at their effects on care quality and patient safety.

“Nephrologists and clinical staff should be involved in decisions about equipment, supplies, and clinical practices. A product or process should not be adopted simply because it is described as environmentally friendly. It must also be safe, reliable, supported by evidence, and capable of consistently meeting the required standards of care,” said Dr Stuard. “Meaningful progress will require health care providers, manufacturers, policymakers, and the wider kidney care community to work together. Environmental impact should become part of the routine assessment of dialysis care, alongside treatment quality, patient experience, and clinical outcomes.”

He said awareness of this issue is also increasing among clinicians, dialysis providers, manufacturers, patients, and policymakers. However, the environmental impact of a technology cannot be assessed on the basis of a single feature. Its entire life cycle, including manufacturing, transportation, clinical use, and disposal, must be considered. A product that reduces transportation or waste, for example, may require more energy or materials during production. Cost, availability, and feasibility in different health care settings must also be taken into account.

Dialysis facilities can reduce their environmental footprint by using water and energy more efficiently, improving waste separation, reducing unnecessary packaging, and better managing supplies and transportation. Dr Stuard said facilities should regularly monitor environmental indicators, including water and energy consumption and the amount and type of waste generated. These measures should be integrated into continuous quality improvement and supported by clinic-level benchmarking to identify variation, set realistic targets, share effective practices, and track progress. “Across Fresenius Medical Care’s NephroCare network in Europe, water consumption, energy consumption, and waste generation are already included in the Balanced Scorecard and routinely monitored at clinic, country, and regional levels. Performance is reviewed monthly, and progressively more ambitious annual targets are set to drive continuous reductions in resource consumption and waste generation,” Dr Stuard said.

“Changes to equipment, materials, treatment processes, or facility operations must be evaluated to ensure that treatment adequacy, infection control, water quality, and access to care are maintained. The aim is to reduce waste and unnecessary resource use without compromising safe and effective dialysis,” Dr Stuard said.

Innovations on the Horizon

Dr Raina said in recent years there have been promising innovations and technology improvements in water purification, heat recovery, low-energy dialysis machines, telehealth monitoring, and home-based therapies. “Point-of-care dialysate generation for peritoneal dialysis and research into more environmentally friendly packaging and biomaterials also has the potential to revolutionize how we think about the carbon footprint of kidney replacement therapy,” said Dr Raina. “While several of these technologies are beginning to be used clinically, broader implementation has been slow due to regulatory barriers, infrastructure investments, reimbursement challenges, and lack of universally accepted definitions and reporting standards for sustainability metrics.”

The dialysis industry continues to rely heavily on single-use plastics and transportation of large amounts of supplies, especially in-center hemodialysis. “So, while I am very encouraged by the progress we have made over the last several years, we still have a long way to go until dialysis can be considered sustainable,” said Dr Raina.

Most transformative technology is still early-stage, including heat energy recovery from dialysis effluent, and shorter bloodlines. “Centralized acid delivery, reverse osmosis reject water reuse, and optimized dialysate flow rates are practical, available-today interventions with demonstrated water, energy, and cost-savings. So, on the operational and clinical practice side, meaningful progress is achievable now, and some centers are already doing it,” said Dr Flythe.

The report notes that even promising ideas like bioplastics aren’t automatically greener once you account for land use, water use, and the underdeveloped recycling and composting infrastructure needed to handle them. Currently, there is a lack of standardized environmental metrics and life-cycle-assessment methods. Additionally, dialysis facilities restrict dialyzer reuse or on-site waste sterilization in many jurisdictions. Another major barrier is that reimbursement and procurement systems don’t yet reward sustainable choices.

Taking a Step-by-Step Approach

The report calls for applying a waste hierarchy (prevention first, then reuse, recycling, recovery, and disposal only as a last resort), and adopting “life cycle thinking” to evaluate any change before adopting it. It is important to not just look at its effect in the treatment room, but its impact from raw materials through disposal. Dr Flythe said US facilities can start with low-risk, well-evidenced changes, such as adjusting dialysate flow rates toward 500-600 mL/min where clinically appropriate, which shows minimal impact on dialysis adequacy.

She also recommends auditing and optimizing reverse osmosis system settings and disinfection schedules. It’s important to improve waste segregation, she added, so material isn’t defaulted into costlier and environmentally burdensome hazardous-waste streams. “Facilities considering capital investments should prioritize reverse osmosis systems and dialysis machines with demonstrated lower water and energy use, and should evaluate whether centralized acid concentrate delivery is feasible, since it reduces plastic waste and emissions substantially, especially in larger units,” Dr Flythe said.

Clinicians can incorporate personalized and incremental dialysis prescriptions where survival and quality-of-life data support it. When having a shared decision-making conversation about modality it may be that home therapies carry a lower carbon footprint, though that shifts some burden (waste, utility costs) to patients, so this needs to be discussed transparently.

Patient safety remains the non-negotiable constraint throughout. The report is careful to distinguish deliberate, evidence-based, patient-centered adjustments (like incremental dialysis) from resource-driven corner-cutting, and it notes that some higher-impact ideas (dialyzer reuse, peritoneal dialysis drain-line reuse, on-site hazardous waste treatment) are currently restricted by US and international regulation because the safety evidence needs further development.

name: IRA Tax Credits
title: Incentives and tax policy: Between growth, fairness and global collaboration
description:
With the increasing use of incentives in industrial and political policy, participants from academia, business and civil society examined what an effective, transparent and legitimate incentive policy could look like.
Industrial policy is back, and incentives are at its core.
The introduction of Pillar Two has altered the landscape of global tax competition.
Yet participants noted that it does not distinguish between “good” and “bad” incentives — for example, between renewable energy tax credits and fossil-fuel subsidies.
Participants noted that in competitive markets, firms prioritize overall conditions — skills, infrastructure and regulatory clarity — above tax incentives alone.
text:
KPMG International hosted a virtual roundtable in November 2025 as part of the Global Responsible Tax Program to explore how governments and businesses can design incentive policies that balance economic growth, fairness and global collaboration.

The discussion took place against a backdrop of shifting industrial strategies, tightening fiscal space and the implementation of global minimum tax rules. With the increasing use of incentives in industrial and political policy, participants from academia, business and civil society examined what an effective, transparent and legitimate incentive policy could look like.

The conversation was held under the Chatham House Rule and included perspectives from multiple regions and sectors. The write-up below summarizes the personal views expressed and does not necessarily represent the position of any particular organization, including KPMG.

Industrial policy is back, and incentives are at its core.

Participants noted that industrial strategy has re-emerged worldwide as governments use fiscal levers to secure supply chains, attract investment and accelerate green transitions. The US Inflation Reduction Act, China’s extensive fiscal support (estimated at over 4 percent of gross domestic product, according to the International Monetary Fund in August 2025), and the EU’s relaxation of state-aid rules are reshaping the global policy environment.

This, several argued, marks a shift from the liberal orthodoxy of neutral tax systems towards a more interventionist era. As one participant observed, “the use of incentives as a policy lever to attract investment is at an all-time high.” Yet the asymmetry in fiscal capacity between large and small economies risks widening disparities: wealthier countries can afford aggressive subsidies, while others must rely on limited or less flexible tax tools.

The discussion highlighted growing trade tensions arising from this imbalance. Some feared that without global coordination, disputes over subsidies could increasingly spill into tariff measures — echoing earlier trade frictions between Japan and the United States in the 1980s.

Effectiveness lies in clarity, stability and purpose.

A central theme was the need to distinguish effective incentives from wasteful or distortionary ones. Participants emphasized three criteria:

Clear objectives and measurable outcomes: Incentives should address specific market failures (such as under-investment in research & development (R&D) or green technology) and include evaluation mechanisms or clawbacks if outcomes are not met.

Certainty and stability: Firms can plan and respond only when policy frameworks remain consistent. Volatility, such as recent UK reforms to R&D credits, undermines behavior change and investor confidence.

Transparency and equal access: Incentives should be rule-based and openly administered, avoiding “sweetheart deals” or opaque discretionary awards.

Several participants stressed that well-targeted incentives genuinely influence decisions when companies can “write them into budgets” — but many schemes simply become windfalls. Others in the group added that full expensing and other timing adjustments are often misunderstood as stimulus measures, when they may just neutralize existing distortions.

The group also debated whether incentives should operate through the tax system at all. Some argued that direct grants or expenditure-based subsidies can be more transparent and efficient; others favored tax mechanisms for their broad reach. The consensus: Incentives should be judged not by form but by function — whether they demonstrably change behavior and serve a public purpose.

International coordination is evolving, but legitimacy gaps remain.

The introduction of Pillar Two has altered the landscape of global tax competition. By imposing a 15 percent minimum rate, it restricts the space for low-tax strategies and certain profit-based incentives. Yet participants noted that it does not distinguish between “good” and “bad” incentives — for example, between renewable energy tax credits and fossil-fuel subsidies.

This bluntness, combined with differences in administrative capacity, risks entrenching inequities. Developing economies may find themselves constrained by minimum-tax rules while wealthier nations shift towards direct subsidies outside those frameworks. Several pointed to emerging middle-income economies caught between these models — too fiscally constrained to match the US or EU, yet too developed to benefit from concessional treatment.

Participants discussed Europe’s move towards recommendation-based guidance under its Green Deal Industrial Plan, reflecting both ambition and political limits. Smaller member states expressed frustration that looser state-aid rules overwhelmingly favor large economies with deeper pockets. As one participant observed, “It will be the richer countries that can afford to take advantage.”

Stability is the ultimate incentive.

Across sectors, participants agreed that credibility matters more than generosity. Multinationals emphasized that unpredictable or short-lived incentives cannot be relied upon in investment planning. Several noted that temporary measures such as accelerated depreciation can provide useful upfront cash-flow benefits, particularly for smaller firms, but offer limited advantages to large, listed companies that already have access to finance and see the benefit reversed through deferred tax effects. For these firms, smaller but permanent tax changes are often more valuable. This “horses for courses” dynamic means governments may spend heavily on temporary incentives that do little to influence investment by large companies, when more modest, enduring measures could be better targeted and more effective.

Participants noted that in competitive markets, firms prioritize overall conditions — skills, infrastructure and regulatory clarity — above tax incentives alone. Yet once other factors align, certainty around incentives can tip decisions. The volatility of the UK’s innovation regime was cited as a cautionary example: repeated rule changes and complexity have eroded trust, making the system “more hostile to business and innovation.”

The group also discussed how different firms experience incentives differently. Large corporates value predictable frameworks; smaller firms rely on refundable or cash-based reliefs to manage liquidity. Designing stable policy requires recognizing these distinct realities.

title: Ford says it converted Louisville plant for Fathom EV work within a year - The Detroit News
description:
Ford Motor Co. on Thursday said it's on track to launch the Fathom all-electric midsize truck next year, after converting Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky from a gas-vehicle plant into a fully electric facility in under a year.
It's the first plant to adopt Ford's new Universal Electric Vehicle Production System, which adopts a three-pronged assembly tree over the Henry Ford-invented moving assembly line to ease the manufacturing process.
The highly automated manufacturing process will help Louisville Assembly be able to build vehicles a net 15% faster than its former products and will help Ford catch up to Chinese competitors and Tesla Inc. that have implemented similar structures to produce EVs, often at lower costs.
WiFi at the plant also has been upgraded to support software quality checks.
Louisville employees have joined engineering teams at Ford's New Model Product Development Center in Allen Park to prepare for launch of production as well.
text:
Ford Motor Co. on Thursday said it's on track to launch the Fathom all-electric midsize truck next year, after converting Louisville Assembly Plant in Kentucky from a gas-vehicle plant into a fully electric facility in under a year.

More equipment installation and quality verification will continue through the end of the year at the former home of the Escape and Lincoln Corsair crossovers as the plant prepares for a first-quarter launch of prototype production of the sub-$30,000 Fathom. It's the first plant to adopt Ford's new Universal Electric Vehicle Production System, which adopts a three-pronged assembly tree over the Henry Ford-invented moving assembly line to ease the manufacturing process.

The highly automated manufacturing process will help Louisville Assembly be able to build vehicles a net 15% faster than its former products and will help Ford catch up to Chinese competitors and Tesla Inc. that have implemented similar structures to produce EVs, often at lower costs. WiFi at the plant also has been upgraded to support software quality checks.

Louisville employees have joined engineering teams at Ford's New Model Product Development Center in Allen Park to prepare for launch of production as well.

Ford announced a $2 billion investment into the Louisville plant in October 2025 to retool the facility for production using the new, streamlined process, which it said would use shorter wiring harnesses, fewer and lighter parts and single-piece aluminum unicastings, among other things, to deliver quicker assembly with more flexibility and profitability.

name: Clean Energy
title: Fix high power bills by ditching bad policies - Carolina Journal
description:
My colleague Kelly Lester and I just released a report titled “Energy Poverty in North Carolina: Securing Affordable, Reliable Power.” Block and Balsari’s op-ed opened with similar concerns to ours.
As our report states, “[w]hen electricity costs grow so burdensome as to force households to cut usage drastically, it takes a human toll in misery and even death.” Naturally, our recommendations address bad policies.
Because it requires replacing working, baseload power plants with expensive, unreliable new renewable facilities paid for by rate increases.
In recent years, North Carolina policymakers have elevated ideological goals in electricity policy.
The answer is to fix the state policies pushing unaffordable, unreliable electricity, not to use unaffordable power as an excuse to push unrelated policy wishes.
text:
USA Today recently published an article from two Harvard representatives concerning the life-and-death risks to workers of not being able to afford electricity. The News & Observer found it so compelling that the editors republished it on Aug. 5.

One author is Sharon Block, a former labor official for the Biden and Obama administrations and current executive director of Harvard’s “Center for Labor and a Just Economy.” The other is Dr. Sanchit Balsari, a Harvard associate professor of emergency medicine.

Block’s center for pro-union euphemism describes itself as “committed to reimagining the law and developing paradigm-shifting policy” and leads with “IT JUST SHOULDN’T BE THIS HARD … for working people to organize and bargain for adequate wages, better working conditions, and dignity in their workplaces.” Like the podiatrist who thinks the cure for a cold starts with better shoes, this background offers a clue to Block’s approach to energy policy.

My colleague Kelly Lester and I just released a report titled “Energy Poverty in North Carolina: Securing Affordable, Reliable Power.” Block and Balsari’s op-ed opened with similar concerns to ours. I was intrigued but ultimately disappointed.

“Workers may die in increased numbers because they can’t afford to stay cool,” they wrote. “This isn’t hyperbole. It’s a predictable consequence of policy choices that leave working Americans choosing between the cost of the cooling they need to recover from work in extreme heat and the costs of other necessities of life, like food, rent and health care.”

Just so. Electricity is indispensable. Higher power bills cause people in poverty to make dangerous trade-offs with other needs. Also, they are a consequence of bad policy choices, as we’ve warned for years. As our report states, “[w]hen electricity costs grow so burdensome as to force households to cut usage drastically, it takes a human toll in misery and even death.”

Naturally, our recommendations address bad policies. We seek to return state electricity policies to “strictly upholding the values of affordability and reliability … to protect households most at risk of energy poverty.”

Block and Balsari’s policy prescriptions, however, have nothing to say about why electricity rates are getting out of hand or how to rein them in. They treat soaring power bills as an unchangeable fact of life and propose living with them in ways that would appeal to labor unions. Here are the policy actions they propose:

Finalize a rule proposed by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration under the Biden administration to “mandate employer-provided heat protections”

Raise the minimum wage

Offer or expand utility assistance programs for workers

Work with unions and worker advocates to protect workers from heat

Heat protections are one thing, but with respect to making energy affordable, raising the minimum wage would not do a thing about why rates are on the rise. It also would affect only so many workers, many in a negative way. Years of economic research have reiterated that minimum-wage increases result in a net harm against the very people they are supposed to help by making it even harder for them to find jobs.

Likewise, utility assistance programs have their place, but they would also be topical solutions only for certain ratepayers and would not address the root cause of rising electricity rates.

Our solutions do, however. For example, we seek repeal of the Carbon Plan law. Why? Because it requires replacing working, baseload power plants with expensive, unreliable new renewable facilities paid for by rate increases.

We want the North Carolina Utilities Commission to compare the all-in costs of new power plants. Why? To ensure they choose the true lowest-cost resource mix.

We propose passing an “Only Pay for What You Get” Act. Why? So ratepayers are charged only for the reliable proportion of any new power facility, and the more unreliable it is, the more of its costs the utility’s shareholders would have to eat.

We call for repeal of the Clean Energy and Energy Efficiency Portfolio Standards. Why? Because they set aside part of a utility’s resource mix for politically favored “clean energy” sources without regard to affordability or reliability.

In recent years, North Carolina policymakers have elevated ideological goals in electricity policy. Affordability and reliability were not considered to be, in the words of Gov. Roy Cooper’s Clean Energy Plan, “[v]alues to prioritize going forward.” No wonder electricity is becoming unaffordable.

The answer is to fix the state policies pushing unaffordable, unreliable electricity, not to use unaffordable power as an excuse to push unrelated policy wishes.

title: How to own profit opportunity on your farm - Farm Progress
description:
But what we must move toward is recognizing farmers as successful businesspeople, as business leaders, and see that as an admirable attribute.
A new U-pick farm opened down the street from their Illinois home, and his wife wasted no time visiting to bring back a good haul of fresh vegetables.
Agricultural business management specialist Dave Kohl sees across surveys and statistics that the sweet spot for farm financial success is three to six revenue streams.
Paying close attention to basis and using options to set floors while holding on to upside price opportunity also is essential.
Let’s switch to being price (profit) makers and leaning into faith in our financial abilities to accompany our well-grounded faith.
text:
When we lean across the decades for the adages and aphorisms that sum up the financial state of farming, we nearly always land on those that strap farmers into an economic corner ruled by everybody but the folks working the land.

It’s favorites like John F. Kennedy in 1959: “The farmer is, after all, the only man in our economy who has to buy everything he buys at inflated retail, sell everything he sells at depressed wholesale, and pay the freight both ways.”

Then there’s the less well-known Wendell Berry conclusion about why some choose to farm: “Why do farmers farm, given their economic adversities on top of the many frustrations and difficulties normal to farming? And always the answer is: ‘Love. They must do it for love.’ ”

And nearly always, people speak of farming as a profession only for optimists, a business built on hope and of character as the most desirable attribute of farmers. And I can agree with all of them. But what we must move toward is recognizing farmers as successful businesspeople, as business leaders, and see that as an admirable attribute.

I’m reminded of a story an ag editor shared many years ago. A new U-pick farm opened down the street from their Illinois home, and his wife wasted no time visiting to bring back a good haul of fresh vegetables. She excitedly reported on her visit and finished with, “And he doesn’t even care whether he makes any money!”

Whoa.

Yet many of us can tell similar stories of such educational conversations in our families. In this moment, when we’re at the most tenuous time for our core row crops in the U.S. — between planting and harvest, when a single storm can crush our financial plan for the year, and we’ve done the bulk of what we can to make this crop profitable — it’s good to take a moment to look at what we can do better to improve a farm’s economic outlook. Not hope. Not even prayer (though I don’t think it hurts). And certainly not throwing up our hands and quoting JFK.

Here’s what we can do: Find a few things we can do a percent or two better. No need to overhaul the operation. No need to dive deep into a new enterprise. Just solid steps toward saving a nickel here and making another nickel there. Nickels, of course, because we no longer deal in pennies.

Here are a few things to consider:

Precision management. Ohio farmer Chad Kemp is using variable-rate fertilizer to cut his costs by 25% to 30% while maintaining yield. That’s a profitable move regardless of the price of inputs.

In Mike Wilson’s article, Kemp speaks specifically to fertilizer, but using precision software to plant and apply pesticides is also an investment that quickly pays dividends. The three generations managing Babb Farms in Windsor, Va., can speak to those advantages.

The Babbs use John Deere RowCommand with Section Control and ExactApply on their planters and sprayers. Using less, well, saves more. While many farmers use precision applications for pesticides and fertilizer, the Babbs also closely meter their seeding rate.

“When I say I put 140 pounds to the acre, I put 140 pounds to the acre,” Bryan Babb said.

Multiple revenue streams. Agricultural business management specialist Dave Kohl sees across surveys and statistics that the sweet spot for farm financial success is three to six revenue streams. As we’ve written about that, farmers have asked: What counts as a revenue stream?

A revenue stream could be an additional crop. At Cardinal Farms in Indiana, Brooks and Brandon Cardinal grow watermelons at commercial quantities, a crop started by their father.

For the Babbs, the additional revenue streams include a field-to-shirt cotton T-shirt company and dog breeding.

That additional revenue stream can also simply be adding a higher premium to an existing crop. Indiana farmer Tom McKinney grows for seed, and the buyer also pays him to store that crop until delivery. The Babbs grow peanuts on a certified seed contract and added edible soybeans to their crop mix.

Marketing tools. Paying close attention to basis and using options to set floors while holding on to upside price opportunity also is essential. Markets are tough to navigate. But you — and any farmer still in business today — are tougher.

The bottom line is, of course, the bottom line. But that’s a business bottom line and a cultural bottom line. That cultural thing means changing up the axioms we hold closest to a few that lend the right attitude to the passion of our aptitude. Let’s switch to being price (profit) makers and leaning into faith in our financial abilities to accompany our well-grounded faith. Toward that end, what do you think about internalizing and prioritizing this axiom:

“Agriculture is our wisest pursuit, because it will, in the end, contribute most to real wealth, good morals and happiness.” — Thomas Jefferson

name: North Carolina American Energy
title: Guest column: Data centers done right can drive grid modernization and energy affordability
authors: JOHN TRULUCK and WILL WILLIAMS Guest columnists, JOHN TRULUCK, WILL WILLIAMS Guest columnists
description:
You have no doubt heard that the rising cost of energy is being driven by data centers.
Data centers, if properly located, can bring much needed grid modernization and energy infrastructure to areas in the state that need it.
For example, AI can identify and unlock unused capacity on existing power lines and thereby more efficiently use existing energy infrastructure.
Some nevertheless argue against data centers of any kind and refuse to acknowledge the daily functions that data centers support.
Finally, there are ways to address the increased demand for energy and the costs of the energy infrastructure.
text:
You have no doubt heard that the rising cost of energy is being driven by data centers.

But the truth is data centers done right can share the costs of modernizing South Carolina’s energy infrastructure and help lower rates for all customers, tap into existing resources, play a critical role in our nation’s defense, place the state at the forefront of the modern technology revolution, and bring critical capital investments and high-skilled, well-paid jobs without causing additional traffic or strains on our roadways.

In reality, South Carolina’s economic growth is multi-layered. The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) ranked South Carolina No. 1 in the nation in economic growth and among the highest in personal income growth, with a Gross Domestic Product (GDP) annual increase of 1.7%. Indeed, Gov. Henry McMaster and the South Carolina Department of Commerce released the 2025 industry recruitment results on Jan. 14, 2026, and from January to December 2025, South Carolina announced a total capital investment of $9.12 billion, representing the third-highest year for industry recruitment on record and more than 8,100 new jobs. Nearly half of that investment ($4.9 billion) and 57 new high-paying jobs were commitments by two data centers who did not receive any state discretionary incentives.

But, we don’t need the BEA study to tell us what we know to be true. We all see the growth in our state every day. When we drive on the highways and roads, we see major manufacturing facilities that are the backbone of our economy like BMW, Mercedes-Benz Vans, Volvo; new industries like Scout Motors, e-VAC Magnetics, Isuzu North America Corporation; and many new housing developments. Simply put, the Palmetto State has more people and businesses locating to our beautiful state.

This economic growth in turn requires electric and gas utilities to meet the demand for power. Meeting this demand means building new generation and transmission facilities, which are expensive.

Data centers, if properly located, can bring much needed grid modernization and energy infrastructure to areas in the state that need it. Everyone benefits from grid modernization. Locating data centers on brownfield sites (unused or abandoned properties) should also be encouraged.

With appropriate and fair safeguards, a data center that locates in an economically disadvantaged area of the state and pays for the transmission lines and associated facilities used to serve it, can be a net positive. The existing energy infrastructure is modernized and financially supported by the data center, paving the way for other businesses offering employment opportunities to locate in the area. Tax revenues increase. And, with proper cost allocation, the energy burden is lowered across all customers, driving rates down.

Additionally, artificial intelligence (AI), which is essential to the nation’s national security, can be a tool to make the grid smarter and more efficient. For example, AI can identify and unlock unused capacity on existing power lines and thereby more efficiently use existing energy infrastructure.

Some nevertheless argue against data centers of any kind and refuse to acknowledge the daily functions that data centers support. Data centers serve as the backbone powering our digital life. Without these facilities, online features like social media apps, AI algorithms, GPS navigation, cloud banking and smart personal assistants/smart home assistants such as Siri and Alexa could not function.

These projects are critical to our national security, which is often a positive that has been overlooked. With President Donald Trump’s “Winning the AI Race: America’s AI Action Plan” released in July 2025, our country has placed an emphasis on growing this critical industry by accelerating innovation, removing regulatory barriers, investing in key infrastructure for these sites and protecting U.S. tech from theft, reducing risks and promoting American AI standard globally.

South Carolina is uniquely positioned to take advantage of the Transco pipeline, subsea cables from Myrtle Beach and Portugal, and high-capacity fiber routes connecting Washington, D.C., and Atlanta. South Carolina should take advantage of the current infrastructure to tap into these existing resources. As Gov. McMaster has said, South Carolina is “pound for pound the most patriotic state in America.” South Carolina has a role in winning the AI race by leading the way in establishing this critical infrastructure.

Finally, there are ways to address the increased demand for energy and the costs of the energy infrastructure. For example, the South Carolina Energy Security Act encourages shared bulk power resources between large customers and electric utilities subject to appropriate protections for existing customers and approval by the Public Service Commission of South Carolina. Also, large customers such as data centers can build their own generation.

Data centers can reduce rates to our residential and commercial customers, help build our State’s energy infrastructure, play a critical role in National Security, support and expand the conveniences they provide in our daily digital lives, place South Carolina at the forefront of AI and the modern technology revolution, and create capital investment without draining our infrastructure, like roads and schools.

description:
Details Sales of battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids rose 9% year-on-year to 1.85 million vehicles in July.
These figures demonstrate the growing divergence between the major electric vehicle markets.
Sales in Europe rose 33% to 450,000 vehicles, with growth since the beginning of the year reaching 28%.
In July, electric vehicle sales in France, Germany and the United Kingdom rose by 81%, 46% and 43%, respectively.
In North America, sales fell 27% to 140,000 vehicles after electric vehicle tax credits in the United States expired.
text:
Global demand for electric vehicles rose for the fifth consecutive month in July, driven by a sharp increase in sales in Europe, while sales in China and North America declined, according to data from consultancy Benchmark Mineral Intelligence released on Thursday. Reuters reports, writes UNN.

Details

Sales of battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids rose 9% year-on-year to 1.85 million vehicles in July. A total of 11.5 million such vehicles have been sold since the beginning of the year.

These figures demonstrate the growing divergence between the major electric vehicle markets. In Europe, demand is being supported by subsidies, while the U.S. market has been affected by the cancellation of federal tax credits for electric vehicles, and Chinese automakers are increasingly relying on exports to drive growth.

Sales in Europe rose 33% to 450,000 vehicles, with growth since the beginning of the year reaching 28%.

High growth rates persisted in Europe's largest automotive markets, many of which have reinstated electric vehicle subsidy programs over the past 18 months

- BMI noted.

In July, electric vehicle sales in France, Germany and the United Kingdom rose by 81%, 46% and 43%, respectively.

Meanwhile, sales in China fell 5% to 980,000 vehicles.

In North America, sales fell 27% to 140,000 vehicles after electric vehicle tax credits in the United States expired.

Sales in the rest of the world rose 97% to 280,000 vehicles.
