text:
Toledo, OH — Today, Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (OH-09), Co-Chair of the bipartisan House Great Lakes Task Force and Ranking Member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Energy and Water, announced that the Toledo-Lucas County Port Authority has been awarded $32,343,000 through the United States Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Great Lakes Restoration Initiative (GLRI) to complete remediation of the Lower Maumee River Sway Bridge Project. Congresswoman Kaptur has championed the GLRI since before its creation, and has worked with Presidents of both parties to ensure its continued funding levels. She continues to lead legislation to reauthorize the GLRI including the GLRI Act of 2025.

“As the largest tributary to the Great Lakes, the Maumee River is a precious natural resource that we must strive to cherish and protect for the generations to come,” said Congresswoman Marcy Kaptur (OH-09). “With this major Federal investment, we return taxpayer dollars back home to Northwest Ohio to allow us to continue our role as stewards of the Great Lakes ecosystem and our mighty Maumee River. The health of our fresh water sources is vital, including that of the Maumee River which is the largest tributary in the entire the Great Lakes region. This is both an environmental and economic priority for our region, as our Great Lakes are home to thousands of unique plant and animal species and generate over $82 Billion in wages and 1.5 million jobs for the Great Lakes Nation on both sides of our northern border.”

"We are proud to partner with the US EPA, Ohio EPA, the US Army Corps of Engineers, the City of Toledo, and the Great Lakes National Program Office on this transformational project," said Thomas J. Winston, President and CEO of the Toledo-Lucas County Port Authority. "This investment demonstrates a continued commitment to restoring one of our region's greatest natural resources while strengthening the Port of Toledo's working waterfront.”

The award will be used to support the removal of tens of thousands of cubic yards of sediment from the Lower Maumee River between the Seneca Petroleum Marine Terminal and the Ironville Marine Terminal. This will be one of the largest sediment remediation efforts in Northwest Ohio. All dredged material will be disposed of within the Port Authority’s Confined Disposal Facility. The site has been designated as a priority for remediation efforts due to high levels of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and other contaminants. Produced both naturally and by human activity, PAHs have been linked to cancer, cardiovascular issues, and developmental defects. The Ohio EPA will also be contributing $1.75 Million to the project.

The Maumee Area of Concern was designated in 1987 and spans across nearly 1,900 miles of streams and 45 miles of Lake Erie shoreline. Industrial and municipal development in the area has led to contamination entering the water, making it less safe for wildlife, recreation, and fresh drinking water. Federal, state, and local partners have joined hands on several projects to advance remediation and restoration efforts.

Through her position as ranking member of the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Energy and Water, Congresswoman Kaptur has secured millions of dollars of funds each year for Northwest Ohio wetlands and shorelines. In 2026 alone, this includes $17.6 Million for harbor dredging in Northwest Ohio, $3.4 Million for the Sawmill Creek Wastewater Treatment plant, and $795,152 for the University of Toledo’s research on harmful algal blooms (HAB). Congresswoman Kaptur remains committed to bringing new funds and Federal investment back home, to ensure your tax dollars uplift our communities.

text:
Dominika Parry never stopped fighting for Jackson, Mississippi, residents even after the Trump administration terminated a multibillion-dollar program last year meant to help the Black city still reeling from a water crisis.

For years, if water did flow out of Black households' faucets in Jackson at all, it was often brown. It left elders and babies with rashes and caused a slew of health problems across the city.

Parry and other community leaders and organizations got some semblance of hope in 2023 with a federal grant. Yet, two years later — before any funds could be distributed — President Donald Trump entered office and terminated a $2.8 billion program meant to help mitigate the harm from climate change and environmental issues in Black, low-income, and disadvantaged communities.

More than a year later, federal courts stepped in and rebuked the administration's effort to dismantle climate funding. The case centers on the administration's effort to roll back climate investments authorized by Congress under the Inflation Reduction Act, President Joe Biden's cornerstone economic policy.

Last month, a South Carolina federal judge ordered the Environmental Protection Agency to resume distributing funds designed to address environmental and health challenges in underserved communities.

The July ruling came just before the D.C. Circuit Court blocked the EPA from rescinding nearly $20 billion in Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund awards. That program is different from the environmental justice grants promised to Jackson and other overburdened communities.

That means that over $22 billion meant for climate and environmental projects in disadvantaged communities may soon be distributed.

Parry did not respond to requests for comment after the ruling, but Matt Sedlar, climate analyst at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, said the outcomes of these lawsuits are "sending a message to the administration that the separation of powers exists and that it must follow the law."

What the billions could be spent on in Black communities

In 2023, a $20 million federal grant offered a life-saving chance for the Jackson's poorest. The money was for a resilience hub that would offer year-round access to housing where the lights would stay on with clean drinking water in the time of disaster by funding a micro electric grid. It would also include backup generators, an independent water well, showers, and overnight shelter for up to 150 people at a time facing water issues in their home.

The goal was building "a place where people can come, stay overnight, have access to energy, be in healthy conditions," Parry said last year. Parry founded the recipient group 2C Mississippi, a Ridgeland-based nonprofit focused on climate resilience in Mississippi.

Since February 2025, the billions made available through the Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant Program have languished as the Trump administration has moved to gut a historic number of environmental rules and protections. The Associated Press estimates that the EPA programs and rules cut were projected to prevent roughly 30,000 deaths per year, particularly in Black and disadvantaged communities.

The Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund was designed as a $27 billion national clean-energy financing program. Its goal was also to make clean-energy investments like home-energy upgrades, solar installations, and electric vehicles more accessible in low-income and disadvantaged communities that have historically been shut out of affordable green financing.

The Trump administration has already moved to legally appeal the judge's ruling regarding the environmental and climate justice grant program, claiming that the EPA now lacks the money and staff to implement the program. (The Trump administration has fired 25% of EPA workers since 2024, bringing the agency to its lowest staff total ever.)

Already, some of the programs that received the initial approval for funding in 2024 have ceased to exist, including a solar installation program for formerly incarcerated people in Houston.

Last year, Leon Dillard, a formerly incarcerated man who was a part of the program before it was cut, said the climate-friendly work gave him a "sense of purpose."

"I really just needed to be a part of [the program], be a part of something," he said. "You have to make a choice to take a chance, or your life will never change. But you need other people with you on that journey."

It is likely that the administration will attempt to appeal the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund ruling as well.

Environmental and Climate Justice Block Grant Program projects include:

More than $14 million to install wastewater systems in Alabama's Blackbelt communities where failing septic systems and untreated sewage have long sickened Black residents.

A $500,000 micro electric grid project in Gentilly, a historically Black New Orleans neighborhood that has faced chronic flooding, heat, and power-outage risk, particularly during hurricane season.

A $20 million grant for four connected disaster hubs in Florida's historically Black areas of Lee County. The hubs would include cooling centers and, during disasters, sites for electricity, communications, water and food distribution, and emergency health support. The project also included money for stormwater treatment, new shade trees, and workforce training.

$500,000 for solar-workforce training for formerly incarcerated Texans, illegal-dumping cleanup, and environmental education in a Black community in Houston overburdened by pollution.

$20 million to weatherize, electrify, repair, and improve air quality in 500 homes in East Alabama and West Georgia. The plan also included 10 solar-and-battery resilience hubs for residents during outages and extreme weather.

Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund projects include:

Mississippi Solar for All: Hope Enterprise Corporation received $62 million to expand residential solar access for low-income and disadvantaged Mississippians.

Arkansas Solar for All: Hope Enterprise Corporation received $94 million for a companion program bringing solar benefits to low-income households across Arkansas.

Georgia BRIGHT Communities Coalition: Capital Good Fund received $156 million to expand access to clean energy and related jobs in Georgia.

EnergizeNC: The North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality received $156 million for its statewide low-income solar initiative.

Industrial Heartland Solar Coalition: Growth Opportunity Partners received $156 million for a multistate solar effort serving Midwestern industrial communities.

text:
EVgo and GM have opened a new flagship DC fast-charging station near Detroit with 12 high-power stalls, CCS and NACS connectors, and pull-through charging for EVs towing trailers.

The station is at the Meijer grocery store in Warren, Michigan, directly across from GM’s Global Technical Center. Its 350-kW chargers can deliver a full charge in as little as 15 minutes, according to EVgo, although actual charging speed depends on the vehicle, battery condition, temperature, and starting state of charge.

An overhead canopy covers the chargers, and the pull-through layout means drivers towing a trailer don’t have to unhitch before plugging in. That’s still an uncommon feature at public fast-charging stations, and a genuinely useful one.

The Warren opening brings EVgo’s US-wide flagship rollout to more than 40 operating stalls. EVgo expects to have more than 100 flagship stalls online by the end of 2026, with sites planned in California, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Michigan, and Texas.

Advertisement - scroll for more content

EVgo’s flagship charging stations average up to 20 stalls and are located near shopping, dining, grocery stores, and other amenities. Along with faster chargers and larger stall counts, the sites feature better lighting and layouts designed to make charging easier.

“The EV-driver customer experience is paramount as American consumers choose whether to drive electric. Through our collaboration with GM, we are meeting EV drivers where they are and seamlessly integrating infrastructure options into drivers’ lives,” said EVgo president Dennis Kish.

EVgo and GM first announced the flagship program in 2024, with plans for 400 fast-charging stalls in major US metro areas. Those chargers are part of a broader buildout: EVgo says it has installed nearly 2,400 stalls across 32 states with GM’s support.

Separately, EVgo, GM, and Pilot Company recently passed 1,300 fast-charging stalls at 300 Pilot and Flying J locations across 40 states.

The new Warren site arrives as Michigan’s EV population grows. EVgo, citing Experian vehicle-registration data, says the number of EVs operating in the state increased sixfold between 2021 and 2025.

text:
For eight years, the Electrify the South Electric Transportation Toolkit for Local Governments has been a reliable guide highlighting actionable EV strategies and policies. The 2026 update includes new learnings and resources, including proven examples for local governments seeking inspiration from their peers. The goal of the Toolkit is to provide information that is easily navigated and ready to be implemented.

The Toolkit is a PDF that can be downloaded and shared among stakeholders. It’s formatted as a series of factsheets based on “big ideas,” and it retains a hyperlinked table of contents that allows users to quickly jump to the factsheet/big idea of interest.

What’s New in 2026?

Electrify My Fleet: Municipal Roadmap Generator Tool

The “Electrify My Fleet” Municipal Roadmap Generator is an interactive tool designed to assist municipal representatives in evaluating their electric vehicle fleet readiness and generate a customized municipal fleet electrification roadmap. It takes users through a structured decision-making process and helps identify baseline metrics and desired goals. Users answer questions in the tool, which takes about fifteen minutes, and the tool then produces an actionable, personalized roadmap for fleet electrification. Click here to learn more about the resource. This resource is found in the Municipal Fleet factsheet/section.

Utility Programs Spreadsheet

The spreadsheet was developed by SACE and is a catalog of investor-owned, municipal, and cooperative utility electric vehicle programs. It can be used to identify utility offerings that can reduce the cost of infrastructure installation or energy costs for commercial and residential customers. There are rebates for the purchase of residential vehicles with some programs. Additionally, some utilities provide fleet support. It is subdivided into tabs arranged by state and has hyperlinks to each of the identified programs. This resource can be found in the Utility Engagement factsheet/section.

Barrier-Reducing Permitting Resources

There are new resources from several sources to help identify and reduce barriers to charging equipment development stemming from permitting. The National Association of State Energy Officials (NASEO), American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO), and Northeast States for Coordinated Air Use (NESCAUM) are working on improving permitting for fast-charging stations. Additionally, there are several playbooks from the Alternative Fuels Data Center and New York, New Jersey, and California. All these new resources can be found in the Regulation: Permitting and Inspection factsheet/section.

Multifamily Housing Resource

The FORTH Charge at Home Program website has a ton of resources to encourage charging installations for both new and existing properties. There are tools and guides for residents and developers. The project also includes technical assistance, including free consultations to multifamily housing developers. These resources can be found in the Residential Charging factsheet/section.

Take-Home Fleet Vehicle Guidance

Many municipalities are considering how to address electric fleet vehicles that employees take home. The charging considerations make it more complex than traditional gas vehicles. The Colorado State Controller’s Office has developed considerations for placement of take-home electric vehicles that are worth examining. This resource and others can be found in the Workplace Charging factsheet/section.

GRID Fast Tool for Utility Communication

Another new resource highlighted in the Utility Engagement factsheet/section is from our partners at Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI) called the GridFAST tool. It is an online portal that allows developers looking to install charging infrastructure to streamline collaboration between themselves and the electric utilities that will be providing power to their project.

Working With One Another

The most important aspect of the Toolkit remains that it is a repository of hard work done by other local governments across the country and, critically, in the Southeast. It is an opportunity to see the policies and practices that have been implemented and are propelling communities into an electric transportation future. Highlighting the outcomes and local governments taking action is important and provides an opportunity for peer-to-peer learning. Fairfax County, Virginia’s EV Readiness Strategy and Raleigh, North Carolina’s EV Implementation Strategy Rollout are examples of this. Their work can be found in the factsheet/section on Community Planning.

Curious about Learning More?

Local government staff who are interested in maximizing the Toolkit to meet their ET goals can schedule a one-on-one consultation with Dory Larsen from SACE.

text:
BOSTON — Governor Healey today announced $6 million in Business Builds Capital Grants to support six major business expansion projects across Massachusetts. The projects will leverage more than $300 million in private investment, create an expected 1,000 new jobs, and will help companies expand facilities, modernize equipment, and advance industry-leading technologies.

“Companies are choosing Massachusetts to grow, invest and create jobs because of our talented workforce and our leadership in innovation,” said Governor Maura Healey. “Through Business Builds, we’re partnering with companies that are making major investments in our state and helping them put down deeper roots here. These projects will create 1,000 new jobs and strengthen communities across Massachusetts.”

“Business Builds is about turning private investment into tangible benefits for our communities,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll. “By partnering with companies that are ready to grow, we’re supporting new jobs, stronger local economies, and investment in communities across Massachusetts.”

Established through the Mass Leads Act, the Business Builds Capital Grant Program is administered by the Massachusetts Office of Business Development (MOBD) within the Executive Office of Economic Development. The program provides targeted capital grants to help businesses grow, relocate, create jobs, and make qualified investments in Massachusetts facilities.

“From established manufacturers to companies developing cutting-edge robotics and autonomous systems, these projects reflect the range of innovative businesses investing and growing in Massachusetts,” said Economic Development Secretary Eric Paley. “By supporting these investments, we’re helping companies expand their presence in the state while creating new opportunities for talent and strengthening the industries that drive our economy.”

Business Builds supports the Healey-Driscoll Administration’s broader strategy to strengthen the state’s economic competitiveness while directing public resources toward projects that provide clear public benefits. The program works alongside existing economic development tools, including the Economic Development Incentive Program, by supporting facility and equipment investments that drive job creation, regional growth, and private-sector investment. Awardees are required to provide a dollar-for-dollar match for grant funds. Through Business Builds, EOED seeks to support business attraction and retention across Massachusetts, including in Gateway Cities, rural communities, and underutilized or redevelopment areas.

Awarded projects for the May 2026 round include:

Boston Dynamics, Waltham - $1.25 million

Boston Dynamics develops advanced mobile robotics used in inspection, warehouse automation, and industrial applications. The $1.25 million award will support the renovation and buildout of approximately 330,000 square feet of space in Waltham for robotics manufacturing, training, research and development, and related operations, including work related to the company’s Spot and Stretch platforms. The project will expand advanced manufacturing capacity and support Boston Dynamic’s plan to create 650 new full-time jobs in Massachusetts over the next three years, while keeping the company’s innovation-to-manufacturing value chain in the state and incorporating energy-efficiency upgrades.

SMC Ltd., Devens - $1.25 million

SMC Ltd. is a global medical device manufacturer and development partner serving original equipment manufacturers in the healthcare and pharmaceutical sectors. The $1.25 million award will support the renovation of SMC’s existing 330,000-square-foot Devens facility and construction of a new 100,000-square-foot building, including high-efficiency HVAC systems, insulated building panels, injection molding machines, and power systems. The expansion is expected to create 190 new full-time jobs and retain 440 existing jobs in Massachusetts, while helping SMC increase production capacity with more efficient building systems and manufacturing equipment.

Autonodyne LLC, Boston - $1 million

Autonodyne is a software company developing collaborative autonomy, command-and-control, and human-machine teaming solutions across air, sea, and land systems. The $1 million award will support construction and equipment for the Autonomy Advancement and Demonstration Center, a 6,500-square-foot demonstration lab and classroom with simulator stations, secure collaboration space, IT systems, demonstration cockpits, and training areas. The project is expected to create 97 new competitive wage jobs, strengthen a local workforce pipeline through internships and training partnerships, and incorporate high-efficiency HVAC, LED lighting, low-VOC materials and Energy Star or EPEAT Gold-certified equipment. The company anticipates in will source most project work from Massachusetts-based vendors.

CBSET Inc., Waltham - $1 million

CBSET is a preclinical translational research institute that supports life sciences companies developing drugs, medical devices, and other medical innovations. The $1 million award will support CBSET’s relocation and expansion from Lexington to Waltham through the renovation of a 104,000-square-foot building with laboratories, procedure rooms, operating rooms, offices, and upgraded building controls for air handling and HVAC systems. The project is expected to create 75 new jobs over the next three years, expand capacity for Massachusetts life sciences companies, and reduce historic building energy usage by an estimated 30 to 40 percent through a new building automation system and HVAC controls.

Helfrich Bros. Boiler Works Inc., Lawrence - $1 million

Helfrich Bros. Boiler Works is a family-owned Lawrence manufacturer of commercial boilers and ASME pressure vessels used in heating and industrial applications, including systems serving renewable energy customers. The $1 million award will help the company acquire land adjacent to its existing Lawrence site and construct a new 65,000-square-foot manufacturing facility with cranes, welding equipment, an automated paint booth, and a testing station. The project is expected to create at least 30 new jobs with competitive wages and benefits, increase the company’s welding school and apprenticeship capacity, support local suppliers, and redevelop a long-underutilized site near the proposed Merrimack Rail Trail.

Entegris Inc., Billerica - $500,000

Entegris develops filtration, purification, and materials-handling products used by semiconductor manufacturers in advanced chip production. The $500,000 award will help the company purchase and install manufacturing, handling, cleaning, inspection, and cleanroom equipment and make upgrades at its Billerica site to expand advanced filter production. The project will support the long-term retention of a 485-person Billerica workforce, strengthen Massachusetts’ semiconductor supply chain, and support filtration technologies that can reduce semiconductor rework, water use, chemical use, and wastewater impacts.

MOBD is currently accepting applications for the next round of Business Builds. The deadline for applications is September 30, 2026.

About the Massachusetts Office of Business Development

The Massachusetts Office of Business Development (MOBD) within the Executive Office of Economic Development (EOED) assists businesses expanding in and relocating to Massachusetts, with specific attention paid to projects that create and retain jobs and invest capital. MOBD administers the Economic Development Incentive Program. The MOBD team provides a highly responsive, central point of contact that facilitates access to resources, expertise, and incentive programs for businesses. The MOBD team is part of EOED’s effort to connect businesses with resources through the Business Front Door at www.mass.gov/bfd.

title: Economic Consequences Of Environmental Degradation - Rio Grande Guardian
description:
Environmental degradation and its consequences to the daily lives of populations around the globe is a sad and worrisome reality.
The World Economic Forum estimates that the global cost of environmental degradation is immense.
Broader economic damage from extreme weather and natural degradation costs the world billions to trillions more annually, impacting health, agriculture, and infrastructure.
Environmental degradation triggers chronic respiratory and heart diseases from air pollution, spread waterborne infections from chemical and sewage runoff, and expands vector-borne illnesses through shifting climate patterns.
Air pollution accounts for more than 1 in 8 deaths globally.
text:
Environmental degradation and its consequences to the daily lives of populations around the globe is a sad and worrisome reality. Wildfires, draughts, floods, higher temperatures, shorter winters, among other phenomena are becoming more common than ever before. The World Economic Forum estimates that the global cost of environmental degradation is immense. Climate and biodiversity damage caused by top global consumers alone reaches 1. 7 trillion to 5. 7 trillion US dollars per year. Broader economic damage from extreme weather and natural degradation costs the world billions to trillions more annually, impacting health, agriculture, and infrastructure.

Environmental degradation triggers chronic respiratory and heart diseases from air pollution, spread waterborne infections from chemical and sewage runoff, and expands vector-borne illnesses through shifting climate patterns. Mosquitoes that could not survive at certain altitudes, now, due to changing weather conditions, are present in cities far from coastal areas where they were traditionally found. Water pollution is responsible for serious diseases, like Minamata disease, a severe and permanent central nervous system disorder caused by mercury poisoning. It was first discovered in Minamata City, Japan, in 1956 after a local chemical factory, Chisso Corporation dumped toxic industrial wastewater into the sea, contaminating the fish and shellfish eaten by local residents from the 1930s to the 1960s. The effects of mercury poisoning include loss of feeling in the hands, feet, and around the mouth; trouble walking, shaking limbs, and poor body coordination (ataxia); reduced field of vision, deafness, and slurred speech; and extreme cases led to madness, paralysis, coma, and death. These effects are permanent, non reversible. The tragedy led to the Minamata Convention on Mercury, a global treaty designed to protect human health and the environment from toxic mercury emissions. This treaty was signed in 2013 and came into force as recent as 2017. Based on the effects of mercury poisoning, the film “Minamata” (2020) by Andrew Levitas with Johnny Depp playing the photojournalist W. Eugene Smith who documented the physical damages of the disease to the inhabitants through pictures released at a special edition of Life magazine exposes decades of negligence and cynicism by the country's Chisso Corporation.

The World Health Organization (WHO) explains that air pollution, including ground-level ozone particulates, and aeroallergens, is associated with respiratory and cardiovascular diseases, allergies, and asthma. Fossil fuel combustion is a major contributor to pollution from particulates and is a leading driver of health harms. It is linked to asthma, respiratory diseases, heart disease, certain cancers, adverse birth outcomes, cognitive impairments, and premature death. Air pollution accounts for more than 1 in 8 deaths globally.

Biodiversity loss is credited as a contributor to zoonotic diseases such as coronaviruses, influenza, HIV, Ebola, Zika and others. This is caused in part by urbanization, a trend that the world is facing at a rapid pace that puts societies in contact with species with which interaction was not possible before due to natural and ecosystemic barriers that now are being destroyed.

Then comes higher temperatures and their contribution to wildfires and extreme heat waves responsible for many deaths all over the world. This year the heatwave has dramatically affected Europe. An estimated 10 000 excess deaths during June's heatwave proves a devastating effect. The heatwave is common every year but not as extreme as seen this year. As of early August, water levels are falling, with the River Danube at a record low and threatening the power supply in Hungary; Italy has put most of its major cities on the highest heat alert; and the UK is facing concerns over crop losses and food supply pressures. Huge wildfires have spread across France and Spain, leading to mass evacuations. The WHO chief, Tedros Adanom Gebreyesus explained a few days ago that Europe is the fastest-warming continent on Earth, heating at twice the global average.

Yet, while looking at the Canada-US border wildfires have created the worst quality air conditions in the world. Thick smoke from Canadian wildfires has blanketed Toronto, Detroit, Minneapolis, Chicago, New York, and Washington, DC, in July on the east coast. There were concerns about the air quality during the final match of the World Cup in New Jersey on July 19. At points, Detroit, Toronto, and other North American cities ranked among the worst in the world for air quality. Some US politicians took to social media, blaming Canada as summer activities were curtailed and residents were warned to stay indoors. But the west also faces its own problems: wildfires in the US west are now sending smoke north across the border into British Columbia.

Both in France and California, the impact of the wildfires in viticulture is a cause of concern. California wildfires threaten wine regions like Napa and Sonoma, risking direct property damage and smoke taint that ruins unharvested grapes with an ashy flavor. Although vineyards can make excellent fire breaks because they are typically clear of burnable plant matter, and grape vines themselves are moist enough to be nonflammable. But heat damage and smoke can still destroy a crop. Grapes may be ruined to smoke exposure -you may not like wine with smokey flavors-, and vines need to be replanted at the owner’s cost. On the other side of the Atlantic, in France, wildfires burning outside Bordeaux are underscoring the climate challenges facing the country’s largest wine region. It is believed fires pose no immediate threat to Bordeaux's famed vineyards -for the reasons explained above-, but nearly two months of drought and repeated heatwaves have intensified stress on vines and brought one of the earliest harvests on record, which of course compromises wine quality.

title: Op-Ed: Steve Crim: America needs more power. We should build it at home.
description:
American energy powers our factories, military installations, hospitals, communications networks and countless other entities that support a robust economy and national defense.
It means American workers building energy technology in an American factory to help power American innovation.
In fact, solar energy technology was invented right here in the USA.
Over the last several decades, U.S. manufacturing struggled to keep up with foreign competitors that invested in building a domestic industry.
If America needs more power quickly — and it does — policymakers should not reject resources that are already adding meaningful supply.
text:
Questions raised about the cybersecurity of foreign-made equipment connected to America’s electric grid should be taken seriously. But the answer is not to abandon solar and battery storage at the very moment the country needs more electricity. It is to manufacture more of that equipment here at home and strengthen our cybersecurity protocols.

America’s energy debate is changing because the demands on the grid are changing. Artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, data centers and a modern defense industrial base all require enormous amounts of electricity. If the United States cannot produce abundant affordable power, we will lose jobs, investment and technological leadership to countries like China that are building faster.

This challenge is about more than economics. It’s about national security. American energy powers our factories, military installations, hospitals, communications networks and countless other entities that support a robust economy and national defense. A weak grid is a strategic vulnerability as well as an economic problem. America has rightly recognized the strategic importance of producing semiconductors and critical minerals at home. The technologies that generate, store and manage our electricity deserve that same priority.

That includes solar inverters, the grid-connected components that convert electricity from solar panels and batteries into power that homes, businesses and the grid can use. Any digitally connected device — an iPhone, Bluetooth connected headphones, for example — are vulnerable to cyberattacks. And as such, concerns about the cybersecurity of foreign-made inverters are understandable. That said, these concerns should strengthen the case for robust cybersecurity protocols and trusted American manufacturing, not weaken the case for solar.

Data shows that the market is already moving in that direction. EPC Power recently opened a 167,000-square-foot inverter factory in Fountain Inn, South Carolina, nearly tripling its production capacity in response to demand from AI data centers and other large power users.

That is exactly the kind of development we should champion. It means American workers building energy technology in an American factory to help power American innovation.

EPC Power is only one part of a much larger manufacturing renaissance. U.S. inverter manufacturing has nearly tripled since the end of 2024 and America is now tied as the world’s second-largest inverter manufacturer.

America’s dominance in the solar supply chain doesn’t stop there. In fact, solar energy technology was invented right here in the USA. Over the last several decades, U.S. manufacturing struggled to keep up with foreign competitors that invested in building a domestic industry. Thankfully, things have changed — and today, the United States ranks third in solar module manufacturing. Today, we have enough module manufacturing capacity to serve the entire U.S. market. We also rank second in battery energy storage manufacturing, a critical technology that allows us to store solar energy and deploy it when the grid needs it the most.

The importance of these achievements is underscored by the necessity to continue building on this success. China has spent years trying to dominate solar, batteries, critical minerals and other technologies that will shape the next generation of energy infrastructure. America cannot afford to replace dependence on foreign oil with dependence on Chinese-controlled energy supply chains. A serious national security strategy should include more domestic production of solar panels, batteries, inverters, transformers and grid equipment.

At the same time, U.S. electricity demands are rising to all-time highs. U.S. electricity generation increased only 2.8 percent in 2025 while prices rose 4.6 percent, even as demand from AI, data centers and high-tech manufacturing continues to climb. Solar and storage made up 91 percent of the new energy coming onto the grid in the first quarter of 2026.

If America needs more power quickly — and it does — policymakers should not reject resources that are already adding meaningful supply. Blocking American-made solar and storage, much less American innovation and industry, would limit our options at the very moment we need every resource capable of adding power to the grid.

America has the workers, resources and ingenuity to lead from a position of strength and build the energy technologies we need to meet this moment. Rather than cede the solar industry to our greatest economic competitor, America should manufacture its future here at home.

text:
A small number of vehicles are discontinued every year. For car shoppers, these cancellations rarely make news. But if you know where to look, there’s an opportunity to get a good deal on a vehicle that’s at the end of its life cycle.

There’s a good chance dealers will be looking to offload their remaining inventory of a discontinued vehicle, which can present an opportunity for you to negotiate on price. It’s also possible that a discounted vehicle might become a high-value classic many years from now. Edmunds’ auto experts have highlighted five of the most notable models that won’t be around after 2026. All of the following prices include destination fees.

Ford Escape

After 25 years and four generations, the Escape is departing dealership showrooms. Ford’s small SUV doesn’t fully measure up to top rivals like the Hyundai Tucson and Toyota RAV4, but there are enough positive attributes to make it worth considering, especially if you can get one at a discounted price.

The Escape has comfortable seating, a smooth ride quality and easy-to-use controls. It’s also available with two powertrains to help you save on gas: a hybrid that delivers an EPA-estimated 39 mpg combined or a plug-in hybrid that can go up to 37 miles on all-electric power before switching over to its gas engine.

2026 Escape starting price: $31,845

Volkswagen ID.4

The ID.4 was one of the first electric SUVs to challenge the Tesla Model Y when it was released in 2021. Its ample driving range and long list of standard features made it a viable choice for an EV, but over time, the ID.4 has been outclassed by competitors such as the Hyundai Ioniq 5 or undercut on price by less expensive options such as the Chevrolet Equinox EV.

However, picking up a 2026 ID.4 makes a lot of sense. Based on Edmunds’ analysis of transaction data, you’ll likely be able to get about $10,000 off the sticker price. For the best value of a 2026 ID.4, check out the Pro trim with standard rear-wheel drive. It comes generously equipped with heated front seats, wireless charging, a 12.9-inch touchscreen and several driver assist features.

2026 ID.4 starting price: $46,570

Jaguar F-Pace

If you’ve ever dreamed of owning a new Jaguar, then the 2026 F-Pace is your last chance at a gas-powered version because the company is transitioning to an all-electric ultra-luxury brand. The F-Pace is the last surviving model from Jaguar’s internal-combustion-engine past, and it won’t be replaced.

Although the F-Pace has soldiered on for 10 years without a redesign, it still boasts an attractive design, potent optional engines and sharp handling. The Jag can’t fully compete with newer small luxury SUVs, but scoring a good deal might be enough to tempt you. As a potential future classic, check out the performance-oriented SVR 575 Edition that comes with a muscular 567-horsepower V8 engine.

2026 F-Pace starting price: $58,375

Toyota GR Supra

The GR Supra is Toyota’s flagship sports car and the modern successor to the iconic Supra from the 1990s. After a seven-year run, 2026 will be its final year. Like its predecessor, the GR Supra boasts a powerful 382-horsepower engine, an engaging driving experience and an available manual transmission. The car’s swoopy styling remains one of the more distinctive shapes on the road too.

The GR Supra’s end isn’t necessarily because of slow sales. Toyota built it as part of a manufacturing partnership with BMW, which sold the related Z4 roadster. With Z4 production ending, there wasn’t a way to keep the Supra going. While it’s possible that a Supra successor is in the works, this GR Supra could easily qualify as a future classic.

Starting price: $59,595

Tesla Model S

The Model S will forever hold a place in automotive history as one of the earliest mass-produced electric vehicles. The 2026 model year is its last, however. The Model S’ longevity has rendered it a bit of an afterthought for a luxury EV, but it is a roomy electric sedan that’s ideal for daily driving and long road trips.

A base Model S has all-wheel drive, an EPA-estimated range of 410 miles, and enough power to get you from zero to 60 mph in a Tesla-cited 3.1 seconds. Another reason to buy the Model S over the competition is Tesla’s Full Self-Driving feature, which enables automated driving on most roads as long as the driver is ready to take control if needed. Tesla is no longer selling new Model S sedans from its website, but used versions are available.

Used 2026 Model S pricing: starting around $110,000

Edmunds says

If you’re in the market for one of these vehicles, act fast because the remaining inventory will likely be limited.

____

This story was provided to The Associated Press by the automotive website Edmunds.

Michael Cantu is a contributor at Edmunds.

text:
The state Public Utilities Commission has approved another round of utility-­scale renewable energy project additions to island power grids through competitive bids.

Under the approval issued Friday, Hawaiian Electric Co. is accepting proposals through late January from renewable energy development firms for projects on Hawaii Island and Oahu.

The effort aims to add nearly 1,650 gigawatt-hours of renewable energy from variable or intermittent sources that can include solar and wind farms, 465 megawatts of “grid forming resources” that can include variable power linked to battery storage, and 111 megawatts of firm power production.

Of the 465 megawatts of grid forming resources, 350 are for Oahu and 115 are for Hawaii Island. Of the 111 megawatts of firm power, 81 are for Oahu and 30 are for Hawaii Island.

Hawaiian Electric expects to select projects in September 2027. Winning projects, which are subject to contract negotiations and PUC approval, are intended to start producing electricity between 2031 and 2034.

This is the fourth round of renewable energy development solicitations being done by Hawaiian Electric under a PUC process to retire decades-old power plants fueled by oil and to meet a state goal to produce 100% of electricity renewable resources by 2045.

Last year, Hawaiian Electric — which serves Hawaii Island, Oahu, Maui, Molokai and Lanai — was at 36.8%, representing 57.3% on Hawaii Island, 41.6% for Maui County and 32.3% on Oahu.

Some of the additional renewable energy projects are being sought to compensate for projects that were approved in a prior round but are no longer moving forward. All the renewable energy projects are intended to meet growing energy needs, modernize power generation and drive down costs by reducing the use of oil.

“Collectively these projects comprise one of Hawaii’s largest-ever energy procurements and will make significant progress toward stabilizing customer bills and achieving the state’s decarbonization goals,” Shelee Kimura, Hawaiian Electric president, said in a statement.

Kimura also said the company expects significant interest in bidding from renewable energy developers, and that the competitive process has proven to be the most effective means to “fairly evaluate projects and ensure our customers’ interests are protected.”

An affiliate of Japan’s largest energy company wants to bypass such competitive bidding by seeking PUC permission to develop a 500-megawatt power plant on Oahu run on liquefied natural gas delivered by ship to an import terminal that would also be built by the company.

JERA Americas, the subsidiary of JERA Co., claims its envisioned $2 billion project endorsed by the administration of Gov. Josh Green could be developed by 2030 and cut the cost of electricity on Oahu by about 20% to save an average household about $42 a month, with a later conversion to run on a renewable fuel by 2045.

The PUC has not received an application yet from JERA, but the agency last week declined a request Hawaiian Electric made in July to allow the addition of 500 megawatts of fuel-­flexible firm generation on Oahu under a competitive procurement process.

One contention from JERA is that the PUC’s framework for authorizing projects via competitive bidding can take years.

The bidding approved on Friday stems from an initiative that the PUC began in August 2024 after groundwork by Hawaiian Electric in 2023.

Earlier phases of renewable energy procurement under the PUC’s competitive bidding framework for Hawaiian Electric were initiated in 2018, 2019 and 2023.

The first two phases led to nearly 450 megawatts of new power production and roughly 1.7 gigawatt hours per year of energy storage for Oahu and Maui.

The third stage of bids sought at least 965 gigawatt hours of variable energy and 300 to 700 megawatts of firm energy to come online between 2027 and 2033 on Oahu, and at least 425 gigawatt hours of variable energy and at least 40 megawatts of firm energy on Maui by 2027.

Hawaiian Electric said its third stage request was the largest energy procurement in company history.

Projects that resulted from the third stage but are still tentative include a 208-megawatt biofuel power plant planned by Kalaeloa Partners on Oahu projected to come online in 2033, and a 99-megawatt biofuel power plant planned by Ameresco Inc. on Oahu projected to come online in 2029.

Third-stage projects approved by the PUC include a 120-megawatt solar farm with battery storage planned by Longroad Energy Holdings on Oahu projected to come online in 2028, and a 253-megawatt biofuel power plant on Oahu planned by Hawaiian Electric projected to come online in three phases from 2029 to 2033.

text:
Louisiana Future Energy, Louisiana Oil & Gas Association (LOGA), Louisiana Mid-Continent Oil & Gas Association (LMOGA), and National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA) hosted the Gulf Coast Energy Forum Tuesday, bringing together energy executives, policymakers, and industry stakeholders in New Orleans one day before the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management (BOEM) opened bids on its third Gulf of America oil and gas lease sale of 2026.

"Yesterday's forum made one thing clear: Louisiana and the Gulf are central to the energy future of the nation and the world," said Michael Hecht, President and CEO of Greater New Orleans, Inc. "Executives, regulators, and elected officials came to Louisiana because this is where the next decade of energy investment gets decided. BOEM's third sale of the year is another chance for the state and region to deliver for the country and globe."

BOEM opened up the public bid reading for Lease Sale Big Beautiful Gulf 3 (BBG3) today, making roughly 80.4 million acres and about 15,100 unleased blocks available for leasing across the Gulf's Western, Central, and Eastern planning areas. The sale is the third of 30 Gulf lease sales required under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, part of a predictable leasing schedule intended to expand domestic energy production and reinforce U.S. energy security.

"Today our LOGA members, both operators and service companies alike, celebrate the Trump Administration’s commitment to the Gulf of America’s oil & gas production," said Mike Moncla, President, Louisiana Oil & Gas Association (LOGA). "These are expensive, long-term investments and without consistent and predictable policy operator’s ability to invest diminishes along with thousands of offshore jobs here in Louisiana. With the gulf’s production representing 15% of the nation’s total output, continued lease sales are of the utmost importance."

For a region that has powered American energy production for more than 70 years, BBG3 sends a clear signal: the Gulf of America is still producing, still attracting investment, and still positioning the U.S. to lead on global energy security. Tuesday's forum captured that momentum and put Louisiana's role in the national energy conversation on full display.

"Louisiana is an energy state, and the companies that operate here are leaders in assuring the United States is an energy leader," said Tommy Faucheux, President, LMOGA. "Gulf of America energy not only meets the needs of economies around the world, but it also employs generations of Louisianians and supports numerous local economies."

Panel discussions throughout the afternoon centered on turning policy into production: the regulatory steps between a lease sale and first oil, what a predictable leasing calendar means for supply chains and capital investment, and how state and federal coordination is shaping the pace of Gulf development. A luncheon was held in conjunction with the program.

Program participants included:

U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow (LA-05)

Kate MacGregor, Deputy Secretary, U.S. Department of the Interior

Matthew Giancona, Acting Director, Marine Minerals Administration

Dustin Davidson, Secretary of Energy, Louisiana

Rick Tallant, EVP of Supply Chain and Contracting & Procurement, Shell

Neil Menzies, VP, Gulf of America, Chevron

Michael Vallejo, President & CFO, Arena Energy

Eric Zimmermann, COO, LLOG Exploration

Michael Hecht, President & CEO, GNO, Inc.

Erik Milito, President, NOIA

Mike Moncla, President, LOGA

Tommy Faucheux, President, LMOGA

Tim Charters, Director of Upstream Policy, American Petroleum Institute

"The people of Louisiana have worked in Gulf exploration and production for generations, and we take pride in our shared history with the offshore industry, providing the fuel and feedstock our nation needs," said Dustin Davidson, Secretary of the Louisiana Department of Conservation and Energy. "The resources of the Gulf of America have been and continue to be a mainstay in our state and nation's role as global energy leaders."

BOEM estimates the Gulf's Outer Continental Shelf holds 26.9 billion barrels of undiscovered, technically recoverable oil and 45.59 trillion cubic feet of natural gas. Blocks available in BBG3 range from three to 231 miles offshore, in water depths from nine feet to more than 11,100 feet.

"The Gulf of America has the resources, infrastructure, workforce, and expertise to attract investment, grow production, and help keep American energy affordable and our nation secure," said Erik Milito, President, National Ocean Industries Association (NOIA).

"This forum brought together the leaders making the decisions that will drive the next generation of offshore investment, jobs, and energy production. The message was clear: long-term certainty and collaboration are essential to keeping the Gulf of America a global energy leader for decades to come."

BOEM is expected to release final bid totals for BBG3 in the hours following Wednesday's bid reading. The numbers will offer the clearest read yet on investor appetite under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's 30-sale schedule, after BBG1 drew $300 million in high bids from 30 companies in December and BBG2 drew just $47 million from 13 companies in March.

Leaders who gathered Tuesday argued the program's value isn't any single sale's total, but the certainty a fixed leasing calendar gives operators planning projects that run years past a single bid reading.

text:
I appear on a lot of podcasts, but I rarely share them here at THB. Today, I make an exception for a conversation I had earlier this week with Darren Samuelsohn, who writes at Love, Journalism on Substack, and until recently served as the White House, Congress, and campaigns editor at USA TODAY.

Readers can find a full transcript of our conversation below. You can also head over to Darren’s site if you’d like to see me beaming out of the THB Global Headquarters or listen to our conversation as a podcast.

I’ve known Darren professionally for going on two decades, and I respect him enormously for his many years of reporting at E&E News and Politico. On a personal level, Darren has always treated me fairly. He never adopted the overt or stealth political advocacy so ubiquitous on the climate beat. Instead, he acts as a journalist should — reporting facts, calling things like he sees them, and recognizing that the world is complex and nuanced.

I share our conversation because Darren asks me some questions that no one else has — as I said, he is a pro. In our discussion I talk about The Honest Broker on Substack, how I approach my work at THB, offer some personal reflections on my career, my thoughts on journalism and journalists, and discuss some of the complexity and nuance that I’ve explored across many topics.

Give Darren a follow over at Love, Journalism — you’ll be glad you did.

HOW ROGER PIELKE JR. BECAME VOLDEMORT

Love Journalism Show by Darren Samuelsohn

Lightly edited for readability.

DARREN: It’s been a while since Roger Pielke Jr. and I caught up. That’s how it’s been with a lot of guests lately. David Roberts, the old E&E crew. Climate has only become more everything since I moved away and into other horizons 15 or so years ago. Roger Pielke of the Honest Broker on Substack, a senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute, is here to talk us back into this discussion. Welcome to the Love Journalism Show. I’m Darren and this is Roger.

ROGER: Hey Darren, good to be with you.

DARREN: Great to have you, Roger. So last time I saw you, you were, gosh, this was a long time ago and you were in academia. You are now quite popular on Substack, writing about all the topics that you and I met on all those years ago. Tell us, tell my audience who your audience is.

ROGER: My audience, that’s a good question. Substack is amazing, as you know. It has an enormous reach. I have more than 40,000 subscribers in every U. S. state in 174 countries around the world. And about half of them are in the U. S., half overseas. And it’s an eclectic, politically diverse, highly educated, smart group. I’d be interested in hearing your views. I have a small proportion of people who Seem to be interested in being regular commenters. But it gets shared around and discussed. And I tell people, it’s no exaggeration. I’ve written a bunch of books as an academic. And I bet you in one week, more people read my Substack than over the last 30 years, all my books combined ever. So it is a remarkable platform. And it’s very rewarding.

DARREN: Do you read the comments?

ROGER: I read all the comments. I respond to some of them. And I do restrict the comments to my paid subscribers, which really elevates the quality. Everyone writes under their own name. And I’ve been doing it for six years now. And I can count it on the fingers of one hand, the incidents I’ve had where I’ve had to intervene. It’s a great community that has sprung up.

DARREN: One of the rules in a newsroom is never read the comments underneath the story. Did you get that memo or do you avert your eyes sometimes?

ROGER: Ha! I enjoy engaging. And for me, and this goes back a long time, more than 20 years, back when what we now call Substacking was called blogging. I use it as a form of extended peer review. I put ideas out there. People critique them, and they’re not shy. Sometimes I push back, and we have a debate and discussion. For me, engaging with the participants is actually a form of learning and getting better at what I try to do.

And I wanted to put the data out there so that normal people, so journalists, policymakers have one stop shopping if they want to know what are flood trends in the US, hurricane trends, drought trends. There are so many claims made, particularly in the media, but also that filter into policy that are based on single studies. And, the headline will say, scientists say hurricanes are getting worse. And so right now, the dashboard has 32 indicators across seven different weather phenomena. IBack in the day, it would have taken me a couple of years and probably a team of PhD students to put this together.

And I was able to put it together in a couple of months. So it’s, it’s work in progress. It’s going to be improved. But, and then I guess the other thing I did is I wanted to align what the official data says with what the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has concluded. And, good news for the IPCC and good news for my Dashboard, they align just fine, just perfectly. So, the IPCC working group one is perfectly consistent with this official data.

It’s funny, I put this out there and I don’t know if it’s yesterday, day before I was reading on X/Twitter, someone was saying, this is all fake information because you can’t believe this guy. And, you take 30 seconds and you’ll see all this is just official data from government sources scraped off the internet, once a week.

ROGER: Ha! DARREN: Fair enough. I will not bore you. But if you bring me on your show, I’ll tell you all about my cloud system, which is crazy and insane. But let’s go back to extreme weather for a second. You spent your entire career pushing back. On the idea that every extreme event in climate change is climate change in action. And I think that’s maybe where I first found my way to you and to your dad for that matter. Here we are. It’s 15 years later. When you look at the data and now you can look at the data in a probably instant way, you’re tracking yourself. What’s changed? What hasn’t from what you were talking about back in 2005, six, seven period even?

ROGER: I’ll go back further than that. I did a postdoc at the National Center for Atmospheric Research, NCAR, in the 90s. I started in 1994. And my mentor, guy named Mickey Glantz, who ran a social science group at NCAR on climate impacts, came in the office in January 1996 with a copy of Newsweek. And it said, hurricanes, floods, and blizzards blame global warming. And at the time, there was some connection of extreme weather and climate change, but not anything like today. And he gave me this. And I tell my students, it was a magazine. It was made out of paper and it had a cover and it came in the mailbox. He gave me this and he said, this looks interesting. Why don’t you take a look at that? And so I blame Mickey for setting me down that path. My postdoc was on hurricanes and floods.

And so at the time, it was pretty clear that the claims that were being made about trends in extreme weather didn’t match with what the data said, even then. And so I started working on hurricanes and floods and branched out to fires and heat waves and things like that, tornadoes.

Everything changed in 2006. And there was this interesting combination of events. I won an award from the National Academy of Sciences, the Roger Revelle Award. Roger Revelle was a professor at Harvard. He happened to be the professor that turned Al Gore on to climate change. And I won an award for my work on extreme weather, in particular demonstrating with data and evidence that rising costs associated with extreme weather events were due to more people, more property, more wealth in harm’s way, not a change in the statistics of the events themselves.

That was in March 2006. In May 2006, Al Gore’s movie came out, An Inconvenient Truth. And people of a certain generation will remember the movie poster had a hurricane coming out of a smokestack, spinning the wrong way, by the way. That was Hurricane Katrina. It was flipped over. And late in the production of that, apparently, as I gather, Hurricane Katrina occurred in October of 2005. And they reoriented some of the movie to focus more on Hurricane Katrina and its impacts, which was a horrific tragedy and obviously badly handled, but a very extreme storm. And for me, that represented a real change in how my work was received and how I was portrayed by journalists and in the media, because all of a sudden extreme weather was the face of climate change. And this was a concerted effort.

People like Matt Nisbet, who’s a professor at Northeastern, have documented how environmental funders, philanthropists gathered together and they thought we have to bring climate change home to normal people. We can’t just say we’re going to have a three-degree temperature change in 2100, that’s not going to get people to act. Extreme weather is very photogenic. It has horrific impacts. It happens everywhere, every day on planet Earth and in the United States. So it feeds the media cycle. I was already well-established as a researcher. I was a young researcher, doing great. But my work, right away, it was palpable. My work was inconvenient because it didn’t fit that narrative. And I remember thinking: Am I still going to work in this area?

And I had colleagues saying, maybe you should downplay your work or it’s going to cause you trouble down the road. And they were probably right about that. But I faced a choice. Do I want to keep doing this stuff or do I just want to go along? In 2006 or 2007, I could have had a very different career track if I would have just joined the bandwagon and said, every hurricane is getting worse. And we need to reduce emissions so that we can modulate future extreme weather events. I might have gone down a very different path than I did.

DARREN: You know who took that path? I remember this so well because I was driving home from a vacation when Katrina hit. And I remember for some reason, because I like listening to, I don’t remember what exactly it was. I remember coming on to Sean Hannity on the radio and the person arguing with him right after Katrina about hurricanes was Robert F. Kennedy Jr. Yeah. ROGER: Well, you might have seen some of this because around that time, 2006, 2007, 2008, first it was Grist. I was one of their favorite punching bags. Then it was the Center for American Progress for a long while. And, as people left their early jobs there and moved on. Some of them, like Dave Roberts, who you had on before, decided I was public enemy number one. And there were journalists at places like the New York Times and elsewhere who decided that the work that I did couldn’t be correct, obviously, because it was contrary to a narrative. But things really changed at that point for me.

DARREN: So around that period, I’m covering climate science, but my focus was the policy. I’m covering the regulations, I’m covering the cap and trade bills that ultimately would crash and burn in 2010. So none of that stuff passed. And yet, I just was for the hell of it looking today, 15, 16 years later to see where emissions went, comparing to what those bills required. And emissions have come down anyway, for reasons most of those lawmakers, presidents, agencies never really had in mind. What’s your read on that? What actually moved the needle? What does it say about climate policy itself versus everything else that happens in energy markets and energy, overall?

ROGER: So I came to climate change ass backwards. I started with adaptation and extreme events, and later moved into energy policy and decarbonization. And one of the, this is down in the weeds again. So down in the weeds on my side, I often talk about decarbonization of the economy. So it’s carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP. It’s a simple metric. And that metric has been declining for as long as we have data for 60 years, which is good news. That means that we’re moving in the right direction. We’re not reducing emissions fast enough to meet targets. But one very fascinating aspect about that particular curve, if you look at the United States or the world, for that matter, it’s a linear, it’s a straight line downward.

And so if climate policy and mitigation policy efforts to reduce emissions, deep decarbonization, if that’s working, we should see an acceleration in that curve. We’re moving it downward faster. And so we don’t. We don’t see that at all. There is no evidence. You start in 1992 with the Earth Summit, 1997, Kyoto, Paris Agreement. In the US, clean power plan, cap and trade, name it, IRA, pick your favorite proposal or outcome. And there’s no evidence that any of it has moved the dial. And people get upset when I say that. Part of the reason is that what we used to call other names, maybe environmental policies, maybe economic policies, we’ve relabeled them as climate policies. So maybe there are things we call climate policies that contribute to decarbonization, but they haven’t accelerated decarbonization.

There are other things, particularly the rise of natural gas over the last 20 years that has displaced coal. Policies that have made coal more expensive and more difficult to build have contributed. Expansion of solar in particular and wind to a lesser degree have also contributed to that. But in terms of reducing emissions, there’s no evidence that our climate policies have done anything to accelerate the rate of decarbonization, which I would think should cause us to think, all right, so what is it we’re doing? And why do we think doing more of the same is going to lead to better outcomes? So I’m a proponent of deep decarbonization. I think it makes a lot of sense just to take that risk off the table. I wrote a book about that 15 years ago, 16 years ago now. But what we’ve been doing is obviously not working.

DARREN: I think I want to go to the politics of this for one second, because over this 26 years that I guess I’ve been in this world in Washington, and this really does overlay with the Bush years and the rejection of Kyoto, we’ve seen the politics of climate rise up, as you said, and it’s dropped down to nothing, and then it’s popped back up again, I think, around maybe the Inflation Reduction Act in Biden is when it gets another swing. And now, again, we’re down into a place where there ain’t nothing happening per se on climate. But the figures have changed. I mentioned RFK Jr., for example, 2005, screaming at Sean Hannity, what the hell are you talking about? It used to be, again, in that Obama era, they needed to win over some Democrats and they couldn’t win over those coal state Democrats. They’re long gone.

And the Tea Party is a brand new thing. And then MAGA is a brand new thing. So talk to me about the politics of climate change for a second, where you see them today versus where they were. And is this Is this one of those issues that’s just going to forever be third rail in the same way as you name it on the other political issues?

ROGER: I’ve been around long enough to remember when George H. W. Bush was campaigning for president saying he was going to counter the greenhouse effect with the White House effect. And there was a good faith battle over the degree to which government and government regulation should be the driving force in decarbonization. And it fell along predictable, old school, New Deal Democrat versus regular Republican conservative lines. But there was a debate about that. And that was, I think, a natural outcome of how climate change, global warming originally was originally framed. And people have to understand that the knowledge of climate change emerged from very sophisticated earth system models. And one, I guess it’s a career risk for modelers is that it’s very easy to map your model onto the real world.

And so if you want to reduce emissions, you put a knob or two in your model that reduces emissions such as going from scenario A to scenario C. And that gets translated into a real world understanding of something like a carbon price or some regulatory fiat to change technologies. And that early framing of climate change, mapping a model onto the real world, did get interpreted by people on the left as, well, we need more regulation. We need some top-down approach to manage the economy. And resistance from the right, who said, well, no, we’ve got to let the free market work. We need more innovation. Basic research is great, but none of this regulation stuff. That, I think, was normal climate politics and normal discussion.

I do think that the Bush versus Gore presidential election, going to the Supreme Court, Al Gore becoming, honestly radicalized on climate issue and making that his signature issue and combining that with the anti-Bush administration stuff helped to make climate change a very powerful wedge issue. And everybody knows what a wedge issue is, but I feel very strongly that folks on the right and folks on the left felt very strongly they could use climate change instrumentally to get political advantage, regardless of what it meant for decarbonization or adapting to climate, that it just became a symbol. And with the debates 20 years ago over the hockey stick mapped very nicely onto that. Honestly, the Republicans, Joe Barton, James Inhofe, they like to pick on climate scientists.

And to be fair, climate scientists, many of them haven’t been shy about advertising their progressive credentials and criticizing Republicans. And so everybody put on their partisan costume, and the politics became pretty poisonous for a long time. And it culminated with, if you look at the Inflation Reduction Act passed with, straight Democratic vote. And, the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act that ostensibly, probably not too significantly, but rolled back a lot of that was all Republican. And so climate change at some point morphed into just another place of the political battles of the U. S. And, the normal politics of climate change is a distant, distant memory.

Bush keeps his dad’s like environmental mantra going all the way through and try and answer it in three minutes because we’re going to run out of time in this particular segment of the Zoom. DARREN: You did so well so we got two and a half minutes left. I’m going to milk this question just one more line. And when I learned this policy back in the days, when I walked into E&E News, my old boss, Kevin Braun, would scream all the time, energy is not a partisan issue. Energy is not a partisan issue. ROGER: Energy is always going to be regional in a country as big as ours. most people don’t realize that California gets a significant part of its finished gasoline product from overseas, from South Korea, from India, from the Bahamas, because the refineries in the US can’t process it. That’s very different than other parts of the country. Texas is an electricity island, and it’s not connected to other parts of the country. If you’re in North Dakota or Wyoming, Natural gas and coal are a big deal. West Virginia, Joe Manchin came out of West Virginia, which coal is part of the history, part of the culture. So yes, of course, energy is going to be a regional issue.

I do think there’s one big change I’ve noticed. really over the long term is that in 2005, the Bush administration and the U. S. Congress led a discussion over national energy policy, which we haven’t had really since then. From 2005 and that time, through Obama and then through Biden, climate policy usurped energy policy. It became the umbrella and energy policy was underneath. And, I think that was a mistake because energy policy means something to everybody everywhere, even if it means different things regionally. In climate policy, it turns out there was just a new report that came out this past week. The working class across ethnic groups in the U. S.—people of all races without college degrees—, climate change is not a big deal. So climate was the umbrella and energy policy was folded under that. And what it meant was that a lot of focus on issues that people care about in different places was lost to this big globally focused issue, but it also meant that things associated.

With energy policy falling out of the discussion other issues go with it, most notably affordability, inflation in an era where energy, particularly electricity demand is picking up, how to meet that demand is lost because you’re talking about reducing emissions, not growing energy systems. The big change has been in really the last couple of years, that’s flipped again. And now energy is the umbrella and climate to the extent that people are still talking about climate, which I think they should be, is underneath that. And I think it’s perfectly compatible to have an agenda that’s an all of the above energy agenda, focused on affordability, energy expansion for growth, for things like data center and AI and reducing emissions.

DARREN: When you add the data center element, which you just said you were digging into, what did you come away with? Because that’s not in the equation 15, 20 years ago.

ROGER: Necessity is the mother of invention. And so for the U. S. for 15 years or so, we were fat and happy. We had plenty of electricity. It wasn’t a lot of demand growth. None was really expensive. There were a lot of projections that we would become ever more efficient and energy demand wouldn’t be as high as it was. And that’s changed. And it’s not just data centers, but the push to electrify heating and electrify the automobile fleet is going to have a greater draw on electricity. And so with the expectations of much greater demand comes questions, well, how are we gonna meet that? What technology is going to meet that? And that forces people to start having a discussion that we haven’t had for a long time.

And so one reason why people often point to China as the true all of the above energy nation is because they have to keep bringing online more and more Energy, not just electricity. And so we’re experiencing a taste of that ourselves in the US.

DARREN: Roger, now you and I have known each other for a long time. I spent a little bit of time looking back through some of my notes where I found your name, thanks to Claude, looking back through things. And I had a chance to look through things. You spent over a decade as a lightning rod. You spoke to that a moment ago.
