Donate Now

Lawrence said that is effectively a pro data-center position, and pointed to what happened in Saline Township, a small municipality where residents overwhelmingly opposed plans for a center supported by Oracle, Open AI, Whitmer and President Donald Trump. The companies threatened to sue, and Saline Township leaders, fearful of being vastly outgunned, quickly buckled. The center is under construction.

“Open AI and Oracle said ‘We have $1 trillion and you don’t so we dare you to take us on in court,’” Lawrence said. “The township feared they would be bankrupted and didn’t think they could stand up to these behemoths because of the imbalance in resources, and that shows you what local control amounts to.”

Four data centers are planned around Ann Arbor, where voters chose Rabhi, who was the utility’s biggest foe during his 2016-2022 legislative tenure. He won along with a council candidate opposed to centers. Rabhi’s opponent in the primary, establishment Mayor Chris Taylor, was not a vocal supporter of the centers, but also did not take a strong stand against them.

“My campaign did an effective job of taking a strong position on data centers, there was no hand wringing on my end, and my point all along was that it’s not just Ann Arbor,” Rabhi said, noting that a new gas plant proposed for just outside of Ann Arbor would have impacted its residents. He was among a coalition of local leaders who pressured Consumers Energy to rescind the plans. Incumbent Ann Arbor leadership was not part of that coalition.

Meanwhile, progressive attorney general candidate Eli Savit, who bucked corporate PAC money and promised to rein in the utilities, beat a utility-backed opponent. Current Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel, who is term-limited, has been a nation-leading consumer advocate in the fight against exploitation by data centers, and that will likely continue under Savit.

The results also bode well for a campaign spearheaded by Voters Not Politicians that aims to ban utilities from making political contributions to state lawmakers. DTE and Consumers Energy, the two largest utilities, are widely loathed because of the state’s poor reliability and cost increases. Their support for data centers has only fueled the anger, but state politicians have failed to take steps to protect residential customers.

Both companies widely donate to state politicians, and residents see the connection, data center opponents say.

“Two years ago we sounded the alarm on what the data center boom meant for Michigan; higher utility bills, more air and water pollution, and regular Michiganders being forced to foot the bill for Silicon Valley billionaire’s infrastructure in their job-killing AI race with each other,” said Christy McGillivray, executive director of Voters Not Politicians. “We knew it wasn’t just bad policy—it’s also terrible politics. Elections since then have proved we were right, and proved that politicians should listen to nonpartisan advocates instead of big tech and utility lobbyists.”

name: Clean Energy
title: Voices of the Energy Transition: Meet the Women of SEforALL's STEM Traineeship in Latin America
description:
The latest cohort of SEforALL’s STEM Traineeship Programme reflects on what it takes to build a just and inclusive energy future.
It gave me a much broader understanding of the energy sector and the complex challenges involved in advancing a sustainable and just energy transition.
The current administration is the first in which the terms “energy justice” and “energy poverty” have been formally incorporated into energy sector legislation.
During my traineeship, I worked on research related to energy access and energy transition challenges in Latin America.
It motivated me to continue my studies in the energy sector with an emphasis on energy for development.
text:
The latest cohort of SEforALL’s STEM Traineeship Programme reflects on what it takes to build a just and inclusive energy future.

Only a fraction of the global workforce holds the skills needed for today’s green economy, and women remain significantly underrepresented across the energy sector, from entry-level roles to boardrooms. Sustainable Energy for All (SEforALL)’s STEM Traineeship Programme was built to change that. In this piece, Sakshi Chandra from UN-Energy speaks with the latest cohort about what that change looks like in practice.

Launched in November 2025 in partnership with The Latin American and Caribbean Energy Organization (OLACDE), the latest edition of the programme brought together four young women from Colombia, Ecuador, Honduras and Mexico for a six-month traineeship combining hands-on technical work with professional development. The trainees conducted landscape analyses of their countries’ energy sectors, examined pathways to unlock financing for SDG7, and supported the advancement of country-specific Energy Compact commitments, working closely with project partners throughout.

They now join a growing network of more than 40 alumni who have completed the STEM Traineeship across Ghana, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Tanzania, a robust community of young women professionals driving national energy goals forward. The programme was also recognized by the COP30 Presidency in the Granary of Solutions as a case study in just and inclusive energy transition.

As this cohort closes its chapter, we sat down with the trainees to hear in their own words: what the experience meant, what they learned, and what comes next.

In conversation with Jessica Sotelo Gil (Mexico)

What inspired you to apply for the SEforALL STEM Traineeship Programme, and what were you hoping to gain from it?

Back then I was coming from a scientific background, I was doing research in electrochemistry, so I was already familiar with energy-related topics, but at the molecular level. At the same time, and ever since I was a teenager, I have been interested in understanding what we need to change as a society to reduce our impact on natural resources and how we can become more resilient to the challenges of climate change. So this traineeship felt like a great opportunity to apply the knowledge and skills I had developed throughout my studies while also stepping outside my comfort zone. It offered the chance to engage with one of the most important challenges we face today: advancing a just and sustainable energy transition.

Can you describe what you worked on during your traineeship?

The main project we worked on was an assessment and diagnosis of the energy sector in our respective countries, in my case, Mexico. We started from the ground up, examining the country’s energy generation mix, climate commitments and GHG reduction targets, institutional and regulatory frameworks, as well as public policies related to energy justice and the main barriers to financing energy transition projects. It gave me a much broader understanding of the energy sector and the complex challenges involved in advancing a sustainable and just energy transition. Beyond this project, I also had the opportunity to contribute to gender and youth-focused initiatives in collaboration with OCLADE, which were equally enriching.

Throughout the traineeship, we participated in regular training sessions led by experts on topics such as sustainable cooling, energy efficiency, clean cooking and energy modelling, and we also received training in professional soft skills such as public speaking, communication, CV writing and interviewing.

Most days were dedicated to advancing our main project, complemented by training sessions, meetings with fellow trainees, and calls with the OCLADE team, which made every week dynamic and engaging.

What has been your single biggest takeaway from this experience?

The biggest mindset shift I experienced was moving from an isolated way of thinking to a systems perspective. I gained a much deeper understanding of how closely energy is connected to water resources, land use and climate change, and how these relationships work in both directions. It is almost like an interconnected web, where changing one node affects everything around it. This realization changed the way I think about the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Achieving SDG7 can have ripple effects across many other areas: improving cold chains for vaccines and medicines (SDG3), supporting industrial electrification and cleaner technologies (SDG9), and contributing to more sustainable water management (SDG6), to name a few.

This reinforced my belief in the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration. No single person can be an expert in everything, and the complex challenges we face today require diverse perspectives. If we want decisions to be as effective and robust as possible, they need to be made collectively.

You were part of a cohort working across Colombia, Ecuador, Honduras and Mexico. What was it like collaborating with peers from different countries?

I loved it! Working in multicultural environments is one of the things I enjoy the most. Building connections with people from different backgrounds helps me recognize the incredible diversity of realities that exist, step outside my own bubble and become more aware of the challenges individuals may face due to the political, economic, social and even climatic conditions of their country.

What are the biggest energy challenges facing Mexico right now, in your view?

One of the main challenges is the insufficient investment in the maintenance, modernization and expansion of Mexico’s transmission and distribution infrastructure in recent years, which has become a significant barrier to the integration of renewable energy sources.

Another key issue is Mexico’s dependence on imported natural gas. Around 60 percent of electricity generation comes from combined cycle plants powered by natural gas, and approximately 70 percent of that gas is imported from the United States. This creates vulnerability to geopolitical tensions and places Mexico in a relatively exposed energy security position. At the same time, this context represents a major opportunity to accelerate renewable energy deployment. Mexico’s national target for 2030 is to reach 25 to 38 percent clean and renewable energy in its electricity mix, which could potentially strengthen the country’s energy sovereignty. The recent regulations on energy storage systems are an important step forward, as they will significantly support the expansion of intermittent renewable technologies such as solar and wind power.

How does the work you did during the traineeship connect to those national priorities?

Our research aimed to identify areas in which Mexico requires financing to advance its energy transition projects, an adequate financing structure is essentially a key enabler for any project. But what stood out most to me was the importance of analyzing the broader sector context through an energy justice lens. The current administration is the first in which the terms “energy justice” and “energy poverty” have been formally incorporated into energy sector legislation. For me, it was especially relevant to assess the extent to which these concepts are not only stated on paper, but effectively implemented in practice. It has been encouraging to see how organizations such as UN-Energy and SEforALL are supporting developing countries to ensure the energy transition is addressed not only from a technical perspective, but more importantly, from a social one.

Is there a specific energy solution in Mexico that deserves more attention globally?

Geothermal energy! This is an area with significant potential in Mexico, as in many other countries, that has not yet been fully developed due to the high level of risk inherent to the resource. But if developed under strong practices, it could bring multiple benefits: lower CO₂ emissions, direct use of thermal energy, generally less water use compared to fossil fuel power plants, and a smaller land footprint compared to technologies such as solar PV.

How has this traineeship prepared you for your next steps?

I have mainly gained much more confidence. The projects we carried out, along with the programme’s training sessions, gave me the knowledge and skills to understand the energy sector in a more holistic way. It has also given me new dreams and aspirations! It broadened my perspective and helped me gain clarity about what I want to pursue moving forward.

What is one thing you would say to a young woman in Mexico who is considering a career in the energy sector?

First and foremost, in both good and difficult times, place your trust in God. After that, a few recommendations: learn English as much as you can, as well as data processing tools. Be open when someone offers you help, and accept it. The energy sector can be challenging, and as women we still face certain disadvantages, but there are many people who genuinely want to support us. Learn to recognize them and take the opportunities when they come, as sometimes they only come once.

Never forget the people who have helped you along the way, try to give back when you can, and stay true to yourself wherever you go.

In conversation with Maria Juliana Otero (Colombia)

What inspired you to apply for the SEforALL STEM Traineeship Programme, and what were you hoping to gain from it?

I applied because I’ve always been interested in the energy sector and wanted to better understand how energy can be used as a tool to improve people’s lives. As an engineer, I was already familiar with some of the technical aspects, but I wanted to learn more about the human side of energy access and the role it plays in development.

Can you briefly describe what you worked on during your traineeship?

During my traineeship, I worked on research related to energy access and energy transition challenges in Latin America. A lot of my time was spent reviewing reports, analyzing information and collaborating with my fellow trainees. Every week felt a little different — we had a lot of trainings with experts, and one of my favourite parts was being able to connect what we were learning with my local context in Colombia.

What has been your single biggest takeaway from this experience?

I think my biggest takeaway was realizing just how much energy impacts every aspect of people’s lives. Before this experience, I knew energy was important, but I mostly thought about it in terms of electricity and infrastructure. Now I see how it affects education, healthcare, economic opportunities, gender equality, and so much more. I was especially surprised by the impact reliable energy access can have on women and youth.

You were part of a cohort working across Colombia, Ecuador, Honduras and Mexico. What was it like collaborating with peers from different countries and contexts?

Honestly, it was one of the best parts of the programme. Before this experience, I hadn’t had many opportunities to interact closely with women from across Latin America who were around my age and interested in similar topics. It was amazing to learn about their experiences, their countries, and the challenges they see in their own communities.

It definitely changed how I approached the work. Even though many of our countries face similar challenges, the realities can be very different, so it taught me the importance of listening, keeping an open mind and understanding local contexts.

What are the biggest energy challenges facing Colombia right now, in your view?

I think one of the biggest challenges is making sure that everyone has access to reliable electricity. Sometimes a community may technically be considered connected, but people still experience outages that last for days or only have electricity for part of the day.

How does the work you did during the traineeship connect to those national priorities?

One thing this traineeship helped me understand is that energy access is about much more than infrastructure. It’s also about affordability, reliability and making sure solutions actually meet the needs of the communities they serve. A lot of what I learned felt very relevant to Colombia, especially when thinking about rural and remote areas where access and reliability continue to be major challenges.

Is there a specific energy issue or solution in Colombia that you think deserves more attention globally?

I think the conversation around energy reliability deserves more attention. When people talk about energy access, they often focus on whether a community is connected or not, but that doesn’t always tell the full story. Reliable and consistent access is just as important. I also think there is a lot that can be learned from decentralized renewable energy solutions that can help serve remote communities more effectively.

How has this traineeship prepared you for your next steps?

This traineeship helped me realize how much I’ve learned and how much there is still to learn. With this experience I confirmed my interest in working in the energy sector, and this motivated me to continue building the knowledge and skills needed to contribute to the energy transition. It motivated me to continue my studies in the energy sector with an emphasis on energy for development.

What is one thing you would say to a young woman in Colombia who is considering a career in the energy sector?

Just go for it. Don’t count yourself out because you think you don’t know enough or aren’t qualified enough.

In conversation with Paula Camila Meneses Polo (Ecuador)

What inspired you to apply for the SEforALL STEM Traineeship Programme, and what were you hoping to gain from it?

Since I was a little girl, I have always felt a deep connection to climate issues. However, what truly inspired me to apply to SEforALL, with the earnest hope of being selected, was the desire to belong to a community composed entirely of women driven to learn about SDG7. In my past experience, I often found myself in environments where youth and gender were perceived as disadvantages.

Finding a programme specifically designed to empower young women in the energy sector through meaningful work felt like a guiding light, both professionally and personally. For me, this represented not just a great career opportunity, but a clear direction forward at a time when I felt lost amidst biased, patriarchal mindsets and age-related skepticism.

Can you briefly describe what you worked on during your traineeship?

My work focused on how to create genuine opportunities for women and youth within our region’s energy sector. A typical week was a dynamic mix of extensive reading, researching what different countries are implementing, learning how to design sustainable energy projects and creating multimedia deliverables.

One of my favorite activities was co-designing the strategic plan for a Regional Youth Council, which I developed alongside my counterpart, Jessica from Mexico. We spent hours brainstorming how to build a framework that actually works, ensuring that young people have a real seat at the decision-making table rather than being mere spectators listening to others talk.

What has been your single biggest takeaway from this experience?

I used to believe that making a real impact or doing meaningful work in this field required a strictly technical background. However, this experience taught me that the energy transition has a place for everyone, regardless of their profession; it is a space where diverse minds complement each other. This programme taught me to open both my heart and my perspective, to realize there is a vast universe of possibilities out there, and to never close doors on myself. I was constantly amazed by the sector’s immense potential for development and the incredible professionals within it.

You were part of a cohort working across Colombia, Ecuador, Honduras, and Mexico. What was it like collaborating with peers from different countries?

Having the opportunity to share this experience with peers from other countries was simply incredible; in fact, it was one of the highlights of my traineeship. I didn’t just learn about their cultures, but also about the vastly different realities each one faces. It was incredibly enriching to discover diverse approaches to achieving our shared goals. Ultimately, I realized that the future of our region relies entirely on learning to look beyond our own borders and supporting one another.

What are the biggest energy challenges facing Ecuador right now, in your view?

Currently, Ecuador is facing a critical situation that directly threatens its energy security due to an over-reliance on hydropower. This leaves the system highly vulnerable to climate crises and periods of drought. The most urgent challenge is building a resilient power grid through deep institutional strengthening, modernizing sector management, and enhancing both technical and administrative capabilities.

How does the work you did during the traineeship connect to those national priorities?

Faced with Ecuador’s complex reality, it is evident that we cannot solve current crises using the same approaches from the past. The work I did during my traineeship focused on gender inclusion and creating spaces for youth. These are fundamental steps to integrate fresh technical and strategic perspectives, giving a voice to underrepresented sectors while driving the participatory governance and innovative solutions that my country’s energy landscape desperately needs.

Is there a specific energy issue or solution in Ecuador that you think deserves more attention globally?

Ecuador possesses immense potential for studying and developing alternative energy sources. I believe the global community should pay closer attention to how we can diversify these resources to achieve greater resilience across the entire energy system, particularly in developing nations.

How has this traineeship prepared you for your next steps?

Through this programme, I realized that there are countless career paths tied to sustainability. Being in daily contact with leading professionals in the sector opened my eyes to new avenues I can pursue. Thanks to this, I am currently researching the best academic and professional paths to continue learning and growing, so I can ultimately return and contribute to my country’s development.

What is one thing you would say to a young woman in Ecuador who is considering a career in the energy sector?

If I could say anything to a young woman who is hesitating to join this sector today, it would be: trust yourself and your capabilities. I know what it feels like to be in environments that make you feel small, but it is vital that you don’t let anyone dim your light. Take every criticism and use it as fuel to forge your own path, never stop learning or being inspired.

The energy world needs women who know how to negotiate, organize, design and see the bigger picture. Walk with your head held high, claim your space in every room you enter, seek out other women to guide you, and always remember that your voice is not an ornament, it is necessary for the future. Some time ago, someone shared Sir Francis Drake’s proverb with me, “sic parvis magna” (greatness from small beginnings), and bit by bit, I have proven it to be true.

A closing reflection, in her own words

Camila chose to answer in English to reach a wider audience — but asked to close in her mother tongue, because, as she puts it, there are feelings that just cannot be translated:

“Al cerrar este ciclo, me doy cuenta de que ni el inglés ni el español son suficientes para abarcar todo lo que he vivido y aprendido aquí, y lo mucho que significó esta experiencia en mi camino profesional y personal. Conocí profesionales admirables, grandes guías, y excelentes compañeras, que ahora tengo el gusto de decirles amigas, incluso un acercamiento con la CEO de la organización, Damilola Ogunbiyi. Cada una de las personas que conocí fue una gran inspiración que me dejó grandes aprendizajes, pero el más grande fue el de confiar en mí misma y no dejar de soñar, porque algún día dejará de ser un sueño y se convertirá en una realidad.

Hay experiencias y sentimientos que no caben en palabras. Cuando me uní al programa, me sentía perdida y decepcionada, y como mencionaba, tener el honor de pertenecer a esta cohorte fue el inicio de un gran sueño. No me llevo de SEforALL sólo un certificado, me llevo la certeza de que el futuro de nuestra región también está en nuestras manos, y ya empezamos a trabajar por él.”

(“As I close this chapter, I realize that neither English nor Spanish is enough to capture everything I have lived and learned here, and how much this experience meant in my professional and personal journey. I met admirable professionals, great mentors and excellent colleagues, who I am now glad to call friends — including a connection with the organization’s CEO, Damilola Ogunbiyi. Every person I met was a great inspiration that left me with great lessons, but the biggest one was learning to trust myself and never stop dreaming, because one day, it will stop being a dream and become a reality.

There are experiences and feelings that don’t fit into words. When I joined the programme, I felt lost and disappointed, and as I mentioned, having the honor of belonging to this cohort was the beginning of a great dream. I’m not leaving SEforALL with just a certificate — I’m leaving with the certainty that the future of our region is also in our hands, and we have already begun working toward it.”)

A growing sisterhood of energy leaders

Jessica, Juliana and Camila now join more than 40 STEM Traineeship alumni around the world — a network of young women turning national energy commitments into action on the ground, from Freetown to Mexico City.

*Grace Morales Ramirez (Honduras) was unfortunately unable to participate in this interview series, but her contributions throughout the traineeship were deeply valued by the cohort and the SEforALL team.

text:
California drivers eyeing their first electric vehicle just got a new incentive to make the switch, as Gov. Gavin Newsom’s administration rolled out a fresh rebate program this month aimed at softening the loss of federal EV tax credits.

The initiative, called MyFirstEV, offers a $3,500 discount to first-time buyers or lessees who purchase a new zero-emission vehicle — a category that includes battery-electric cars as well as hydrogen fuel cell vehicles — as long as the manufacturer’s suggested retail price stays under $50,000. Shoppers looking at the used-EV market can also benefit, though at a reduced rate: a $1,750 rebate on pre-owned vehicles priced below $25,000.

The state program arrives roughly a year after President Donald Trump’s sweeping tax and spending package, often referred to as the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” eliminated federal EV tax credits nationwide. Those credits had previously allowed buyers to claim up to $7,500 for a new electric vehicle or $4,000 for a used one.

When he announced the program in July, Newsom framed it as California stepping up while Washington pulls back. The instant rebate, he said, would make it easier for families “to drive clean vehicles, breathe clean air and save money.”

State officials have secured $270 million to fund the program, with half coming from California’s budget and the other half contributed by participating automakers.

Who qualifies

Only California residents purchasing or leasing an electric vehicle for the very first time are eligible. Buyers will need to sign paperwork at the dealership confirming this is their first EV purchase or lease before driving off the lot, according to Lindsay Buckley, communications director for the California Air Resources Board, which oversees the program.

“Participants will be required to sign a legal document attesting that this is their first EV purchase or lease,” Buckley said. “So if you’ve previously purchased or leased an electric vehicle, you would not be eligible for this program.”

Restricting eligibility to first-time buyers could actually be a smart strategy for growing the EV market, according to Scott Moura, a civil engineering professor at UC Berkeley. “Giving incentives to people who have already bought EVs doesn’t really help grow the pool of buyers,” he said. “The funds can be used more effectively if they’re targeted at first-time buyers.”

No advance application needed

Unlike some past state rebate programs — including the now-defunct e-bike voucher program — MyFirstEV doesn’t require an application before making a purchase. Buyers simply need to visit a dealership representing one of the 15 automakers currently participating.

Rebates through Hyundai, Lucid and Tesla are already available. The remaining automakers are expected to launch their versions of the program throughout the fall.

Before finalizing a purchase or lease, buyers should confirm two things with the dealer’s sales and finance staff: that they qualify for the MyFirstEV rebate, and that funding is still available for that particular automaker.

Under the old federal EV rebate system, buyers typically had to wait until filing their taxes the following year to claim their credit. State officials say that won’t be the case here.

“Californians will be able to go to dealerships of participating automakers and access the rebates at the point of sale,” Buckley said. “They won’t have to wait to get this discount.”

Not every EV qualifies

The rebate applies only to battery-electric and hydrogen fuel cell vehicles sold by the automakers enrolled in the program. Hybrid vehicles are excluded, state officials confirmed.

There’s also a price ceiling — the vehicle must be priced under $50,000 if new, or under $25,000 if used, to qualify.

There is one notable exception: automakers headquartered in California are exempt from the price cap, meaning rebates apply to their vehicles regardless of sticker price. More than a dozen EV brands are based in California, and several offer models well above the $50,000 mark.

Extra help for lower-income buyers

While the MyFirstEV rebate amount doesn’t change based on income, buyers can stack it with other existing incentive programs, such as the Driving Clean Assistance Program and Clean Cars 4 All.

To qualify for Clean Cars 4 All, applicants must have household income at or below 300% of the federal poverty level. That program can provide additional savings of up to $12,000.

Are some automakers offering better deals?

Funding is being divided equally among all participating manufacturers, so no single brand receives a larger pool of rebate money. However, officials note that higher demand for certain models could cause rebate funds for those specific automakers to run out faster at some dealerships than others.

This report includes reporting contributed by KQED’s Laura Klivans.

text:
South Korea's Samsung SDI has acquired a 49.99% stake in the joint venture SynergyCells with General Motors and has become the sole owner of the battery plant under construction in Indiana. Meanwhile, the companies agreed to jointly develop the next generation of batteries for electric vehicles.

The facility in New Carlisle will be the first fully controlled Samsung SDI battery manufacturing base in North America. Construction of the plant began in 2024.

Initially, Samsung SDI and GM planned to invest about $3.5 billion in the joint project. The plant was expected to produce up to 27 GWh of EV batteries per year, but the partners revised the cooperation format due to slower-than-expected growth in demand for electric cars.

After completion of construction, Samsung SDI plans to primarily use the plant for the production of batteries for energy storage systems. The company aims to take advantage of the rapid growth of the U.S. energy storage market, demand for which is increasing along with the development of renewable energy and data centers.

Despite GM's exit from the joint venture, the companies continue to cooperate. Samsung SDI and the U.S. automaker have signed a separate agreement to develop next-generation prismatic battery cells.

The future batteries should have high energy density and support fast charging. They could be used in upcoming GM electric vehicle models, and later, production of such cells might be arranged at the Indiana plant.

Samsung SDI explained that the stake acquisition takes into account changes in the EV market and, at the same time, allows for maintaining a strategic partnership with General Motors.

title: In Puerto Rico, Trump admin backs big battery project but snubs solar - Canary Media
description:
The Department of Energy is backing a major battery project to bolster Puerto Rico’s fragile electric grid — even as the Trump administration axes funding for key clean energy initiatives across the U.S. territory.
Notably, the DOE loan scrapped an earlier plan for Pattern to include a utility-scale solar project.
Experts say new gas facilities would leave Puerto Rico even more exposed to the high costs and price swings that come with imported fossil fuels.
Pattern’s utility-scale battery project is advancing as the Trump administration disrupts efforts in Puerto Rico to deploy networks of smaller batteries paired with rooftop solar systems, including for medically vulnerable, low-income residents.
Jenniffer González-Colón, the Trump-allied governor of Puerto Rico, has recently backed away from the island’s ambitious renewable energy goals in favor of expanding fossil fuels.
text:
The Department of Energy is backing a major battery project to bolster Puerto Rico’s fragile electric grid — even as the Trump administration axes funding for key clean energy initiatives across the U.S. territory.

Last week, the DOE said it closed a nearly $490 million loan to a subsidiary of Pattern Energy to support two battery storage systems totaling 220 megawatts in the coastal cities of Arecibo and Santa Isabel. The loan was finalized by the agency’s renamed Office of Energy Dominance Financing, known as the Loan Programs Office under previous administrations.

Pattern’s battery systems are expected to provide backup electricity for more than 100,000 customers during power shortages — a chronic problem that has only gotten worse in the nine years since Hurricanes Irma and Maria all but destroyed the centralized electricity system. Batteries can help keep the lights on by delivering power to the grid during hours of high demand or when large power plants trip offline, as well as by managing voltages to avoid dips in electricity flows.

Notably, the DOE loan scrapped an earlier plan for Pattern to include a utility-scale solar project. In January 2025, at the tail end of the Biden administration, the office conditionally committed to providing San Francisco–based Pattern with a loan guarantee worth the same amount for a 70-MW solar project and three stand-alone batteries totaling 180 MW.

But not long after, Trump’s DOE began an ​“exhaustive” review of the Biden-era loan portfolio, which resulted in the office ​“restructuring, revising, or eliminating” over $83 billion in financing.

Any projects moving forward have been reshaped to reflect the Trump administration’s priorities, which do not involve advancing wind or solar projects. Pattern’s newly announced loan instead includes potential support for developing natural gas–fired generation in Puerto Rico, though the company and the DOE did not provide details on the gas component.

The Puerto Rican government has backed other efforts to build new power plants fueled by gas, which, like the oil that produces most of the island’s electricity, must be brought in by ship. Experts say new gas facilities would leave Puerto Rico even more exposed to the high costs and price swings that come with imported fossil fuels.

Gregory Beard, the director of Energy Dominance Financing, said the office analyzed Pattern’s loan and collaborated with the company ​“to restructure it using common sense, data driven solutions to ensure Puerto Rico gets the reliable and secure baseload power the Commonwealth deserves.”

A spokesperson for Pattern said the DOE loan will allow the developer to ​“continue advancing energy storage projects that improve grid reliability and resilience.” Pattern didn’t specify when it expects to begin construction or start operating the battery systems, or what their total energy capacity will be in terms of megawatt-hours.

That the Trump administration didn’t scrap the loan entirely underscores the peculiarities of its energy policy. Wind and solar are out, but batteries, geothermal, and hydropower are still in favor — though they haven’t received nearly as much support as natural gas, coal, and nuclear energy.

“The federal government is not pro-solar, but batteries seem to be generally uncontroversial on both sides of the aisle in the States,” said Javier Rúa-Jovet, chief policy officer for the Solar and Energy Storage Association of Puerto Rico. He noted that while batteries can soak up wind and solar power to provide around-the-clock clean energy, they also enable gas-fired power plants and generators to operate more nimbly to meet demand.

Rúa-Jovet spoke earlier this week from San Juan, which is grappling with not only a faulty electric grid but also an aging, underfunded water system. Authorities recently began rationing water in the capital and other major cities as an intense drought exacerbates long-standing infrastructure issues.

On the Pattern project, Rúa-Jovet said he applauded the DOE’s loan, despite losing the solar component. ​“Batteries of all sizes, in all places on the grid, are great for everyone,” he added.

The new storage projects ​“could also support the integration of greater renewable energy onto the system,” said Cathy Kunkel, an energy consultant at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis.

Pattern’s utility-scale battery project is advancing as the Trump administration disrupts efforts in Puerto Rico to deploy networks of smaller batteries paired with rooftop solar systems, including for medically vulnerable, low-income residents. Under Trump, the DOE has redirected hundreds of millions of dollars in federal resiliency funding away from such initiatives in order to shore up the island’s fossil-fuel power plants and gas pipeline infrastructure.

Congress originally meant for the funding to broaden access to Puerto Rico’s solar-plus-storage boom, which has provided a lifeline for many residents amid an onslaught of blackouts, electrical surges, and soaring electricity rates. In 2025, utility customers experienced an average of 36 hours of power interruptions not related to major events like hurricanes, up by 19% from 2024. By contrast, people on the U.S. mainland typically lack power for an average of just two hours per year, according to federal data.

Most of Puerto Rico’s energy storage capacity is divided across roughly 200,000 households and businesses, whose batteries totaled almost 2,900 MWh at the end of 2025.

Jenniffer González-Colón, the Trump-allied governor of Puerto Rico, has recently backed away from the island’s ambitious renewable energy goals in favor of expanding fossil fuels. Last year, the Puerto Rico Energy Bureau approved a new 560-MW gas plant in San Juan, and regulators are looking to procure another 3 gigawatts of power capacity to replace the existing power fleet — and they appear to prefer natural gas.

At the same time, over 1.2 GW of utility-scale battery projects are in development. That includes a 430-MW project from Tesla and Genera PR, a subsidiary of New York–based New Fortress Energy, which operates Puerto Rico’s legacy power plants. The companies plan to install Megapack systems at six aging facilities to improve grid stability, using $767 million in funding from the Federal Emergency Management Agency and disaster recovery funds.

“While the Puerto Rico government has pushed new natural gas plants as a solution to the island’s reliability problems, the reality is that utility-scale storage can be installed on a much shorter timeframe,” Kunkel said.

text:
“The Weight” was written by Robbie Robertson and appears as the fifth song on side one of The Band’s debut album, Music from Big Pink. The lyrics are a pastiche of Southern images regarding strange characters you might meet on the backroads of rural America. “Nazareth” comes from the brand inside of Robertson’s Martin D-28 that he was using while composing the song; it is the hometown of the Martin guitar manufacturing plant in Pennsylvania. “Fanny” refers to Robertson’s friend, Fanny Steloff, who founded the New York City Gotham Book Mart he was fond of visiting. “Anna Lee” is singer/drummer Levon Helm’s lifelong friend, Anna Lee Amsden from Turkey Scratch, AR. “Crazy Chester” was a bizarre character in Fayetteville, AR, who carried a holstered cap gun with him everywhere he went. Released as a single in August 1968, “The Weight” only went to #63 on the Billboard Hot 100 Singles chart but became a staple of airplay on progressive FM radio in the U.S. in the late 1960s. The song appears in the film Easy Rider, but the version heard on the soundtrack album is by A Group Called Smith, due to licensing issues. Personnel on the record were: Levon Helm (lead, backing vocals, drums), Rick Danko (lead, backing vocals, bass), Robbie Robertson (acoustic guitar), Richard Manuel (Hammond organ), and Garth Hudson (piano).

Music from Big Pink was recorded in early 1968 at A&R Recorders (Studio A) in New York City and Gold Star Studios and Capitol in Hollywood. Produced by John Simon, the album was released in July 1968 and went to #30 on the Billboard 200 Albums chart. Al Kooper said in Rolling Stone magazine, “This album was recorded in approximately two weeks. There are people who will work their lives away in vain and not touch it.” The album title refers to the pink house — aka Big Pink — that Band members Danko, Hudson and Manuel were living in at 2188 Stoll Road (later re-addressed as 56 Parnassus Lane) in West Saugerties, NY, while their first album was being written and recorded. The house is still there — and actually available for rent on VRBO. One single was released from the LP.

The Band was a Canadian-American rock band formed in Toronto in 1967 by Rick Danko, Garth Hudson, Richard Manuel, Robbie Robertson and Levon Helm. They were formerly known as Ronnie Hawkins’s backing band, The Hawks. They toured with Bob Dylan as his first electric backing band in 1966. They released their debut album for Capitol Records in 1968. In 1976, the band filmed and recorded The Last Waltz at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco, a documentary celebrating The Band before they officially broke up in 1978. The band, minus Robertson, began touring and occasionally recording again in 1983 until 1998. They have released 10 studio albums, nine live albums, 10 compilation albums, and 32 singles. They were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1994. All the band members had successful careers as solo artists. Richard Manuel died in March 1986, Rick Danko died in December 1999, Levon Helm died in April 2012 and Robbie Robertson died in August 2023.

text:
Physical infrastructure underpins major factors driving the global economy, including AI advancement, the clean energy transition and supply chains.

However, despite accounting for up to 13% of global GDP, the built environment and infrastructure sector struggles to attract entry-level talent.

To better understand and drive action on this challenge, the World Economic Forum is partnering with built environment and other industry communities to create a First Mile Sandbox.

Underpinning the advancement of artificial intelligence (AI), the transition to secure and clean energy, and the rerouting of supply chains as geoeconomic fragmentation accelerates is the physical infrastructure that enables it all.

Accounting for 11-13% of gross domestic product globally, the buildings and construction industry employs nearly 1 in 10 people worldwide.

Yet despite this momentum, the sector faces a talent gap, as it continues to struggle to attract the entry-level talent required to capture the growth opportunity at hand.

Why there's a talent gap in the built environment industry

As outlined in the Future of Jobs Report 2025, 40% of infrastructure employers highlight the sector’s inability to attract talent as the single-biggest barrier to industry transformation by 2030. This situation is particularly acute for in-demand skill sets such as AI and green skills, where there is significant competition for talent across industries.

Beyond AI and green skills, there is a broader evolution in skills demand by the infrastructure industry, as growth in skills such as talent management and analytical thinking points to changing expectations and a need for hybrid skill sets.

“The built environment is shaping the future of our planet, but it cannot thrive without young talent,” says Ebru Özdemir, Chairperson of the Board, Limak Holding.

While industry expectations are changing, so are those of entry-level talent. To address the industry talent gap, we need to consider how we might better understand the expectations of entry-level talent to calibrate where we should begin.

Understanding entry-level talent drivers and expectations

The World Economic Forum’s flagship report on youth perspectives, Youth Pulse 2026: Insights From the Next Generation for a Changing World, draws on insights from nearly 4,600 young people from 489 locations worldwide, representing diverse regions and contexts, providing a place for us to start.

According to the report, 42.7% of youth respondents think the growing gap between education and job market needs is one of the economic trends shaping the future the most.

Additional economic trends shaping the future include more remote work and flexible job opportunities (28%) and the expansion of sustainable industries (26.1%).

When asked “What matters most to you when thinking about your future career?”, 61.8% of respondents emphasized a sense of purpose or meaning, followed by flexibility and work-life balance at 58.1%.

Ranking significantly higher in importance than job and financial security at 45.1% and learning and career advancement opportunities at 40%, these priorities signal that young people today emphasize meaning, flexibility and alignment with personal values over more traditional measures of success.

Beyond the above drivers, labour market uncertainty is influencing broader shifts in how entry-level talent approaches entering the labour market.

Recent figures from the United States suggest that 42% of Gen Z workers are working in, or pursuing, skilled trade or “blue collar” roles, including 37% of those with a bachelor’s degree. Entry-level talent is attempting to navigate macro-level economic and labour market trends, while remaining true to their career and workplace priorities.

From Global Shaper Edwin Lai, we heard that “the built environment offers purpose in abundance. But too often, it is still shown through traditional professions rather than the missions it enables.

“If the built environment wants to attract the next generation, it should start inspiring people around missions. Young people are not simply choosing careers. They are choosing the future they want to help build, and few industries offer a greater opportunity to shape it.”

How the built environment industry can address the talent attractiveness gap

The expectations and priorities identified in the Youth Pulse survey provide insight into where the industry might begin to address the talent attractiveness gap. In fact, there are innovative programmes working towards that goal already.

Through the Global Engineer Girls (GEG), Limak Holdings is actively building pathways to address the entry-level talent disconnect. Started in Türkiye, the programme has expanded across eight countries – from Kosovo and Saudi Arabia to Spain and Côte d'Ivoire – and empowered more than 2,000 young women in engineering. By equipping them with scholarships, mentorship and trainings, Limak seeks to turn potential talent into the future leaders of the industry.

Loading...

Harking back to the Global Shapers Community and other youth-based organizations and initiatives, Edwin Lai shares how the "UN Sustainable Development Solutions Network Youth Initiative (SDSN Youth) Local Pathways Fellowship is empowering young urban leaders to advance sustainable development through practical, place-based solutions aligned with Sustainable Development Goal 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities).

“To date, over 700 fellows from more than 100 cities have undertaken initiatives – from tackling traffic congestion in Thailand to improving sanitation and waste management in Nigeria and creating safe and inclusive public spaces for women in Brazil – proving that young people want to actively create the built environment.

“Together, these initiatives reveal that young people are not just on the sidelines. They are already transforming their communities, tackling local challenges and influencing urban policy. The challenge now is to ensure the built environment tells this story more clearly, and creates pathways that enable more young people to see themselves within it.”

What’s next for entry-level talent readiness and industry attractiveness?

Ensuring the industries driving global growth have the talent they need, addressing changing entry-level talent expectations, and correcting the widening structural gap between how early-career talent is developed and how entry-level work is changing is beyond the role of a single industry, educational institution or region.

To better understand and drive action on this challenge, the World Economic Forum is partnering with built environment and other industry communities to create a First Mile Sandbox.

The sandbox connects universities, employers and other stakeholders with an invitation to scale best practices, pilot new partnership models, and anticipate future workforce transformation pressures on entry-level talent. Join us as we work together to reinvent talent readiness for the next generation.

After 20 years of mandates, subsidies, seasonal waivers, and RIN credit schemes, the proposed changes to the RFS demonstrate how the renewable fuels industry still struggles to compete without federal support.
Section 12501 should be removed from the Agricultural Act of 2026, as the Renewable Fuel Standard has not delivered on the promises made by its advocates 20 years ago.
text:
Established in 2005 to “reduce dependence on foreign sources of petroleum, increase domestic sources of energy, and help us make progress in moving beyond a petroleum-based economy,” the Renewable Fuel Standard has failed to deliver on each of these promises. As a result, the RFS remains one of the nation’s most expensive and misguided energy policies.

Dependence on foreign energy sources

While the program has displaced some gallons of gasoline and diesel with biofuels, it has simultaneously created a new form of import dependence. EPA’s Set 2 rule was finalized in March 2026, requiring 26.81 billion RINs, the compliance credits assigned to each gallon of renewable fuel, in 2026 and 27.02 billion in 2027, after the 70% reallocation of prior small-refinery exemptions. To meet these aggressive renewable fuel volume requirements, the U.S. will have to rely heavily on imported feedstocks and fuels, such as vegetable oils and animal fats.

Updated S&P Global analysis prepared for the American Fuel & Petrochemical Manufacturers confirmed that domestic (and even broader North American) origin feedstocks cannot meet the new targets without sustained imports. The EPA has imposed a policy that trades one form of foreign dependence for another while imposing compliance costs that some estimates place as high as 37 cents per gallon for obligated gasoline and diesel. This equates to a total market value of more than $60 billion.

Homegrown technologies like fracking provide a far more effective means of achieving energy independence goals. Fracking has caused an “eight-fold increase in [domestic] extraction productivity for natural gas and a nineteen-fold increase for oil,” allowing the U.S. to lead the world in oil and gas production.

Increase domestic energy sources

Corn ethanol production is largely domestic, but the RFS’s design keeps any advantage from scaling cleanly. EPA actions this year expanded the implied conventional renewable fuel mandate to near 15 billion gallons even though the market cannot absorb that volume given the ethanol blend wall and recently declining gasoline demand.

When the market is unable to absorb the mandated levels of ethanol, the shortfall must be covered by more expensive advanced biofuels, like biodiesel, which end up setting the marginal RIN price for the entire conventional category. Meanwhile, the high compliance burden and chronic uncertainty around small-refinery exemptions discourage investment in domestic refining capacity—the infrastructure that supplies the bulk of the nation’s transportation fuel.

The most recent version of section 12501 of the Agricultural Act of 2026 is intended to address the challenges that small refineries face by discarding the extreme company-focused changes to the definitions of what makes a “small refinery” found in the House bill. Despite that attempted correction, the bill would still compound problems for small refiners.

The Senate version of the bill, as released by Sen. John Boozman (R-Ark.) on July 31, would end traditional small-refinery exemption petitions after 2027 and replace them with a permanent compliance level based on a refinery’s peak production during 2023–2025. Any small refinery that grows beyond the 75,000-barrel-per-day threshold permanently loses that exemption.

This provision penalizes ambitious refiners — the ones that invest, hire, and expand — while redistributing the exempted volumes (minus a 500-million-gallon buffer) onto every other refiner (or “obligated party”). As the American Energy Association and others have noted, this creates structurally favored and disadvantaged refiners rather than a competitive energy sector.

Policies that discourage domestic refining investment undermine one of the principal ways the U.S. converts domestic energy resources into usable transportation fuels

Move beyond a petroleum-based economy

Higher ethanol blends such as E15 remain gasoline. They operate within the same petroleum infrastructure, vehicle fleet, and liquid-fuel distribution system, but mandates forcing them into the mix make that system less efficient. Permanent year-round E15 authority — the other half of Section 12501 — does not represent a transition beyond petroleum; it is simply a higher percentage of an inefficient fuel that is being forced into the mix by bad policy decisions.

After 20 years of mandates, subsidies, seasonal waivers, and RIN credit schemes, the proposed changes to the RFS demonstrate how the renewable fuels industry still struggles to compete without federal support. The push to legislate year-round E15 locks the industry’s dependency into statute and prevents markets and consumers from deciding which fuels they prefer.

Section 12501 is only the latest example of the political bargain that keeps the RFS alive: agricultural interests seeking guaranteed demand allied with a very narrow set of small refiners seeking permanent insulation from compliance costs. American drivers, along with refiners without political cover, and any small refinery that wants to grow, will pay the price for this policy.

Large refiners and industry trade associations have also supported requiring year-round E15, while small independent refiners warn that the intended changes could speed up closures and further consolidate the sector. Neither outcome would strengthen energy security.

Agencies and legislators should deal with small-refinery exemptions quickly and base renewable fuels mandates on realistic expectations for ethanol consumption and available North American feedstocks, not unrealistic predictions of import-dependent growth.

Section 12501 should be removed from the Agricultural Act of 2026, as the Renewable Fuel Standard has not delivered on the promises made by its advocates 20 years ago. Access to E15 should be driven by demand, not federal meddling in energy markets. Doubling down in the proposed Farm Bill will not change that record.

Jason Hayes is a Senior Research Fellow in the Heritage Foundation’s Center for Energy, Climate, and Environment.

text:
SEOUL, South Korea: South Korean battery maker Samsung SDI will acquire General Motors' 49.99 percent stake in their Indiana battery joint venture, ending the partnership after citing slower-than-expected growth in electric vehicle demand.

Samsung SDI said in a regulatory filing on August 11 that it plans to use the wholly owned unit, SDI-GM Synergy Cells Holdings, to meet demand for batteries across a range of applications, including energy storage systems (ESS) and electric vehicles.

The company said its existing investment plan would change following the transition to a wholly owned business, although specific investment plans have not yet been finalized. It said further details would be disclosed in accordance with regulatory requirements.

"The ownership change was made in consideration of market changes since the joint venture was announced, including the slower-than-expected growth of EV demand. The two partners have now decided to seek other forms of cooperation other than the joint venture," Samsung SDI said in a statement.

Separately, Samsung SDI said it has signed an agreement with GM to jointly develop next-generation prismatic batteries for potential future EV applications.

Reuters reported earlier this year that construction at the Indiana plant had slowed amid weak demand for electric vehicles.

GM and other automakers pulled back on EV manufacturing after the loss of a US$7,500 federal tax credit last September. While automakers continue to build and sell electric vehicles, they have reduced factory output to better match demand.

The joint venture was announced two years ago and was initially expected to have an annual production capacity of 27 gigawatt hours, with mass production targeted to begin in 2027.

In March, GM and LG Energy Solution also announced plans to convert another EV battery plant in Tennessee to manufacture batteries for energy storage systems.

text:
A US energy exploration company has sparked an outcry by unloading drilling equipment without authorisation on the east coast of Greenland, the autonomous Danish territory coveted by US President Donald Trump.

Texas-based Greenland Energy, which insists it has no connection to the US president's territorial ambitions, maintains that it was merely taking a preliminary step toward exploration activities when it unloaded the gear last month in Nunap Qeqqa, also known as Jameson Land.

Greenland Energy did not respond to an AFP request for comment, but it told Danish media in July that it believed that authorisation to unload and store its equipment, which was located in another part of Greenland, was only required within the oil exploration licence area.

"It was a mistake on our part, a mistake that will not be repeated," its managing director Roderick McIllree told Danish public broadcaster DR in late July.

The equipment is currently stored in a hangar at Nerlerit Inaat Airport, near the village of Ittoqqortoormiit, the closest settlement to the licence area.

The company has received a "strong warning" from the Greenland government, which in a statement last month added "that all future logistical arrangements must be notified to and approved by the mineral resources authority before they are carried out".

Greenland Energy's chairman, Larry Swets, has been described as being close to Trump.

And at a time when the US president still wishes to control the vast Arctic island, the prospect of a US energy company potentially carrying out exploration activities is making people uneasy.

"There is this vague sense of a connection to Trump," Ulrik Pram Gad, a researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies, told AFP.

- 'Anxiety' -

"This creates anxiety and tensions, all the more so because with Trump you can expect anything," he added.

"With this unauthorised unloading of equipment, the company has really not improved its chances with the Greenland authorities," said Anne Merrild, a professor at Aalborg University and Arctic specialist.

In 2021, the Greenlandic government, which manages the island's natural resources, declared a moratorium on the exploration and extraction of oil across the Arctic territory, which has been profoundly disrupted by climate change.

But the exploration licences under which Greenland Energy operates were issued earlier, in 2015 and 2018, and therefore remain valid.

"One of the conditions for keeping the licence is to actively explore the area," Pram Gad pointed out, while noting that "the company is under pressure", as it is not active currently.

Activities are subject to specific permits, and Greenland Energy still hopes to obtain full approval to begin drilling soon in order to determine the quality of potential deposits.

There is a need to double down on preparations and equipment on land that is inherently hostile due to the harsh Arctic conditions.

"We continue to be encouraged by the progress being made toward the remaining approvals required for drilling," Greenland Energy said in a letter to shareholders.

Greenland's government is less optimistic.

"Given the current situation, I do not consider it realistic that the company can drill in the autumn," Greenland Foreign Minister Mute Egede, who is responsible for natural resources, told the territory's broadcaster, KNR.

- Global tensions -

The environmental and social impact studies required to approve the project have not yet been submitted, the Greenland government has noted.

"The few inhabitants of the region depend on the surrounding nature: they are hunters, fishers," Merrild explained.

"Drilling causes a lot of disturbance, and increased human activity would have an impact on wildlife."

In Ittoqqortoormiit, more than a hundred people -- out of the 325 inhabitants of the village -- demonstrated in mid-July against the project, according to KNR.

The geological survey of Denmark and Greenland (GEUS) estimates that the region could contain the equivalent of 2.35 billion barrels of oil, a considerable volume for a single oil project, but limited when compared with reserves around the globe.

"In the company's logic, given current geopolitical tensions, the project sends a signal; it's a way of saying 'we have access to resources elsewhere'," Merrild stressed.

text:
Researchers are working to determine how chemical compounds can make products with characteristics like conventional plastics, but that can be tossed in a composting bin instead of a trash can to avoid leaving microplastics in the environment.

According to The Associated Press, traditional plastics last for a long time as they fragment into harmful microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics.

Microplastics have been found in the ocean and the air, in food and water, and in body tissues.

Sugar-based plastics may solve microplastic pollution issue

Dig deeper:

CJ Biomaterials, a biotechnology company based in Massachusetts, stimulates sugar to make plant-based chemical compounds that microorganisms will consume. The AP reported that alternatives to traditional plastics made of fossil fuels are viewed by some as one of several solutions required to tackle global plastic pollution.

The organization feeds sugar to microorganisms that transform it to PHAs for energy. CJ Biomaterials collects the PHA (polyhydroxyalkanoates) and turns it into small particles.

Pellets of this are then sold to other companies that can melt them down and mold them into products. These same bacteria will consume PHA in a compost pile, breaking it down within six months, Leah Ford, marketing director for CJ Biomaterials, explained to the AP.

Bioplastics growing share of the market

Big picture view:

The Associated Press reported that biobased plastics worldwide account for less than 1% of 440 million tons of plastics produced yearly, according to the industry group European Bioplastics.

China, Sweden and the United States are major exporters of natural polymers, which is a chemical compound or mixture of compounds.

Bioplastics usually cost more than conventional plastics. Major cities have municipal composting programs, but they are limited elsewhere.

According to the AP, many composting facilities accept compostable bioplastic products, though some refuse out of concern about degraded soil quality. Since bioplastics and conventional plastics look the same, they can be mixed up, creating issues for composters.

title: General Motors hands its $3.5 billion battery dream to Samsung - ArenaEV
description:
The grand plan in New Carlisle, Indiana, was supposed to be a cornerstone of that brave new world - a £2.55 billion joint venture between General Motors and Samsung SDI sprawling across a 680-acre site.
In a handbrake turn, Samsung SDI is buying GM's 49.99% stake in their Synergy Cells venture, converting the massive Indiana complex into a wholly owned subsidiary.
Where does that leave Samsung SDI?
Taking full control of the Indiana plant gives Samsung SDI the freedom to add a dedicated Energy Storage System (ESS) production line.
The North American passenger EV market goes through a sluggish recalibration, but the demand for stationary grid storage and power-hungry AI data centers is off the charts.
text:
12 August 2026

Detroit has been making cars long enough to learn that nothing tests a carmaker's resolve quite like a sudden shift in consumer trends. A couple of years ago, you couldn't pass an automotive press conference without hearing corporate executives preach the gospel of total electrification, backing up their sermon with eye-watering checks for mega-factories.

The grand plan in New Carlisle, Indiana, was supposed to be a cornerstone of that brave new world - a £2.55 billion joint venture between General Motors and Samsung SDI sprawling across a 680-acre site. It promised thousands of jobs and enough battery capacity to power hundreds of thousands of heavy-duty electric haulers.

Then reality hit. In a handbrake turn, Samsung SDI is buying GM's 49.99% stake in their Synergy Cells venture, converting the massive Indiana complex into a wholly owned subsidiary. The purchase price is locked in a vault, and the headline is painful: GM is officially stepping out of the battery business in Indiana.

Instead of co-owning the brick-and-mortar, Detroit's largest automaker is retreating to a simpler supply and co-development agreement for next-generation prismatic cells. This exit is the aftermath of a massive demand hangover that ripped through the North American EV market when Washington pulled the plug on the £5,500 federal EV tax credit on September 30, 2025.

Without that government cushion softening the blow on window stickers, retail buyers slammed on the brakes. GM felt the burn pretty much straight away, taking an agonizing write-down of over £4 billion as it throttled back EV assembly lines and idled facilities within its Ultium Cells partnership with LG Energy Solution - eventually selling its stake in a third Ultium plant for £1.56 billion.

To anyone familiar with GM's playbook, this sudden decision isn't really surprising. General Motors has a rich history of pulling off sharp retreats whenever the market gets choppy - the legendary EV1 that was crushed in the desert after all the enthusiasm is a great example. Or the Chevrolet Volt, a genuinely decent plug-in hybrid that was abandoned just as the market started asking for PHEVs.

The Bolt EV wasn't spared from a chaotic cycle of cancellations and rewrites either. GM is notorious for bowing to political winds, flying forward when subsidies offer tailwinds, only to hit the brakes the very moment those incentives vanish into thin air.

The main issue is that building batteries for GM's electric cars needs an astronomical amount of raw capacity - capacity that only makes financial sense if showrooms are emptying at breakneck speed. Consider the Chevrolet Silverado EV - that beast is 232.9 inches long and crushes the scales at over 8,378 lb. Park it next to a rival like the Ford F-150 Lightning - which spans 232.7 inches long, or the sleeker Rivian R1T, stretching 217.1 inches end-to-end, and you realize that feeding these multi-ton road locomotives takes enormous battery packs. And that makes any dip in vehicle demand a catastrophe for a half-owned cell plant.

It is a similar story over in the luxury aisle. The Cadillac Lyriq commands respect with its portly curb weight of 6,116 lb. That gives it a larger footprint than European class rivals like the Audi Q8 e-tron, which weighs 5,699 lb. GM built machines with genuine road presence and serious battery requirements, but when buyers hesitate to sign on the line for luxury EVs or heavy-duty electric haulers, co-funding a 27 GWh to 36 GWh battery factory becomes a very expensive hobby.

Where does that leave Samsung SDI? Rather than panicking over GM's retreat, the South Korean battery giant is executing a clever pivot of its own. Taking full control of the Indiana plant gives Samsung SDI the freedom to add a dedicated Energy Storage System (ESS) production line. The North American passenger EV market goes through a sluggish recalibration, but the demand for stationary grid storage and power-hungry AI data centers is off the charts. Samsung is repurposing the production lines to feed gigawatts to energy-starved server farms instead of full-size pickup trucks - a pragmatic shift that keeps the lights on.

Under the new deal, Samsung SDI and GM will still work together on developing next-generation nickel-rich prismatic cells under Samsung's PRiMX brand, promising high energy density and great charging performance. But from GM's perspective, this arrangement shifts the risk onto supplier shoulders. GM gets access to high-tech cells down the road without carrying billions in real estate and factory debt on its balance sheet.

Detroit recalibrating its electric transition is a masterclass in automotive survival. We all love the idea of tire-shredding EVs with silly power numbers, but the truth is that mass adoption is dictated by consumer wallets, not corporate promises. GM's exit from Indiana is not a total surrender on electric cars - at least not yet - but it is a sobering dose of reality.

text:
The joint venture EV battery plant near New Carlisle has somewhat changed owners.

General Motors and Samsung entered into that partnership, and now Samsung is taking over.

This comes after both companies announced a joint development agreement to co-develop prismatic batteries.

On Tuesday, both General Motors and Samsung announced that both companies will co-develop prismatic batteries.

Also in their deal, Samsung will take over the New Carlisle location to create those batteries.

It's been nearly three months since General Motors announced it was pausing construction on the battery plant near New Carlisle.

But with the news of Samsung taking over, questions of uncertainty regarding the location are starting to be answered.

"We were excited at one point about GM and Samsung advancing a major project. But when things changed in Washington, D.C., it really put that whole project in limbo when the tax credits went away. So there's been a lot of uncertainty around the building," said Jeff Rea, South Bend Regional Chamber president.

According to Rea, this could be a real positive for the area regarding the economic impact.

The agreement will allow both companies to co-develop prismatic batteries, used for EV's, residential solar energy storage systems and other consumer electronics.

The new agreement also makes Samsung the majority owner of the battery plant.

"If you look internationally at what's happening with Samsung, the company is growing like crazy. A lot of different opportunities. They're moving into new technology. We always thought this was going to be a great chance for us to be in the middle of emerging technologies. And I think you'll see that happen as Samsung advances their project," said Rea.

The battery plant is still under construction.

When it's supposed to be done, and what a timeline looks like, are unknown.

The GM battery plant was expected to provide nearly 1,700 jobs.

Rea says he expects a similar number due to the size of the property.

"We think, though, this still is going to take a lot of humans out there to produce these values, and so it should be a big economic impact. It was slated to be one of our top five private sector employers," said Rea.

St. Joseph County Council Member Joe Thomas told WSBT 22 on Tuesday "I’m glad to see the building is not going to stay empty with Samsung announcing the manufacturing of batteries. We are hoping this development will bring a positive impact to the community, while keeping the New Carlisle and Olive Township residents a priority."

In a release, Samsung says they are ready to utilize the location in a fast-growing Energy Storage System market.

text:
Doubles Fermi power to market to 4.8 gigawatts (GW) over the next ~30 months

Build-Own-Operate-Transfer structure accelerates one of America's largest AI campus power programs - with no capital outlay by Fermi

Fermi Inc. (NASDAQ:FRMI)(LSE:FRMI), operating as Fermi America™ ("Fermi" or the "Company"), announced the execution of a framework agreement with Hillcore Energy Capital Corporation ("Hillcore") under which Hillcore will finance, build, own and operate the Hillcore Power Center, an approximately 2.6 GW power complex at Fermi's Project Matador campus in Carson County, Texas, under a Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT) structure. The Hillcore Power Center will comprise approximately 2.5 GW of natural gas-fired generation, developed in phases, together with approximately 100 megawatts (MW) of solar generation and battery energy storage. Construction of the first power block, approximately 350 MW, will begin on execution of definitive agreements, with first power targeted within 24 months of notice to proceed.

Strategic Alliance Summary

Speed to power. The construction of the Hillcore Power Center will run in parallel with Fermi's Main Campus power generation buildout. The strategic alliance is designed to bring the Project Matador campus to approximately 4.8 GW of on-site power years faster than a self-build path - a decisive advantage for AI and hyperscale customers.

Capital-efficient growth. Hillcore and its partners will finance and own the facility on their own balance sheets. Fermi adds gigawatts of dedicated, behind-the-meter power with no upfront capital expenditure.

De-risked commercial structure. Fermi purchases power only as customer leases are signed, on terms matched to each customer's lease, with fuel costs passed through. Construction, operating, and performance risk sit with Hillcore.

Path to ownership. Fermi holds an option to acquire the facility after 10 years at fair market value, preserving long-term ownership upside without committing capital today.

Alignment. Hillcore and its partners bring long-duration private capital and, through affiliates including JV Driver, more than 35 years of heavy-industrial and power-generation experience spanning natural gas, steam, biomass, and power boiler facilities from project development and construction through commissioning and operations.

"Power is the gating asset for AI, and this alliance brings gigawatts to our customers faster than any self-build path in the market," said Jacobo Ortiz, Fermi Co-President & Chief Operating Officer. "Hillcore finances, builds, and operates the plant; Fermi delivers dedicated, behind-the-meter power matched to every tenant lease, with our balance sheet intact and a clear path to owning the asset."

"This is the long-duration infrastructure Hillcore was built for," said Russell Negus, President at Hillcore Energy Capital Corporation. "Backed by Hillcore and our partners' capital platform, and JV Driver's execution capabilities, we intend to deliver first power within 24 months of notice to proceed and to stand behind this plant for decades. Fermi's customer demand and the strategic alliance structure make the Hillcore Power Center immediately financeable, and we're proud to anchor this power program at Project Matador."

Next steps will be for the parties to finalize the constituent agreements and obtain customary approvals.

About Fermi's Project Matador

Fermi America is where AI gets power. The Company is developing one of the world's largest advanced energy and AI ecosystems, on an area in the Texas Panhandle that's more than half the size of Manhattan. text:
Modern AI data centers use an enormous amount of electricity — as much as a city in one location. Because local grids often can’t keep up, new power plants are being built for these data centers along with backup diesel generators, which are designed to run in case of emergency. These generators are extremely polluting and increasingly used in non-emergency situations, as tech companies look to grow at all costs.

Rather than addressing the pollution these generators create, the Trump administration doubled down by:

ordering the AI data centers to run their dirty generators more frequently

letting certain power plants not install any pollution controls for acid rain

Now, its proposing a rule that would allow companies to seek and receive “minor source” air permits without gathering public input.

Since “minor source” permits are less stringent, tech companies often divide large projects into smaller ones to qualify — bypassing normal Clean Air Act requirements. This loophole has fueled the recent explosion of AI data centers and health harming pollution. The administration’s new rule will supercharge it by keeping the public in the dark.

Limiting the transparency of the buildout of these dirty generators will have real consequences. The large-scale generators at AI data centers are usually powered by diesel and are polluting the air we breathe with dangerous chemicals. This type of permit applies to all kinds of facilities, from chemical plants to sterilizers to hazardous waste combustors, exacerbating the damage that this rule will cause.
