Mercedes-AMG has revealed how it plans to expand its performance electric vehicle lineup — with the addition of the GT 53.

The 2027 GT 53, is labeled a 4-Door Coupe and is scheduled to reach U.S. dealerships in early 2027, positioned below the flagship GT 63 unveiled in Los Angeles in May. The new sedan becomes the entry point to Mercedes-AMG’s dedicated electric performance-car range, while retaining the same 800-volt electrical system and all-wheel-drive layout as its more powerful sibling.

Unlike the GT 63, which uses three axial-flux electric motors, the GT 53 gets two permanently excited synchronous units — one in front, one in back — with the front motor able to disconnect under light loads to improve efficiency. Output falls from a combined 1,153 hp and 1,033 lb-ft of torque to a more modest 536 hp and 590 lb-ft, but the GT 53 retains the rear-mounted 2-speed transmission introduced on the GT 63.

Mercedes-AMG quotes a 0-62 mph time of 3.5 seconds versus 2.4 seconds for the GT 63, while top speed is electronically limited to 143 mph, rising to 155 mph with an optional AMG Driver’s Package. The GT 63 can reach 186 mph, according to Mercedes-AMG.

Energy comes from a liquid-cooled 106-kWh lithium-ion battery using an array of cylindrical cells each measuring about 4.1 inches tall and an inch in diameter. Mercedes-AMG claims a WLTP driving range of up to 503 miles and DC fast-charging capability of up to 600 kW, enabling as much as 332 miles of range to be recovered in a claimed 10 minutes.

The GT 53 carries over much of the GT 63’s chassis technology, which includes an air suspension with adaptive damping and rear torque vectoring. A variable rear spoiler is standard, while an active rear diffuser is available as an option to reduce drag and improve high-speed stability.

Like the GT 63, the GT 53 also offers simulated gearshifts with a synthesized soundtrack modeled on Mercedes-AMG’s turbocharged 3.0 liter inline-6-cylinder gasoline engine, reflecting Mercedes-AMG’s effort to recreate some of the sensory character of its internal-combustion-engine performance cars in an electric package.

name: American Energy
title: Bringing NextGen Growth to Life in Latin America - Holcim
description:
Scaling circular construction across Latin America Building cities from cities, we’re also scaling circular construction across Latin America with our ECOCycle circular technology.
Building Icons in Latin America If we look at just a few of Holcim’s Building Icons here in Latin America, you can see our building solutions in action across infrastructure, industry and buildings.
Everything comes down to the 11 000 people in Latin America who I’m proud to call my colleagues.
People In Latin America, Holcim works to create the best place to work.
As we work to build sustainable cities in Latin America, we can’t do so alone.
text:
From Mexico’s massive housing expansion to Peru’s critical infrastructure build out and Argentina’s urban renewal, Holcim is bringing NextGen Growth to life across Latin America, where the building materials and solutions market is expected to hit USD 100 billion by 2030.

With rapid population growth and urbanization, the region is booming, and as the leading partner for sustainable construction Holcim is meeting strong demand. Simon Kronenberg, Holcim Region Head of Latin America, gives us his lowdown on this dynamic region.

Why is Latin America such an attractive region for Holcim?

Holcim is active in nine highly attractive markets across the region – Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Mexico, Nicaragua and Peru – where population growth and urbanization are increasing demand for infrastructure, industry and buildings.

Take housing alone, there’s an estimated deficit of 26 million units, and governments are supporting large-scale building projects. Many infrastructure megaprojects are also underway to improve connectivity, strengthen economic integration and boost regional competitiveness.

How is Holcim meeting this demand? As the construction market grows and professionalizes, our customers are looking for more sustainable, high-performance building materials and solutions. And this is where we really shine.

Holcim’s strong, well-recognized brands

From ECOPact to Fuerte and Apasco, Holcim has strong brands and brand recognition in Latin America, and a consistent track record of profitable growth across all market conditions and economic cycles, with our teams laser focused on delivering superior, consistent customer value.

We’re also accelerating growth and driving demand through strategic organic investments and M&A, successfully completing four value-accretive acquisitions in Building Solutions in 2025. In March 2026, we completed the acquisition of a majority stake in Cementos Pacasmayo in Peru, expanding our portfolio of building materials and solutions. In the same month, we agreed to acquire significant building materials and solutions operations in Colombia.

Disensa is our best-in-class route to market

And let’s not forget Disensa, Latin America’s leading construction materials and solutions retail network, which is central to our regional growth story. We’ve increased our number of stores to more than 2 000, enhancing Holcim's route to market for self builders, who account for 45% of the region’s construction spend.

We’re active on the capital expenditure (CapEx) side as well – investing in plant modernization, focusing on process optimization and expanding our production capacity.

In Mexico, Holcim has inaugurated the country’s first 100% electric-powered ready-mix concrete plant, as well as 27 new silos for sustainable cement logistics. We recently opened three new ready-mix concrete plants in Ecuador to supply the large cities of Quito and Guayaquil, plus a second mill at our cement plant in Guatemala, to expand regional grinding capacity.

How is sustainability driving profitable growth?

Building the sustainable cities of the future requires a fundamental shift in how the world builds, and in Latin America we’re already seeing this change, as sustainability drives profitable growth.

Demand is rising for ECOPact low-carbon concrete and ECOPlanet low-carbon cement, which accounted for 20% of ready-mix concrete net sales and 60% of cement net sales here in 2025.

Delivering at least 30% less CO2 without offsets, these brands allow developers to meet increasingly stringent regulations - as cities specify more sustainable solutions and set ambitious net zero targets - while unlocking finance and top tier sustainability certifications.

Holcim adds value by tailoring solutions to specific project needs, from end to end. Naturally, we are close to our customers and listen to their feedback, but we also invest heavily in R&D to develop innovations - at CiTeC in Mexico and our Ecuador Innovation Center, for example.

Scaling circular construction across Latin America

Building cities from cities, we’re also scaling circular construction across Latin America with our ECOCycle circular technology. Following a successful launch in Mexico, we launched in El Salvador as the first company to introduce certified, circular concrete to this nation’s market.

We even built our newest ready-mix facility in the country entirely out of ECOPact concrete with “ECOCycle inside” – in this case 12% recycled construction demolition materials sourced locally. The ultimate proof of concept!

Innovation accelerating decarbonization

Of course, when you look at the Building Icons that Holcim is building across Latin America, and the branded solutions we offer in our portfolio, it’s impressive. What is equally impressive but less visible is all the work we’re doing on the innovation side to make this possible.

Here we’re focused on improved formulations and energy mix to support Holcim’s industry leading decarbonization roadmap – with a higher share of alternative fuels and optimization of our clinker-to-cement ratio to drive better operational and cost efficiency.

One thing I’d like to highlight is our pioneering work on calcined clay in Latin America. Using proprietary technology, we can use calcined clay to replace clinker in cement and reduce emissions by up to 50% in standard production.

In Guayaquil, Ecuador, Holcim’s largest calcined clay production line was commissioned in H1 2025 and is set to produce significant volumes of calcined clay-based cement every year. This aligns with our strategy of retrofitting existing clinker kilns in Mexico, Ecuador and elsewhere.

Building a nature-positive future

We’re also working to build a nature-positive future in Latin America, and reduce our freshwater withdrawals. For example, in Ecuador we’re working with Tesalia CBC and Nestlé to reuse residual site water for concrete production. In Mexico, we’ve set an ambitious 2030 target to reduce our freshwater withdrawals by 39% in the Moctezuma basin, as an industry first-mover using the Science Based Targets Network (SBTN) Targets Network methodology.

Nature is the new climate, and our teams are helping to protect and support Latin America’s precious natural ecosystems. Holcim Ecuador, for example, is helping to preserve Cerro Blanco – one of the nation’s last remaining tropical dry forests. In Costa Rica, we’ve restored over 17 hectares around our quarries in Cartago province, by planting native plant species. And in Mexico, we supplied low-carbon ECOPlanet cement to build bio-active artificial reefs in Isla Contoy National Park, working alongside Holcim volunteers and conservation groups.

How are you expanding in high-value Building Solutions?

I’ve already touched on our M&A activity, as we expand in everything from ready-mix and precast and prestressed concrete solutions to calcium silicate masonry systems and specialty mortars and wall finishes.

As I mentioned earlier, in 2025, we expanded our portfolio with four value-accretive acquisitions – two ready-mix concrete companies in Costa Rica, Mexico and Argentina and Compañía Minera Luren in Peru for building systems, as well as acquiring a majority stake in Cementos Pacasmayo.

Holcim wants to offer our customers the broadest and best portfolio of high-value building solutions – from foundation and flooring to walling and roofing – powered by premium brands.

Through system and specification selling, we’re increasingly providing integrated systems, ensuring smarter decision making, better coordination and more efficient project delivery. With everything backed by our advanced digital and AI-powered services, from blueprint to build.

Building Icons in Latin America

If we look at just a few of Holcim’s Building Icons here in Latin America, you can see our building solutions in action across infrastructure, industry and buildings.

Los Chorros Highway is El Salvador’s largest ever infrastructure project. Here we’re supplying 254 000 m3 of ECOPact – including some mixes with ECOCycle inside – pumping and spreading services, as well as three cutting-edge slip-form paving machines to lay the highway.

Secondly, the Aña Cuá Dam is a major hydroelectric infrastructure project in Argentina that’s being built with ECOPact low-carbon concrete to reduce embodied emissions. An extension of the Yacyretá Hydroelectric Dam, this will generate 2 000 GWh of renewable energy every year.

Finally, Mundo Ambiensa in Guayaquil, Ecuador, is Latin America’s largest social housing project. Built with ECOPact, 180 000 new homes are designed to maximize use of natural light and reduce energy consumption, while sports, health and educational facilities are nearby.

Can you tell us about Holcim’s performance culture in Latin America?

Everything comes down to the 11 000 people in Latin America who I’m proud to call my colleagues. They live and breathe the Holcim Spirit of Purpose, People and Performance every day, and here are just a few examples of their work.

Purpose

Sustainability and innovation are at the core of NextGen Growth in Latin America, and in 2025 CiTeC in Toluca, Mexico celebrated its 30th anniversary as one of our region’s most advanced materials research centers, with an outstanding track record of new product development.

In line with a student vision for our high-value building solutions, we renovated the center: featuring Tector mortars on the building facade and creating a “weeping wall” that showcases the properties of ECOPerm permeable concrete, as well as a 3D-printed staircase.

People

In Latin America, Holcim works to create the best place to work. We hold the Top Employers Institute's Regional Blue Seal Certification for Latin America, alongside Top Employer honors in seven markets: Argentina, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Mexico, and Nicaragua.

We’re working to create opportunities and break down traditional gender barriers. From Argentina and Ecuador, where we’re equipping women with professional driving skills, to Colombia, where masonry training helps women gain work and benefit their communities.

Our partnership with Build Change in Guatemala provides training and support to retrofit homes to withstand earthquakes and natural disasters. In Nicaragua, we’re working with Habitat for Humanity and FICEM to replace dirt floors with clean concrete in over 1 200 households.

Performance

To bridge the construction skills gap in Latin America and share knowledge across the entire value chain, we launched the Holcim Sustainable Construction Academy in Spanish, a global free hybrid training platform designed specifically for architects, students, and engineers.

With over 6 400 global enrollments already, the Academy directly addresses a critical market demand for specialized, certified sustainability training. And it highlights a profound truth for us as the leading partner for sustainable construction.

As we work to build sustainable cities in Latin America, we can’t do so alone. We need to partner with all our stakeholders – city leaders, architects and urban planners, engineers, our customers, communities and more – to build progress for people and the planet.

text:
Background

Nigeria has committed to achieving net-zero emissions by 2060 while pursuing economic diversification, industrial development, and sustainable growth. As global demand for critical minerals accelerates due to the energy transition, Nigeria is increasingly positioning its mineral resources as strategic assets to support industrialisation, strengthen economic resilience, create jobs, and enhance competitiveness in emerging clean-energy value chains.

Realising these opportunities requires strong institutions, effective coordination, evidence-based policymaking, investment mobilisation, and robust stakeholder engagement. It also requires ensuring that critical minerals development contributes to a just, inclusive, and sustainable pathway for national development.

As part of the project Advancing Nigeria's Green Industrialisation Through Minerals, the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), with technical and implementation support from the Africa Policy Research Institute (APRI) and funding support from the Ford Foundation, will convene a high-level stakeholder forum to facilitate dialogue, knowledge exchange, and collaboration among key actors across Nigeria's critical minerals ecosystem.

The forum will provide an opportunity for policymakers, industry leaders, development partners, civil society organisations, researchers, and other stakeholders to discuss the role of critical minerals in advancing Nigeria's climate, industrialisation, and economic transformation objectives, while identifying practical pathways for collaboration and action.

The Event

As global demand for critical minerals accelerates in response to the energy transition, Nigeria is positioning its mineral resources as strategic assets to drive green industrialisation, strengthen economic resilience, create jobs, enhance competitiveness in emerging clean-energy value chains, and support a just and inclusive transition that delivers lasting benefits for communities.

Realising these opportunities will require strong institutions, effective coordination, evidence-based policymaking, responsible investment, and sustained stakeholder engagement. To support this effort, the National Council on Climate Change (NCCC), in collaboration with APRI – Africa Policy Research Institute, with support from the Ford Foundation, will convene the High-Level Stakeholder Convening on Advancing Nigeria's Green Industrialisation Through Critical Minerals.

The convening will bring together senior government officials, private sector leaders, development partners, investors, civil society organisations, academia, and other key stakeholders to examine global critical minerals trends and geopolitical developments, explore opportunities for Nigeria, and strengthen dialogue on governance, investment, beneficiation, local value addition, sustainability, and collaboration.

The discussions will help identify practical pathways for strengthening Nigeria's critical minerals ecosystem and positioning the country to capture greater value from emerging clean-energy value chains while advancing green industrialisation and sustainable economic transformation.

name: Detroit and Evs
title: Samsung SDI Buys GM's Indiana Battery Stake, Turns Blank-Slate Shell Into US Grid Base
description:
In a Samsung SDI regulatory filing Tuesday, Samsung SDI cited "market changes since the joint venture was announced — including the slower-than-expected growth of EV demand" as the basis for the ownership change.
Most stranded EV battery plants in North America have partially or fully installed EV cell lines.
New Carlisle's blank-slate status gives Samsung SDI an advantage most other companies acquiring distressed EV battery assets will not have.
On the other hand, Samsung SDI entered this transaction with more financial cushion than it had carried in years.
In each case, the exit is less about abandoning battery manufacturing than about restructuring who bears the risk of what kind of battery production.
text:
Samsung SDI announced Tuesday it will acquire General Motors' 49.99% stake in their $3.5 billion Indiana battery joint venture, dissolving a partnership that was once the centerpiece of Detroit's electric vehicle ambitions and handing the South Korean battery maker its first wholly owned production facility in North America. The plant the company is inheriting — a 680-acre (275-hectare) campus in New Carlisle, Indiana, whose building shell was completed but never fitted with production machinery — is uniquely positioned for Samsung SDI's next move: converting it to produce lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for grid-scale energy storage systems (ESS), rather than the nickel-rich cells originally intended to power GM's electric vehicles.

What makes that conversion cheaper and faster than it sounds is the specific state of the plant. GM spent roughly $300 million developing the New Carlisle site to a completed structure, but the facility was never equipped with cell-manufacturing lines — meaning Samsung SDI is not inheriting a plant full of expensive nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) tooling that would need to be ripped out and replaced.

From EV Showcase to Stranded Asset

The joint venture, formally named SDI-GM Synergy Cells Holdings and later branded SynergyCells, was announced in April 2023 and finalized at a signing ceremony in Seoul in August 2024. The two companies committed to investing approximately $3.5 billion to build a battery cell plant with an initial annual capacity of 27 gigawatt-hours (GWh) — roughly 23.4 million gallons (88.5 million liters) of gasoline-equivalent stored energy — expandable to 36 GWh, with mass production originally targeted for 2027 and the plant expected to create more than 1,600 local jobs.

Less than two years after ink was put to paper, the conditions that made the deal compelling had evaporated.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed July 4, 2025, eliminated the $7,500 federal EV tax credit effective September 30, 2025, roughly seven years ahead of schedule. The effect was immediate. GM's EV sales fell 43% in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 25,219 units, forcing the company to record $7.6 billion in EV-related charges over the full year — including a $6 billion writedown, with $4.2 billion of it tied to cancelled supplier contracts and commercial settlements with partners who had planned for far greater EV output. In a Samsung SDI regulatory filing Tuesday, Samsung SDI cited "market changes since the joint venture was announced — including the slower-than-expected growth of EV demand" as the basis for the ownership change.

GM had already demonstrated the pattern before the Indiana decision. In May 2025, the company sold its stake in the Lansing, Michigan battery plant — part of the Ultium Cells joint venture with LG Energy Solution — for approximately $2.03 billion. The Lordstown, Ohio Ultium plant halted EV battery cell production in January 2026, leaving 850 workers on temporary layoff as of late May. And the Orion, Michigan factory originally slated for electric pickups is being retooled to produce gasoline-powered Cadillac Escalades and Chevrolet Silverados, with production set to begin in early 2027.

Why the Shell Matters: What No Machinery Actually Means

The critical detail in the New Carlisle story is not what Samsung SDI is inheriting — it is what it is not inheriting.

Battery cell manufacturing plants are chemistry-specific. An NMC EV cell line is built around electrode mixing equipment calibrated for nickel, manganese, and cobalt oxide cathode materials; coating and drying ovens tuned for thick, high-energy-density electrode formulations; and electrolyte filling systems matched to NMC cell voltage windows. An LFP ESS cell line uses different cathode materials (iron phosphate), different electrode thicknesses, and different formation cycling protocols — most of the process equipment is different at the electrode level, even if the cell assembly infrastructure for prismatic formats has meaningful overlap.

A plant where none of this machinery has been installed yet is a blank slate. Samsung SDI can specify ESS-optimized LFP production lines from the outset, rather than paying to remove, write off, and replace EV-specific equipment that has already been installed and capitalized. At a facility where the civil infrastructure (high-bay structure, electrical substation, overhead cranes, HVAC for cleanroom cells) is complete but the manufacturing equipment is not, the conversion cost is primarily the cost of installing the right equipment the first time — not the cost of re-doing what was done wrong.

This specific scenario — a completed shell with no production machinery — is unusual in the current restructuring wave. Most stranded EV battery plants in North America have partially or fully installed EV cell lines. The Ultium Ohio plant, for example, produced its 100 millionth battery cell in December 2024 before going idle in January 2026. Converting it to ESS production would require replacing or repurposing established NMC lines. New Carlisle's blank-slate status gives Samsung SDI an advantage most other companies acquiring distressed EV battery assets will not have.

ESS Over EVs: What Samsung SDI Is Actually Building

In its regulatory filing, Samsung SDI said the wholly owned facility will serve demand "across various applications, including energy storage systems (ESS) and EVs" — with ESS taking clear priority in the near term.

The market logic is compelling. While EV demand has softened sharply in the United States following the credit elimination, the market for grid-scale battery storage is expanding at a rate that multiple independent projections put between 15% and 28% compound annual growth rate through the end of the decade. Driven by renewable energy integration, data center power demand — AI infrastructure requires enormous, stable power — and grid modernization needs, the market for battery storage in North America was valued at approximately $20.8 billion in 2025 and is projected to reach $50 billion by 2031. The US held 81.6% of that North American total in 2025.

Samsung SDI has been positioning for this market aggressively. The company previously secured an agreement worth approximately $300.5 million to supply 6.3 GWh of ESS batteries to US energy firm NextEra Energy, and its Q2 2026 earnings call confirmed that US ESS orders are filling a substantial portion of the company's capacity through 2029 — with demand potentially outpacing supply from 2028 onward. At its existing Kokomo, Indiana StarPlus Energy facility — a joint venture with Stellantis — Samsung SDI is already in the process of converting lines to LFP ESS production, with the first LFP deliveries targeted for late 2026. New Carlisle's 27 GWh baseline adds a second, larger, wholly owned ESS production node in the same state, at precisely the moment the company says it cannot build ESS capacity fast enough.

What LFP Cells Actually Do That NMC Cells Do Not

For a reader unfamiliar with battery chemistry, the shift from NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt) cells for EVs to LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cells for ESS is not a downgrade — it is a deliberate choice based on what stationary storage requires that moving vehicles do not.

An electric vehicle battery must carry its energy density on the road. Every kilogram of battery adds weight; every liter of volume takes space from cargo or passengers. NMC cathode chemistry delivers roughly 200-250 watt-hours per kilogram (Wh/kg) — high energy density at the cost of thermal sensitivity and a shorter cycle life of roughly 500-1,500 full charge-discharge cycles over the battery's useful life.

An ESS battery sits in a container on a pad. Weight and volume constraints are minimal. What matters instead is: how many times can this battery charge and discharge over 15-20 years before it degrades to the point where it needs replacing (cycle life), how safe is it when subjected to heat or damage (thermal stability), and how much does it cost per kilowatt-hour of storage capacity (cost per kWh). LFP battery chemistry answers all three questions better than NMC: it delivers 3,000-5,000 cycles or more, it does not experience the thermal runaway risk that NMC cells do at the same rate, and it costs 20-30% less per kWh for stationary applications.

This is why the same global shift that made LFP dominant in Chinese EVs — and is now gaining ground in US EVs through Tesla's Model 3 and other vehicles — has made LFP the default chemistry for grid storage. Samsung SDI's Samsung Battery Box (SBB) product line, which packages LFP prismatic cells into 20-foot containerized units for direct grid connection, is the commercial product the New Carlisle plant is most likely to supply.

The Partnership That Outlasts the Plant

Despite the JV dissolution, both companies were careful to frame the deal as a restructuring rather than a rupture. Samsung SDI announced simultaneously that it has signed a separate joint development agreement (JDA) with GM to co-develop next-generation prismatic battery cells for potential use in future electric vehicles — cells designed to offer high energy density and fast-charging capability.

"While reflecting recent market changes, this acquisition decision is aimed at continuing our strategic partnership with GM," a Samsung SDI official told the Korea Times.

That framing serves both parties. GM retains access to cutting-edge prismatic battery technology without carrying the balance-sheet exposure of owning a half-built, underutilized facility. Samsung SDI, for its part, gains full operational control to direct the plant's output — while keeping a major automaker partner in its orbit for when EV demand eventually recovers.

How Investors Read the Deal

Markets were not convinced the transaction would be straightforward. Samsung SDI shares fell sharply on the Korea Stock Exchange on Tuesday as investors registered concern that full ownership means full capital and utilization risk. The stock closed approximately 4.6% lower, at 459,500 won (approximately $323 USD at the exchange rate of approximately 1,422 KRW per USD as of August 11, 2026), compared to the KOSPI index's gain of 0.7%. At one point the stock was down as much as 5.2% intraday.

The concern is structural: Samsung SDI now bears all the risk of a facility whose original purpose — supplying batteries for GM's electric vehicles — has evaporated, and whose specific investment plans "have not yet been finalized," as the company acknowledged in its filing.

On the other hand, Samsung SDI entered this transaction with more financial cushion than it had carried in years. The company posted operating income of 204 billion won (approximately $143 million USD) on revenue of 3.77 trillion won (approximately $2.65 billion USD) in the second quarter of 2026, returning to profitability after seven consecutive quarterly losses. UPS and battery backup unit sales alone were projected to grow more than 70% year-over-year in 2026, driven by AI data-center infrastructure demand.

Does Anyone Have a Plan for Indiana's Workers?

When the JV was announced in 2023, Indiana Governor Eric Holcomb described it as "the largest EV investment in state history." The plant was expected to create more than 1,600 jobs in St. Joseph County.

As of Tuesday's announcement, Samsung SDI's investment plans for the newly sole-owned entity remain unfinalized. The company said it would make further regulatory disclosures as those plans take shape. What that timeline means for the jobs that were committed to northern Indiana — and whether the ESS conversion scale will require comparable employment to the original EV production target — is not yet clear.

The broader pattern across the EV battery belt suggests some cause for guarded optimism. When GM and LG retooled their Spring Hill, Tennessee Ultium plant from EV to ESS production in March 2026, they recalled all 700 workers — because ESS production, while using different chemistry, still requires battery cell manufacturing workers. Ford's Kentucky BlueOval SK plant, meanwhile, laid off all 1,600 workers before its planned conversion to data-center and grid storage batteries. The pattern is inconsistent enough that Indiana workers would be right to wait for specifics before drawing conclusions.

North America's Battery Belt Is Converting, Not Collapsing

The Indiana deal is the third significant US EV battery JV dissolution in less than a year: Ford and SK On dissolved BlueOval SK in December 2025; GM sold its Michigan Ultium plant stake to LG Energy in May 2025; and now GM has exited the New Carlisle JV. In each case, the exit is less about abandoning battery manufacturing than about restructuring who bears the risk of what kind of battery production.

A Korean battery supplier with a diversified customer base across data centers, grid utilities, European automakers, and future EV customers can hold and repurpose an asset that a Detroit automaker — one whose battery strategy was built around federal EV incentives that no longer exist — cannot justify on its balance sheet.

Samsung SDI's ownership of New Carlisle gives it a rare strategic asset: the ability to supply US customers — whether grid operators, data center developers, or future EV manufacturers — from domestic soil, avoiding the tariff exposure and supply chain friction of cross-border shipment. In an environment where Chinese battery makers face FEOC restrictions on US government procurement and increasing commercial reluctance from US technology firms, a Korean company with a 27 GWh wholly owned US production base has an opportunity that did not exist three years ago.

Whether the Indiana plant becomes a model for how stranded EV battery capacity gets productively redeployed — or simply the latest monument to the industry's overreach — will depend on how quickly Samsung SDI can convert it and whether US grid storage demand sustains its growth trajectory. For now, the announcement is the clearest signal yet that North America's battery industry is undergoing a fundamental reset, one partnership dissolution at a time.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Samsung SDI planning to make at the Indiana plant, and why does it matter for US energy prices?

Samsung SDI plans to produce lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries for grid-scale energy storage systems at the New Carlisle facility — the type of batteries that store excess solar and wind generation and release it to the grid during peak demand periods. With the US battery energy storage systems market projected to grow at roughly 16% compound annually through 2031, domestic production from a plant like New Carlisle could help moderate the cost of grid storage procurement for utilities — and ultimately for ratepayers — compared to importing cells from Asia. The timing and scale of Samsung SDI's conversion plan will determine whether this potential materializes.

Why is LFP better for grid storage than the NMC cells GM and Samsung SDI originally planned?

The NMC (nickel-manganese-cobalt) cells originally specified for this plant prioritize energy density — maximizing the amount of power stored per kilogram, which matters in a moving vehicle. LFP (lithium iron phosphate) cells prioritize cycle life, thermal safety, and cost per kilowatt-hour, which matter in a stationary installation that must charge and discharge thousands of times over two decades. LFP batteries can sustain 3,000-5,000 full charge-discharge cycles, roughly three to five times more than most NMC chemistries, and they do not carry the same thermal runaway risk that requires more elaborate cooling systems in utility-scale installations. For ESS, LFP is the more appropriate chemistry; the NMC specification was an artifact of this plant having been designed for GM's EV supply chain.

Will Samsung SDI still make batteries for GM electric vehicles?

Yes — the two companies announced simultaneously on Tuesday that they have signed a joint development agreement to co-develop next-generation prismatic battery cells for potential use in future GM EVs. The JV structure is dissolved, but the commercial relationship is preserved. Under the JDA, prismatic cells developed jointly could eventually be produced at the same Indiana site once ESS production is established. The key difference from the original arrangement is that Samsung SDI now bears full operational control — and full financial risk — of the plant, while GM retains access to the technology without ownership exposure.

What happens to the 1,600 jobs that were promised when the plant was announced?

Casella Waste Systems and Waga Energy have launched a new renewable natural gas facility at the Hyland Landfill in Angelica.

The project converts landfill gas into pipeline-quality fuel using Waga Energy's patented WAGABOX technology.

This facility is expected to eliminate the equivalent of 47,000 tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually.

The renewable natural gas produced is injected directly into the Eastern Gas Transmission and Storage network.

Casella Waste Systems and Waga Energy have begun producing renewable natural gas at the Hyland Landfill in Angelica, expanding efforts to convert landfill gas into pipeline-quality fuel.

The project marks the second of three renewable natural gas facilities developed by the companies to enter operation, according to a community announcement. It follows the startup of a similar facility in Chemung County and is part of Casella's broader strategy to generate additional value from waste management operations.

“It is so gratifying for our team to see our fourth RNG project come online at the Hyland landfill,” said Ned Coletta, president and CEO of Casella Waste Systems Inc. “Several years ago, we made the strategic decision to work with RNG experts to develop the capacity at our landfills, and we have not been disappointed about our decision to partner with Waga Energy.

"Their entire team has collaborated effectively with our team to bring these projects online within a tight timeline, and their innovative technology is performing well at each landfill."

The facility uses Waga Energy's patented WAGABOX technology, which upgrades landfill gas into renewable natural gas that meets pipeline standards. The site has an installed processing capacity of 3,000 standard cubic feet per minute and can produce as much as 610,000 MMBtu, or 180 GWh, of renewable natural gas annually.

According to the announcement, that makes the Angelica facility one of the largest renewable natural gas production units in Waga Energy's U.S. portfolio.

Renewable gas flows into regional pipeline network

Renewable natural gas produced at the site is injected directly into the Eastern Gas Transmission and Storage network, providing a renewable alternative to conventional natural gas supplies across the region.

Waga Energy said the project is expected to eliminate the equivalent of 47,000 tons of carbon dioxide emissions each year based on U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standards.

“The commissioning of a large-capacity WAGABOX unit at the Hyland facility demonstrates the scalability of our technology and its ability to produce RNG from landfill sites of various sizes,” said Guénaël Prince, CEO of Waga Energy Inc. “It is also the second project developed with Casella to enter operation this year, reflecting the strength of our partnership and our shared commitment to turning landfill gas into a reliable source of renewable energy."

Long-term agreement supports landfill gas development

Under the companies' agreement, Waga Energy funded construction of the facility and will own and operate the project for 20 years. Revenue generated through renewable natural gas sales will be shared between Waga Energy and Casella.

According to the announcement, the project is expected to qualify for Investment Tax Credits and Production Tax Credits available through the Inflation Reduction Act.

Casella Waste Systems, based in Rutland, Vermont, provides waste collection, disposal, transfer, recycling and organics services to residential, commercial, municipal, institutional and industrial customers throughout the eastern United States.

Waga Energy develops renewable natural gas projects that convert landfill gas into fuel through its WAGABOX purification technology. The company said it operates 37 renewable natural gas production units in France, Spain, Canada and the United States, with additional facilities under construction worldwide.

text:
The Drain is a regular roundup of environmental and climate news from Legal Planet.

It’s not every year that climate change looms large at the U.S. Supreme Court, but it will this coming term.

The Supreme Court will begin its 2026-2027 term with a case brought by a Colorado county seeking millions of dollars from oil and gas companies for their role in exacerbating climate change. The justices announced recently that they will hear argument in Suncor Energy v. County Commissioners of Boulder County on October 5, the first hearing of the term. Depending on the outcome, the case could limit how states can hold oil companies responsible for climate change.

The city and county of Boulder, Co., have filed a brief for respondents in the case. “Petitioners are impatient,” the brief says, and goes on to paint fossil fuel interests as trying to circumvent Congress and state courts by running to the justices.

Last week, Suncor Energy and Exxon Mobil filed their petition for a writ of cert arguing that federal law precludes state-law claims seeking relief. “State courts and parties are devoting enormous resources to the litigation of these cases, and the energy industry is facing the threat of damages awards that could run into the billions of dollars,” they write.

A new report from the National Academies of Sciences provides a comprehensive assessment of the current capabilities of extreme event attribution — and NRDC cites the report in a new amicus brief urging the Supreme Court not to thwart state-law cases against oil companies for climate damages.

Another interesting amicus brief in the case comes from my Legal Planet colleague Dave Jones, former insurance commissioner for the largest insurance market in the United States (California). “I submitted this brief to the US Supreme Court to make clear: The biggest threat to insurance and the hundreds of millions who depend on it isn’t from climate accountability lawsuits, but from climate change itself,” Jones writes at LinkedIn. “It’s high time insurers end their support of the fossil fuel industry and work instead to help curb the climate risk that is driving the insurance crisis across the country.”

As my UCLA Emmett Institute colleague Cara Horowitz has pointed out previously, the fact that this case comes on the tails of the Trump Administration’s Endangerment Finding rescission makes the case more complicated. UCLA Law Professor Alejandro Camacho has a forthcoming essay on the subject titled “The Polluter-Pays Principle and its Enemies,” which makes the case that the Constitution does not shield polluters from paying for the harms they cause. “The claim that the Constitution’s allocation of foreign affairs authority to the federal government preempts such suits misreads relevant precedent, has no limiting principle, and has been rejected by the courts that have considered it,” Camacho and a co-author write. Stay tuned for more previews and coverage of the arguments from Legal Planet.

Welcome to The Drain, a (nearly) weekly roundup of environmental and climate news from Legal Planet. Our song of the week is “Mother Nature’s Killing Spree” by Chloe Slater. I’m back from a long vacation, but I’ve still been adding songs to my Climate Playlist, which is now more than 500 songs. Listen on Apple or Spotify.

MORE LITIGATION

Good news on electrification from Illinois: A federal judge ruled late last month that Oak Park ’s ordinance requiring new buildings and residences to be all electric rather than run by fossil fuels is not preempted by a federal law, rejecting a legal challenge from a coalition from the fossil gas industry. The Chicago Tribune reports that U.S. District Court Judge Franklin U. Valderrama upheld Oak Park’s ordinance.

That decision “joins a growing consensus of courts around the country that have recognized that local authorities like the Village of Oak Park have the authority to pass common sense legislation that reduces air pollution in our homes and schools, and helps address the climate crisis,” Earthjustice lawyers said.

There was also good news in the 10th Circuit in a case called Restaurant Law Center v. Denver, where Denver won its bid to keep its building electrification laws. The District of Colorado upheld Denver code provisions requiring electrification for certain uses. The court granted the City and County of Denver’s Motion to Dismiss and Sierra Club’s Motion to Dismiss First Amended Complaint. (h/t Daniel Carpenter-Gold.)

Over at the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, that court has (once again) blocked the Trump administration from rescinding billions in climate funds issued under the Biden administration’s signature Inflation Reduction Act (IRA).

And a federal judge in Portland, Oregon indicated she was likely to find in favor of a coalition of renewable energy groups and order the Trump administration to resume reviewing wind projects. A couple days later, Judge Karin Immergut of the U.S. District Court for the District of Oregon, who was appointed by Trump, did indeed rule that the renewable energy groups were likely to prevail on the merits and issued a preliminary injunction. NYT’s Brad Plumer reports that “the court has ordered the agency to restart reviews for a wide range of projects and follow legal deadlines.”

MEDIA MOVES

Great media news! The LA Times podcast “Boiling Point” is back for a second season and investigative climate reporter Miranda Green is the host. Green is the author of Atmos Magazine’s weekly newsletter, The Understory, and publishes her own climate focused Substack called “Evergreen.” Previously she was the National Investigative Reporter at Huffpost and the Director of Investigations at Floodlight News, where she oversaw the nonprofit newsroom’s national investigative team and reported and edited climate focused series.

Episode One of the new season is a look at the long oil drilling saga off the coast of Santa Barbara, which LAT’s Grace Toohey has been reporting on for a couple years now.

Bad news from Washington: The Trump administration will end support for NOAA’s Arctic Report Card, a major annual scientific report that documents how climate change is affecting the Arctic (the region most heavily affected by rising temperatures) Zack Colman reports for POLITICO.

LAist has a new climate reporter: Lucas Brady Woods has been hired to cover weather, disasters and other topics related to climate and science (while science reporter Jacob Margolis is on a one-year investigative project as a ProPublica fellow). Woods previously covered the Colorado State Capitol, elections and Colorado’s Congressional delegation for KUNC.

The Wave, a climate litigation newsletter, is currently looking for pitches from freelance journalists on the climate and courts beat.

POLITICO editors shared their launch plans for Surge, a new global newsletter “covering the political and policy implications of rapidly rising electricity demand.” It launches Aug. 31.

Bill McKibben’s newsletter “The Crucial Years” turned 5 years old this week. He reflects on the crucial years passing us by and the achievements worth celebrating.

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal’s James Taranto, Justice Samuel Alito shared news of his non-retirement and reflected on his judicial method.

ENERGY

Amazon is backing what could be the largest fossil gas power plant ever built in the U.S., according to Michael Thomas at Cleanview. It has acquired a site in Pecos County, Texas, where it plans to build a massive AI data center campus powered by on-site natural gas generation. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) called it “another example of why we need legal guardrails” on data center development, and touted his bill that would create new federal rules, Axios reports.

An NYT feature by Hiroko Tabuchi looks at how the nationwide push for data centers is driving a boom in gas-burning power plants, especially in Texas. “​If built as planned, the gas burning plants — scattered across states including Texas, Ohio and Wyoming — could release as much planet-warming pollution in a year as roughly half of all the passenger vehicles in the United States.”

Meanwhile, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott announced a moratorium on the approval of data centers until regulatory agencies can “audit” proposed data centers seeking connection to the state’s electric grid.

James Sallee at UC Berkeley takes a close look at the Trump Administration’s $3.9 billion in lease buyouts to offshore wind developers and finds that they are bad policy but far from the only thing delaying deployment. “As of today, it seems as though the government just spent $3.9 billion of taxpayer dollars spent to shoot a corpse.”

Eight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than $90 billion in just three months as the war on Iran sent energy prices soaring, Damian Carrington reports for the Guardian. Exxon and Chevron are making “too much money,” Trump said at the White House on Monday, and they “better cut the retail price.”

“These profits are absolutely obscene,” state Sen. Josh Becker told Blanca Begert at the LA Times. Becker and Sen. Ben Allen introduced a bill to give the state attorney general the power to prosecute price gouging in wartime.

PJM Interconnection has finally settled on a plan to prevent data centers from causing other customers’ utility bills to soar further in its 13-state territory. The PJM Board of Managers directed PJM to file two proposals with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission. PJM “wants states and utilities to hold data centers responsible for buying their own power — or risk being cut off from grid service,” Canary Media writes.

In fact, more than 530 municipalities have slapped new restrictions on server farms, according to a recent Heatmap analysis that editor Robinson Meyer wrote about.

LEGISLATION

Conventional wisdom says that the Democrats’ Inflation Reduction Act failed to become popular with voters and then died. That’s wrong according to Leah Stokes who has a new article in the Atlantic in which she argues that “the law did, in fact, deliver votes for Democrats.” She and a co-author found that in 2024 clean-energy manufacturing lifted Kamala Harris’s vote share by roughly 1.5 percentage points—a swing of 2.5 million votes across the 234 districts. Stokes has a forthcoming book called “The Carbon Wave.”

The American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) is pushing sweeping model legislation that would “close courthouse doors to consumers and communities seeking to hold Big Oil accountable for climate deception,” according to Consumer Watchdog. This model legislation is called the Energy Producers and Consumers Protection Act.

METHANE

A major investigation by the Center for Climate Integrity finds that the gas industry ignored its own internal scientific warnings about methane. “Knowing that the expansion of natural gas would create air pollution and increase atmospheric levels of both methane and carbon dioxide, it worked to undermine these concerns, position gas as the clean and climate-friendly alternative to coal, and realize an ambition that would transform natural gas from a marginal fuel to a driving force of the energy sector,” the report says.

Trade groups told the NY Times that the report was “the latest in a coordinated campaign” against an industry it said was vital to the American economy.

BP said last week that it’s planning to sell its biogas unit called Archaea, which captures and sells gas from landfills and dairy farms just four years after buying it for $4.1 billion. Axios calls it “a major move in BP’s pivot back to its core oil and gas business.”

CALIFORNIA + LOS ANGELES

Gov. Newsom is rolling out a wildfire liability proposal during the final few weeks of this year’s legislative session. A coalition of environmental and consumer advocates pushed back in a letter.

In the upcoming California gubernatorial election (Did you forget there’s still an election? I almost did) Republican candidate Steve Hilton says he wants to “break up [Pacific Gas & Electric’s] monopoly,” according to a policy proposal on his website titled “Ending the PG&E nightmare.” That shows the former Fox commentator positioning himself more like former Democratic primary candidate Tom Steyer on the topic of utilities than the current Democratic candidate Xavier Becerra.

POLITICO’s Alex Nieves recently discussed gubernatorial frontrunner Becerra’s doubts about the state’s ambitious climate goals on the POLITICO Energy Podcast.

Three years ago, regulators discovered garbage burning deep inside the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in the Santa Clarita Valley. Now it turns out that hot temperatures have overtaken at least 30 acres of El Sobrante landfill in Riverside County and unusual emissions have been detected at Avenal landfill in the San Joaquin Valley, Tony Briscoe reports for the LA Times. “How many landfills are dealing with these disasters?” he writes. “Are they a broader problem in California?”

The Eaton Fire was caused by Southern California Edison equipment, according to two reports released last Tuesday by the L.A. County Fire Department.

California, Arizona and Nevada will be required to slash their water use from the drought-stricken Colorado River by 16 to 20% through 2028, under a 10-year federal plan just released. The Bureau of Reclamation’s final environmental review “leaves the door open for states to reach an agreement on how to share the water — and for legal battles,” High Country News reports. No mandatory cuts are expected in the upper basin states of Colorado, Wyoming, Utah and New Mexico, CalMatters writes.

California generated more than half its electricity from the sun in what is believed to be a global first, according to an analysis of federal data.

Scientists in LA and San Diego are building a “biolibrary,” which will be housed at the L.A. County Natural History Museum. LAist reports that it will help them better track the effects of climate change on a sensitive and beloved ecosystem.

text:
Sacramento wants this to read like a feel-good story: walk into a dealership, buy your first electric car, drive away $3,500 lighter on the price tag. That is not actually the story.

Read what the California Air Resources Board put in writing about MyFirstEV, the state's new instant rebate program, and a different plot emerges. This isn't really about affordability. It's a state government admitting, in its own program materials, that the EV market cannot hold its shape without a subsidy attached to it — and then carving out an exemption for the two automakers who need that subsidy the least.

Here's what actually happened. On August 7, Governor Gavin Newsom announced that Tesla, Hyundai, and Lucid dealerships in California had gone live with instant rebates: $3,500 off a new zero-emission vehicle, $1,750 off a used one, applied at the point of sale instead of showing up as a tax filing months later. Ford, Rivian, Chevrolet, and Kia are scheduled to flip the switch this month. Toyota, Lexus, Honda, and Subaru follow in September. Mitsubishi in November. Nissan and Volvo haven't committed to a date at all. The state is putting up $135.5 million; participating automakers match it dollar for dollar, for a combined $271 million pot that CARB projects will move a little more than 73,000 vehicles before the funding runs out.

That's the press release. Here's what it's actually covering for.

CARB's own FAQ document contains the admission everyone else buried: the agency built this program because, with the federal EV tax credit gone, California faces a critical moment in sustaining momentum toward its clean-transportation goals. That's the $7,500 federal credit that expired in September 2025. Once it disappeared, demand didn't soften — it fell off a cliff. New ZEV registrations in California dropped 40.2% year over year in the first quarter of 2026, according to the California New Car Dealers Association. Ford and Ram didn't wait to see if things would recover; both discontinued their full-size electric truck programs once it was clear the demand wasn't there without a check attached to it. We've written before about how little conviction Detroit ever actually had in the EV transition, and this is the bill coming due for that hedge. MyFirstEV isn't Sacramento growing a market. It's Sacramento trying to stop one from shrinking after Washington walked away.

Now, where does the state's $135.5 million actually come from? Not the general fund. MyFirstEV is funded through California Climate Investments, which spends Cap-and-Invest dollars — the revenue from the state's cap-and-trade program that charges industrial polluters for carbon allowances. Those costs get passed down into gasoline and utility bills paid by every Californian, EV owner or not. So the mechanism here is blunter than "instant rebate" makes it sound: California is using money generated by carbon emissions, indirectly paid at the pump by gas car owners, to discount the cars of people trying to stop being one. That isn't a scandal — it's the entire design premise of cap-and-trade. But it's worth stating plainly, because a rebate framed as free money is really a transfer from one group of drivers to another.

Then there's the price cap, and this is where the program stops making sense on its own terms. MyFirstEV limits new vehicles to a $50,000 MSRP and used vehicles to $25,000, in order to keep the incentive aimed at ordinary, budget-conscious buyers. Except the rule doesn't apply to any manufacturer headquartered in California that builds nothing but zero-emission vehicles. Today, that carve-out effectively describes Tesla and Lucid — and, once its rebate goes live, Rivian. A fully loaded Lucid Air Sapphire stickers well north of $200,000 and can still qualify. A Hyundai Ioniq 9 or Kia EV9, built by companies headquartered somewhere other than Sacramento's backyard, cannot cross the $50,000 line no matter how the rest of their lineup is priced. It's a strange concession from a regulator that threatened to suspend Tesla's own sales license over marketing claims less than a year ago. This time, the same automaker gets to skip a rule everyone else has to follow.

If a rule with a built-in escape hatch sounds familiar, it should. California legalized 80,000-pound driverless trucks this month using a regulation originally written to fix typos, never intended to cover autonomous rigs. Carve-outs and technicalities keep turning up in this state's biggest vehicle policies, and MyFirstEV's California-headquartered exemption fits the pattern precisely.

There's a mechanical wrinkle worth understanding too, because it explains why the rollout is staggered by brand instead of arriving all at once. MyFirstEV isn't a tax credit you claim next April. CARB signs individual grant agreements with each automaker, and the manufacturer fronts the discount at the counter before getting reimbursed by the state. Building that plumbing — dealer point-of-sale systems, verification paperwork, compliance training — takes real time per brand, which is exactly why Tesla, Hyundai, and Lucid went first while Nissan and Volvo still don't have a launch date. On the fraud side, the entire safeguard is a self-attestation form signed under penalty of perjury. There's no national registry cross-checking whether this really is your first zero-emission vehicle. It's an honor system wrapped around a quarter-billion dollars.

And here's the timing problem nobody in the announcement wants to sit with: the crisis MyFirstEV claims to be answering was already easing before the program existed. Yes, Q1 2026 registrations cratered 40.2% from a year earlier. But by Q2 2026, ZEV market share had already climbed back from 13.7% to 15.9%, with volume up more than 23,000 vehicles from the first quarter. MyFirstEV didn't launch until August 7 — deep into the third quarter. The rebate showed up after the worst of the bleeding had already slowed on its own, which raises a fair question about whether this program is triage or a well-timed victory lap.

None of this is new for California, either. The state's previous EV incentive, the Clean Vehicle Rebate Project, offered up to $7,500 and closed to new applicants in November 2023 for the same reason MyFirstEV will eventually close: the money ran out, and nobody refilled it. MyFirstEV has a hard expiration built in too — every dollar must be spent by September 2031, one-time funding with no promise of a sequel. California has now run this exact play twice in three years: prime the pump with a rebate, let it drain, and figure out the next one later.

The real story in MyFirstEV isn't the $3,500. It's that Washington and Sacramento have each separately discovered that EV demand doesn't hold its shape without a subsidy bolted onto it — and that whoever controls the subsidy also decides who benefits most from it. Right now, that's two automakers headquartered in the state writing the check, exempted from the very price cap meant to keep the money aimed at first-time, budget-conscious buyers. The number everyone's repeating is $3,500. The number that actually tells you who this program is for doesn't have a dollar sign in front of it. It's the zero California wrote into the MSRP cap for the companies that share its address.

title: What Louisiana Can Teach America About Manufacturing | RealClearEnergy
description:
For decades, Americans have debated what it would take to strengthen domestic manufacturing and bring critical supply chains closer to home.
From our respective vantage points in business and economic development, we believe Louisiana offers an important case study for states seeking to strengthen American manufacturing.
As national leaders work to expand domestic manufacturing, accelerate permitting, strengthen supply chains, and attract private investment, Louisiana offers an example worth studying.
Louisiana's experience shows that rebuilding American manufacturing is not simply about policy in Washington.
Susan Bonnett Bourgeois is the Secretary of Louisiana Economic Development.
text:
For decades, Americans have debated what it would take to strengthen domestic manufacturing and bring critical supply chains closer to home. Today, that conversation has become more urgent. Today, that conversation has become more urgent as Washington has renewed its focus on rebuilding American manufacturing, strengthening domestic supply chains, and encouraging private-sector investment.

The disruptions of recent years — from global supply chain bottlenecks to geopolitical uncertainty — have underscored the importance of producing more of what the nation needs within our own borders. Policymakers in Washington have renewed their focus on expanding domestic manufacturing, strengthening supply chain resilience, reforming permitting, and ensuring the United States remains globally competitive. Companies across sectors are responding by reevaluating where they invest and build.

The question is no longer whether the United States should strengthen its industrial base. The question is where that growth can happen.

From our respective vantage points in business and economic development, we believe Louisiana offers an important case study for states seeking to strengthen American manufacturing.

Earlier this year, Air Liquide announced a significant new investment in Louisiana, further expanding the company's presence in a state where it has operated for over six decades. This $350 million investment will support more efficient industrial processes with a lower CO2 footprint. And while every project is unique, this investment reflects a broader reality: companies are increasingly choosing Louisiana because it offers the conditions needed to compete in a global economy and build the economy for future generations.

Those conditions are not unique to one company or one project. They offer broader lessons about what it takes to attract long-term industrial investment in today’s competitive global economy.

Manufacturing growth depends on more than ambition. It requires infrastructure, access to energy, a skilled workforce, favorable policies, and an environment where major projects can be developed efficiently and operate reliably for decades. Louisiana offers that combination at a scale few places can match.

The state's strategic position along the Gulf Coast has long made it one of America's most important industrial corridors. An extensive network of ports, pipelines, transportation assets, and energy infrastructure supports industries ranging from chemicals and refining to advanced manufacturing and logistics.

For companies making long-term capital investments, these advantages are not theoretical. They translate into lower costs, greater reliability, and faster timelines. Access to affordable and dependable energy remains one of the most important factors in site selection decisions, and Louisiana continues to distinguish itself in that regard.

Just as importantly, the state understands that infrastructure alone is not enough.

Louisiana's economic success is increasingly driven by its people. Major industrial investments create direct jobs, but their impact extends much further. Construction workers, suppliers, contractors, small businesses, and local communities all benefit when new projects move forward. These investments create opportunities for career growth, workforce development, and long-term economic stability, while the development of cleaner and more advanced industrial processes delivers lasting benefits for society as a whole.

Recent years have demonstrated the strength of this approach. Louisiana has attracted billions of dollars in new investment and secured projects across a range of sectors that are shaping the future of American industry. Those announcements represent more than economic activity – they reflect confidence in Louisiana's ability to compete globally.

That confidence is especially important as the United States works to strengthen its industrial resilience.

While reshoring is often discussed in terms of jobs, its strategic impact extends far beyond employment. Revitalizing domestic manufacturing capacity means ensuring that the materials, products, and industrial capabilities critical to our economy can be produced here at home. It also means reducing vulnerabilities in global supply chains and strengthening America's long-term competitive edge.

Louisiana plays a central role in that effort. The state supports the production of essential industrial inputs that underpin manufacturing across the country, its infrastructure enables companies to scale operations efficiently while serving domestic markets, and its continued success demonstrates how states can position themselves to compete for next-generation manufacturing investment.

Perhaps most importantly, Louisiana demonstrates what is possible when government and industry work together toward a shared goal. Businesses need predictability when making investments that will operate for decades and communities need confidence that economic development will create lasting opportunities. Effective public-private partnerships help deliver both.

Louisiana's collaborative approach to economic development has helped create an environment where major projects can move from concept to reality. By aligning infrastructure, workforce development, and economic strategy, the state has positioned itself as a place where industrial growth can succeed.

As national leaders work to expand domestic manufacturing, accelerate permitting, strengthen supply chains, and attract private investment, Louisiana offers an example worth studying.

If the United States is serious about reshoring critical industries, enhancing supply chain resilience, and creating durable economic opportunity, it must invest in places that are already demonstrating how those goals can be achieved.

The lessons extend beyond Louisiana. States that invest in competitive infrastructure, cultivate skilled workforces, provide reliable energy, and foster strong public-private partnerships will be best positioned to attract the next generation of manufacturing investment.

Louisiana's experience shows that rebuilding American manufacturing is not simply about policy in Washington. It also depends on creating the right conditions for investment in communities across the country.

The state's success is not only a local story. It’s also a story about American competitiveness, resilience, and a bright industrial future. The investments being made today will help determine whether the next generation of manufacturing growth occurs in the United States.

As the United States seeks to usher in a new era of American manufacturing, Louisiana offers a practical blueprint for turning national priorities into tangible investment, new jobs, and long-term industrial growth.

Susan Bonnett Bourgeois is the Secretary of Louisiana Economic Development.

Matthieu Giard is the CEO of Air Liquide Americas.

text:
Charged readers know Vingroup as the parent company of automaker Vinfast. Another of the Vietnamese conglomerate’s units is Green SM, which offers an electric car booking service and electric car and motorbike rental. The company currently operates some 20,000 cars and 60,000 motorbikes in Vietnam, Laos, Indonesia, the Philippines, India and Kazakhstan.

Now the company has announced its most far-flung international expansion: an electric taxi service in Copenhagen. Green SM chose the Danish capital as its first European market because it is “one of the world’s leading cities in sustainable urban mobility.”

In Denmark, the company operates a fleet of VinFast VF 6 and VF 8 EVs. Unlike many ride-hailing platforms, which primarily connect passengers with independent drivers, Green SM directly owns and manages its fleet and oversees driver operations to ensure consistent service quality. Before hitting the streets, every driver completes comprehensive training in road safety, customer service and EV operation.

text:
For months, Louisiana residents have watched as major decisions about economic development and the state’s energy future have taken place largely out of public view. They have involved the use of non-disclosure agreements and backdoor proceedings among state and local leaders, Entergy and Meta to create a $50 billion artificial intelligence data center in Richland Parish.

NDAs have become a standard tool in the state’s approach to major industrial projects, including Meta’s data center in Richland Parish, the Amazon data center in Northwest Louisiana and the Hyundai steel mill near Donaldsonville.

These agreements limit what elected officials can share with their constituents. Though not technically illegal, the use of NDAs in public projects sets a dangerous precedent for transparency and accountability in dealings with corporations and government. By withholding information, corporations can fast-track projects and unpopular initiatives to avoid public scrutiny.

The dispute over transparency came to a head recently when an administrative judge ordered Meta to produce records supporting its projections for investment, permanent job creation and electricity demand — key information needed to evaluate whether Entergy’s proposal is truly in the public interest.

Meta has challenged that order, placing it before the Louisiana Public Service Commission, which is scheduled to discuss the matter at its meeting Wednesday. The panel of five elected utility regulators will determine whether the public gains access to critical information about the project’s costs, jobs and electricity needs.

Their vote will not decide the fate of the Richland Parish data center, which will be determined in December when the Public Service Commission will consider whether Entergy can build seven new power plants for the massive Meta campus. But it will set an important precedent about whether transparency will be the rule or the exception in this process.

The stakes for this project could not be higher. Meta originally announced its Hyperion AI data center as a $10 billion project, but has now doubled its planned size, pushing the cost to as much as $50 billion.

If completed, the facility would consume a staggering 7.5 gigawatts of electricity, more than seven times the electricity consumed by the entire city of New Orleans.

Consumer and environmental advocacy groups — including the Alliance for Affordable Energy, the Union of Concerned Scientists and the Sierra Club — have raised serious concerns about the financial risks to Entergy Louisiana’s ratepayers. Documents the company submitted to the Public Service Commission estimate its average household customer’s bill could increase up to $40 per month once the new power plants are built.

Louisianans must pay attention to decisions that will affect their energy costs, environmental health and economic future for decades to come. The Public Service Commission belongs to the people it serves, and the public has a right to be heard when billions of dollars and the welfare of communities are at stake.

text:
Minnesota and Wisconsin's gubernatorial primaries on Tuesday feature two candidates situated at the far end of their parties' ideological spectrums. Former MyPillow CEO and 2020 conspiracy promoter Mike Lindell is running for the Republican nomination in Minnesota and Democratic socialist Francesca Hong is seeking the Democratic nomination in Wisconsin.

Both would face off against more conventional candidates in November's mid-terms and create electability questions for their respective parties.

The race is expected to test the progressive energy that has recently propelled left-wing Democrats to the top of their tickets, while also indicating whether the endorsement of U.S. President Donald Trump still holds the sway over Republicans it has in previous elections.

Minnesota Republicans weigh Trump's endorsement of Lindell

Seven Minnesota Republicans are vying to face off against likely Democratic gubernatorial nominee Senator Amy Klobuchar in November. Seven Democrats are also running, with Klobuchar receiving the state's Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party nomination in May.

Lindell is among the most visible of those Republicans, an enduring Trump ally and proponent of the baseless idea that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. Speaker of the Minnesota House of Representatives Lisa Demuth and businessman Kendall Qualls are also top hopefuls.

This year could be a tough one for the Minnesota GOP, with one of its top contenders, lawyer Chris Madel, dropping out of the race in January, in the aftermath of "Operation Metro Surge," the immigration deportation campaign in Minneapolis that led to the deaths of two American citizen protesters earlier that month.

"I cannot support the national Republican's stated retribution on the citizens of our state nor can I count myself a member of a party that would do so," Madel said in a video posted on X. "The national Republicans have made it nearly impossible for a Republican to win a statewide election in Minnesota."

But Lindell told Reuters in an interview that he could win over Democratic voters. "I believe I'm the only candidate that can win. I not only have the name, but I can raise the most money and I can do the best marketing," said Lindell, who stepped down as CEO of MyPillow in early August to devote himself full-time to his campaign.

Lindell received Trump's endorsement in May, when the president wrote on Truth Social, “Mike will be SPECTACULAR!!! He truly loves Minnesota, as do I, and wants to bring it back from oblivion and embarrassment. He can do it!”

In Wisconsin, democratic socialist faces off against party favorite

In Wisconsin's Democratic primary, Francesca Hong is looking to become the first democratic socialist governor of the state, and some polls show her leadingGovernor Tony Evers' pick, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley.

Hong recently drew criticismfor the reappearance of old tweets, including a November 2020 post, at the height of a COVID-19 wave in Wisconsin, in which she wrote, "Please DON'T gather for the colonizer holiday," and another when she said, "Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621."

In recent interviews, Hong has walked back those statements, saying that as a chef, she had fond memories of the Thanksgiving holiday, but that Thanksgiving was a time that is painful for many people. In another interview she said that she did not want to cancel Thanksgiving.

Hong did not respond to a request for an interview.

Hong's left-leaning policy goals, including abolishing the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, a one-year moratorium on data centers and increased taxation of billionaires and corporations, may be growing in popularity among Democratic voters.

A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll shows Democratic voters ​want their party's candidates to track further to the left. More than seven in 10 liberal Democrats say it’s “essential” for their party’s candidates to support increasing taxes on corporations and billionaires (76%), expanding access to abortion (72%) and universal government-provided health care (71%).

But unlike Abdul El-Sayed, another left-winger who captured the Michigan Senate primary earlier this month, Hong is running without the endorsements of progressive heavyweights, independent Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, New York Democrat.

Dems Minnesota Senate matchup

Among the aspirants for Minnesota's Democratic Senate nomination are left-leaning Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan, who was elected on a ticket with Governor Tim Walz in 2018, and Representative Angie Craig, who took office in 2019 and is seen as a more moderate candidate who sometimes votes with Republicans.

The candidates are seeking the seat left open by Democratic Senator Tina Smith, who announced her retirement in February 2025.

Craig was the only Minnesota Democrat to vote for the Laken Riley Act, which gave ICE broader authority to detain immigrants charged with some crimes. She later wrote in a March op-ed for the Minnesota Star Tribune that she regretted her vote.

Flanagan has said ICE is out of control and must be dismantled.

title: Why Contract Enforcement Drives Energy Investment in Africa
description:
Evidence from the African Development Bank’s Electricity Regulatory Index shows that countries with similar regulatory designs can deliver very different results.
Energy transition: Clean energy projects typically have long tenors, which make those projects highly sensitive to “enforcement risk,” rendering it a primary driver of bankability.
In countries with predictable enforcement, investors accept lower returns and longer tenors.
